20  Readable Regular Expressions with rebus

title: 20  Readable Regular Expressions with rebus
text:
20.3 Metacharacters

20.3.1 Character classes
To match any one of a group of characters, we put them in a class with the function char_class(). Bill numbers are often written with different separators. Let us find the separators in a few bill numbers.

bill_nos <- c("BL/2024/001", "BL-2024-002", "BL.2024.003", "BL 2024 004")
# matches a slash, a dot, a space or a hyphen. A hyphen goes last, or it would mean a range
str_view(bill_nos, char_class("/. -"))

[1] │ BL</>2024</>001
[2] │ BL<->2024<->002
[3] │ BL<.>2024<.>003
[4] │ BL< >2024< >004


To match a range of characters or numbers, we separate the two ends with a hyphen inside the class. So, char_class("A-D") matches any one of A, B, C or D. Suppose cheque books of series A to D were issued to an office, and the cheque numbers start with the series letter.

cheques <- c("A 500301", "b 500302", "E 500303", "D 500304")
# Match a series letter from A to D, in upper case
str_view(cheques, char_class("A-D"), match = NA)

[1] │ <A> 500301
[2] │ b 500302
[3] │ E 500303
[4] │ <D> 500304

# The same, irrespective of case
str_view(cheques, case_insensitive(char_class("A-D")), match = NA)

[1] │ <A> 500301
[2] │ <b> 500302
[3] │ E 500303
[4] │ <D> 500304


The first pattern misses b, because it is in lower case. The cheque of series E matches neither, so it is not from the books issued to the office.
For negated character classes, there is an equally clear function, negated_char_class(). It matches any character not in the class. Amounts typed into a spreadsheet often carry extra characters. Let us find every character which is not a digit.

amounts_text <- c("25000", "25,000", "Rs 25000", "25000/-")
# Match everything except digits
str_view(amounts_text, negated_char_class("0-9"), match = NA)

[1] │ 25000
[2] │ 25<,>000
[3] │ <R><s>< >25000
[4] │ 25000</><->


These are the characters to remove before the amounts can be converted to numbers.

20.3.2 Built-in character classes
We can also use the ready-made character classes of rebus, listed below.

ALPHA

<regex> [:alpha:]

ALNUM

<regex> [:alnum:]

BLANK

<regex> [:blank:]

DIGIT

<regex> [:digit:]

LOWER

<regex> [:lower:]

PRINT

<regex> [:print:]

PUNCT

<regex> [:punct:]

SPACE

<regex> [:space:]

UPPER

<regex> [:upper:]

HEX_DIGIT

<regex> [:xdigit:]

ANY_CHAR

<regex> .

GRAPHEME

<regex> \X

NEWLINE

<regex> \R

DGT

<regex> \d

WRD

<regex> \w

SPC

<regex> \s

NOT_DGT

<regex> \D

NOT_WRD

<regex> \W

NOT_SPC  # Equivalent to "\\S"

<regex> \S

ASCII_DIGIT

<regex> 0-9

ASCII_LOWER

<regex> a-z

ASCII_UPPER

<regex> A-Z

ASCII_ALPHA

<regex> a-zA-Z

ASCII_ALNUM

<regex> a-zA-Z0-9


Let us use two of them on our narration.

# Match TAB or SPACE characters
str_view(narration, BLANK)

[1] │ Paid< >to< >M/s< >Gupta< >Traders< >against< >Bill< >No.< >45< >dated< >12.04.2024.

# Match all UPPER CASE characters
str_view(narration, UPPER)

[1] │ <P>aid to <M>/s <G>upta <T>raders against <B>ill <N>o. 45 dated 12.04.2024.


Besides these constants, there are lower case functions for the same character classes. They are more useful for building patterns, because they also take a repetition.
alnum(lo, hi, char_class = TRUE)
alpha(lo, hi, char_class = TRUE)
blank(lo, hi, char_class = TRUE)
cntrl(lo, hi, char_class = TRUE)
digit(lo, hi, char_class = TRUE)
graph(lo, hi, char_class = TRUE)
lower(lo, hi, char_class = TRUE)
printable(lo, hi, char_class = TRUE)
punct(lo, hi, char_class = TRUE)
space(lo, hi, char_class = TRUE)
upper(lo, hi, char_class = TRUE)
hex_digit(lo, hi, char_class = TRUE)
any_char(lo, hi)
grapheme(lo, hi)
newline(lo, hi)
dgt(lo, hi, char_class = FALSE)
wrd(lo, hi, char_class = FALSE)
spc(lo, hi, char_class = FALSE)
not_dgt(lo, hi, char_class = FALSE)
not_wrd(lo, hi, char_class = FALSE)
not_spc(lo, hi, char_class = FALSE)
ascii_digit(lo, hi, char_class = TRUE)
ascii_lower(lo, hi, char_class = TRUE)
ascii_upper(lo, hi, char_class = TRUE)
ascii_alpha(lo, hi, char_class = TRUE)
ascii_alnum(lo, hi, char_class = TRUE)
char_range(lo, hi, char_class = lo < hi)
number_range(lo, hi, allow_leading_zeroes = FALSE, capture = FALSE)
In these functions, lo and hi take positive whole numbers. They give the smallest and largest number of repetitions. The argument char_class takes TRUE or FALSE. Let us try them on the address line of a vendor.

address <- "Shop 12, Station Road, Kota  PIN 324001"
# one to three digits at a time
str_view(address, digit(1, 3))

[1] │ Shop <12>, Station Road, Kota  PIN <324><001>

# exactly six digits, the PIN code
str_view(address, digit(6))

[1] │ Shop 12, Station Road, Kota  PIN <324001>

# five characters which are not digits
str_view(address, not_dgt(5))

[1] │ <Shop >12<, Sta><tion ><Road,>< Kota><  PIN> 324001

# two spaces together
str_view(address, space(2), match = NA)

[1] │ Shop 12, Station Road, Kota<  >PIN 324001


The last pattern finds the double space before PIN. Such stray spaces are a common reason why two copies of the same address fail to match.

20.3.3 Word boundaries
To match a word boundary, or its negation, we have BOUNDARY and NOT_BOUNDARY in rebus. The function whole_word(x), on the other hand, wraps the pattern in boundaries, so that it matches only a whole word.
Suppose we want to find the vouchers paid in cash, from their narrations.

narrations <- c("Paid in cash to the contractor", "Cashier advance for petty expenses",
                "Encashment of leave", "Cash withdrawn for wages")
# Note the match inside "Encashment"
str_view(narrations, "cash", match = NA)

[1] │ Paid in <cash> to the contractor
[2] │ Cashier advance for petty expenses
[3] │ En<cash>ment of leave
[4] │ Cash withdrawn for wages

# Only the whole word, in lower case
str_view(narrations, whole_word("cash"), match = NA)

[1] │ Paid in <cash> to the contractor
[2] │ Cashier advance for petty expenses
[3] │ Encashment of leave
[4] │ Cash withdrawn for wages

str_view(narrations, case_insensitive(whole_word("cash")), match = NA)

[1] │ Paid in <cash> to the contractor
[2] │ Cashier advance for petty expenses
[3] │ Encashment of leave
[4] │ <Cash> withdrawn for wages

# Words that begin with "cash", in any case
str_view(narrations, BOUNDARY %R% case_insensitive("cash"), match = NA)

[1] │ Paid in <cash> to the contractor
[2] │ <Cash>ier advance for petty expenses
[3] │ Encashment of leave
[4] │ <Cash> withdrawn for wages

# "cash" inside a word
str_view(narrations, NOT_BOUNDARY %R% "cash", match = NA)

[1] │ Paid in cash to the contractor
[2] │ Cashier advance for petty expenses
[3] │ En<cash>ment of leave
[4] │ Cash withdrawn for wages


The plain pattern "cash" picks up Encashment of leave, which is not a cash payment at all. case_insensitive(whole_word("cash")) finds exactly the two cash payments.

title: 20  Readable Regular Expressions with rebus
text:
20.4 Quantifiers
We learnt the following quantifiers in regular expressions.


+ 1 or more occurrences

* 0 or more


? 0 or 1


{} specified numbers


{n} exactly n

{n,} n or more

{n,m} between n and m



rebus has a clearly named function for each of them.

one_or_more(x, char_class = NA)
zero_or_more(x, char_class = NA)
optional(x, char_class = NA)

repeated(x, lo, hi, lazy = FALSE, char_class = NA)

where lo and hi stand for n and m.



Each of them has an argument char_class = NA. It takes TRUE when x should be wrapped in a character class.
Round amounts are a well known sign of estimates or made-up figures. We may find amounts ending in three or more zeros with repeated("0", 3, Inf) %R% END. We may also pull out the quantities of material from bill descriptions.

amounts_text <- c("125000", "48750", "200000", "3500")
# three or more zeros at the end
str_view(amounts_text, repeated("0", 3, Inf) %R% END, match = NA)

[1] │ 125<000>
[2] │ 48750
[3] │ 2<00000>
[4] │ 3500

items <- c("10 bags cement", "5bags sand", "25 tins paint")
# a number followed by "bags", with an optional space
str_view(items, one_or_more(DIGIT) %R% optional(BLANK) %R% "bags", match = NA)

[1] │ <10 bags> cement
[2] │ <5bags> sand
[3] │ 25 tins paint

20  Readable Regular Expressions with rebus

title: 20  Readable Regular Expressions with rebus
text:
20.5 Anchors
Anchors match a position in the string, not a character. In rebus, the constants START and END match the beginning and the end of the string.

narrations2 <- c("Paid to Gupta Traders", "Advance paid to Gupta Traders")
str_view(narrations2, START %R% case_insensitive("paid"), match = NA)

[1] │ <Paid> to Gupta Traders
[2] │ Advance paid to Gupta Traders


Only the first narration matches. In the second, paid is not at the start. There is one more function, exactly(x), which makes the pattern match the whole string, from start to end. It is a shortcut for START %R% x %R% END.

modes <- c("Cash", "Cheque", "Cash/Cheque", "Petty Cash", "RTGS")
str_view(modes, exactly("Cash"), match = NA)

[1] │ <Cash>
[2] │ Cheque
[3] │ Cash/Cheque
[4] │ Petty Cash
[5] │ RTGS


Only the value which is exactly Cash matches. This is how we must check codes and identifiers. A pattern without anchors would also pass Cash/Cheque and Petty Cash.

title: 20  Readable Regular Expressions with rebus
text:
20.6 Capture groups
We have seen that a capture group keeps a part of the match as a separate piece. This is useful when we want to extract or replace a specific part of a string. In regular expressions, capture groups are written in parentheses (). We also learnt that a captured piece can be referred back to with a back reference. \1 refers to the match in the first pair of parentheses, \2 in the second, and so on.
In rebus, there are two functions for this, capture(x) and group(x). capture() makes a capturing group, (x), whose match can be referred back to. group() makes a non-capturing group, (?:x), which only keeps its contents together, as we need with alternations. It does not remember its match.
Let us remove the separators from our bill numbers, and pull out the mode of payment from a narration.

## capture(x)
str_remove_all(bill_nos, capture(char_class("/. -")))

[1] "BL2024001" "BL2024002" "BL2024003" "BL2024004"

## group()
pay_modes <- group("cheque" %|% "RTGS" %|% "NEFT")
narration3 <- "Part payment by cheque, balance by RTGS after deduction of TDS."
str_extract_all(narration3, pattern = pay_modes)

[[1]]
[1] "cheque" "RTGS"  


Back references for replacement are written with the constants REF1 to REF9. We can also use them inside the pattern. Account and mobile numbers with the same digit repeated four times in a row are often dummy entries. Let us find them.

account_nos <- c("30114567892", "99999012345", "20188880123", "50100234567")
# a digit, followed by the same digit three more times
str_view(account_nos, capture(DGT) %R% REF1 %R% REF1 %R% REF1, match = NA)

[1] │ 30114567892
[2] │ <9999>9012345
[3] │ 201<8888>0123
[4] │ 50100234567


As in Chapter 19, we can use capture groups to rearrange a value. Let us turn names written as last name, first name into first name last name.

# We have names in last_name, first_name format
staff_names <- c("Sharma, Ramesh", "Verma, Sunita", "Iyer, Lakshmi")
# Pattern to capture the last name and the first name
pat <- capture(whole_word(one_or_more(ALPHA))) %R% "," %R% optional(SPACE) %R%
  capture(whole_word(one_or_more(ALPHA)))
repl <- REF2 %R% " " %R% REF1
# Using this regex, we can convert these to first_name last_name format
str_replace_all(staff_names, pat, repl)

[1] "Ramesh Sharma" "Sunita Verma"  "Lakshmi Iyer"

title: 20  Readable Regular Expressions with rebus
text:
20.7 Lookarounds
As we learnt, lookaheads and lookbehinds are zero-width assertions. They match a pattern only if it is followed or preceded by another pattern. The pattern inside the lookahead or lookbehind is not part of the match.
rebus has clearly named functions for all four lookarounds.
lookahead(x)
negative_lookahead(x)
lookbehind(x)
negative_lookbehind(x)
Let us find invoice numbers where INV is not followed by a hyphen.

invoices <- c("INV-101", "INV102", "INV")
# With lookahead
str_view(invoices, "INV" %R% negative_lookahead("-"), match = NA)

[1] │ INV-101
[2] │ <INV>102
[3] │ <INV>

# Without lookahead. Notice the difference
str_view(invoices, "INV" %R% negated_char_class("-"), match = NA)

[1] │ INV-101
[2] │ <INV1>02
[3] │ INV


The negative lookahead finds both INV102 and the bare INV. The negated class needs one more character after INV, so it misses the bare INV. It also takes that character into the match.
Now let us use all four lookarounds on the remarks column of an advance register. Advances which are not adjusted are a regular audit point.

remarks <- c("advance adjusted", "advance not adjusted", "advance")

# Lookahead
str_view(remarks, "advance" %R% lookahead(optional(SPACE) %R% "adjusted"), match = NA)

[1] │ <advance> adjusted
[2] │ advance not adjusted
[3] │ advance

# Note that "adjusted" is not included in the match

# Lookbehind
str_view(remarks, lookbehind("advance" %R% optional(SPACE)) %R% "adjusted", match = NA)

[1] │ advance <adjusted>
[2] │ advance not adjusted
[3] │ advance

# Negative lookahead
str_view(remarks, "advance" %R% negative_lookahead(optional(SPACE) %R% "adjusted"), match = NA)

[1] │ advance adjusted
[2] │ <advance> not adjusted
[3] │ <advance>

# Negative lookbehind
str_view(remarks, negative_lookbehind("advance" %R% optional(SPACE)) %R% "adjusted", match = NA)

[1] │ advance adjusted
[2] │ advance not <adjusted>
[3] │ advance


The negative lookahead picks out exactly the two advances that are not shown as adjusted.
A lookahead is also handy for pulling out numbers that belong to a particular word.

supply <- "Supplied 10 bags cement, 6 bags sand and 5 tins paint"

# lookahead to match the number of bags
bags_pattern <- one_or_more(DIGIT) %R% lookahead(optional(SPACE) %R% "bags")
str_view(string = supply, pattern = bags_pattern, match = NA)

[1] │ Supplied <10> bags cement, <6> bags sand and 5 tins paint

text:
20.8 Ready patterns for dates and times
rebus has ready patterns for the parts of dates and times, and for whole dates and times.

# Individual date-time components
DTSEP             # optional selected punctuation or space

<regex> [-/.:,\ ]?

CENTURY           # exactly two digits

<regex> [0-9]{2}

YEAR              # one to four digits

<regex> [0-9]{1,4}

YEAR2             # exactly two digits

<regex> [0-9]{2}

YEAR4             # exactly four digits

<regex> [0-9]{4}

MONTH             # number from 1 to 12, leading zero

<regex> (?:0[1-9]|1[0-2])

WEEK_OF_YEAR      # number from 0 to 53, leading zero

<regex> (?:[0-4][0-9]|5[0-3])

DAY               # number from 1 to 31, leading zero

<regex> (?:0[1-9]|[12][0-9]|3[01])

DAY_SINGLE        # leading space

<regex> (?: [1-9]|[12][0-9]|3[01])

HOUR24            # 24 hour clock, leading zero

<regex> (?:[01][0-9]|2[0-3])

HOUR12            # 12 hour clock, leading zero

<regex> (?:0[1-9]|1[0-2])

HOUR24_SINGLE     # 24 hour clock, leading space

<regex> (?:[ 1][0-9]|2[0-3])

HOUR12_SINGLE     # 12 hour clock, leading space

<regex> (?: [1-9]|1[0-2])

MINUTE            # number from 0 to 59, leading zero

<regex> [0-5][0-9]

SECOND            # number from 0 to 61 (leap seconds), leading zero

<regex> (?:[0-5][0-9]|6[01])

FRACTIONAL_SECOND # a second optional decimal point and up to 6 digits

<regex> (?:[0-5][0-9]|6[01])(?:[.,][0-9]{1,6})?

AM_PM             # AM or PM, any case

<regex> (?:am|AM|pm|PM)

TIMEZONE_OFFSET   # optional plus or minus, then four digits

# ISO 8601 formats
ISO_DATE          # %Y-%m-%d

<regex> [0-9]{4}-(?:0[1-9]|1[0-2])-(?:0[1-9]|[12][0-9]|3[01])

ISO_TIME          # %H:%M:%S

<regex> (?:[01][0-9]|2[0-3]):[0-5][0-9]:(?:[0-5][0-9]|6[01])

ISO_DATETIME      # ISO_DATE followed by ISO_TIME, separated by space or "T".

<regex> [0-9]{4}-(?:0[1-9]|1[0-2])-(?:0[1-9]|[12][0-9]|3[01])(?:[ T](?:[01][0-9]|2[0-3]):[0-5][0-9]:(?:[0-5][0-9]|6[01]))?

# Compound forms, separated by DTSEP
YMD

<regex> [0-9]{1,4}[-/.:,\ ]?(?:0[1-9]|1[0-2])[-/.:,\ ]?(?:0[1-9]|[12][0-9]|3[01])

YDM

<regex> [0-9]{1,4}[-/.:,\ ]?(?:0[1-9]|[12][0-9]|3[01])[-/.:,\ ]?(?:0[1-9]|1[0-2])

MYD

<regex> (?:0[1-9]|1[0-2])[-/.:,\ ]?[0-9]{1,4}[-/.:,\ ]?(?:0[1-9]|[12][0-9]|3[01])

MDY

<regex> (?:0[1-9]|1[0-2])[-/.:,\ ]?(?:0[1-9]|[12][0-9]|3[01])[-/.:,\ ]?[0-9]{1,4}

DYM

<regex> (?:0[1-9]|[12][0-9]|3[01])[-/.:,\ ]?[0-9]{1,4}[-/.:,\ ]?(?:0[1-9]|1[0-2])

DMY

<regex> (?:0[1-9]|[12][0-9]|3[01])[-/.:,\ ]?(?:0[1-9]|1[0-2])[-/.:,\ ]?[0-9]{1,4}

HMS

<regex> (?:[01][0-9]|2[0-3])[-/.:,\ ]?[0-5][0-9][-/.:,\ ]?(?:[0-5][0-9]|6[01])

HM

<regex> (?:[01][0-9]|2[0-3])[-/.:,\ ]?[0-5][0-9]

MS

<regex> [0-5][0-9][-/.:,\ ]?(?:[0-5][0-9]|6[01])


Let us check some dates and times exported from a system in ISO format.

# Some dates, valid and invalid
some_dates <- c("2000-13-01", "2025-08-09","2000-01-32", "2000-00-01", "2000-01-00", "2020-05-20")

str_view(some_dates, ISO_DATE)

[2] │ <2025-08-09>
[6] │ <2020-05-20>

# Similarly some time formats
some_times <- c("24:00:00", "23:60:59", "23:59:62", "23 59 59", "23:55:55", "00:00:00")
str_view(some_times, ISO_TIME)

[5] │ <23:55:55>
[6] │ <00:00:00>


Only the dates with a possible month and day match. Among the times, only 23:55:55 and 00:00:00 match. In 24:00:00, 23:60:59 and 23:59:62, the hour, the minute or the second is out of range. And 23 59 59 uses spaces in place of colons.

section: 20.10 Audit use case, readable validation patterns
text:
20.10 Audit use case, readable validation patterns
In Section 19.10 we wrote patterns for Indian identifiers. Written with rebus, they can be read almost like the official description of the format. Let us build three of them, and print the regular expressions they produce.

# PAN. Five letters, four digits, one letter
pan_rx  <- exactly(ascii_upper(5) %R% ascii_digit(4) %R% ascii_upper(1))

# IFSC. Four letters for the bank, a zero, six letters or digits for the branch
ifsc_rx <- exactly(ascii_upper(4) %R% "0" %R% repeated(char_class("A-Z0-9"), 6))

# GSTIN. State code, PAN, entity number, Z, check character
gstin_rx <- exactly(ascii_digit(2) %R%
                    ascii_upper(5) %R% ascii_digit(4) %R% ascii_upper(1) %R%
                    char_class("1-9A-Z") %R% "Z" %R% char_class("0-9A-Z"))

pan_rx

<regex> ^[A-Z]{5}[0-9]{4}[A-Z]$

ifsc_rx

<regex> ^[A-Z]{4}0[A-Z0-9]{6}$

gstin_rx

<regex> ^[0-9]{2}[A-Z]{5}[0-9]{4}[A-Z][1-9A-Z]Z[0-9A-Z]$


These are exactly the patterns we wrote by hand in the previous chapter. Notice that for the IFSC we used char_class("A-Z0-9") and not ascii_alnum(), because ascii_alnum() would also allow lower case letters. Printing the pattern is how we catch such differences.

str_detect(c("ABCPK1234D", "ABCP1234D"), pan_rx)

[1]  TRUE FALSE

str_detect(c("SBIN0001234", "SBIN1001234"), ifsc_rx)

[1]  TRUE FALSE

str_detect(c("27AAPFU0939F1ZV", "27AAPFU0939F1Z"), gstin_rx)

[1]  TRUE FALSE


A pattern only checks the format. The check character of a GSTIN still needs the function gstin_valid() of Section 19.11.

20.10.1 Checking a vendor master
Let us now run the patterns over a small vendor master. A few errors have been planted in it.

Code to create the vendor mastervendor_master <- tibble::tibble(
  vendor_id = sprintf("V%03d", 1:8),
  vendor    = c("Gupta Traders", "Shree Balaji Enterprises", "Narmada Builders",
                "Om Sai Caterers", "Kaveri Suppliers", "Laxmi Hardware",
                "Rajdhani Travels", "Yamuna Cleaning Services"),
  pan       = c("AAKPG4521K", "ABJPS7788Q", "AAFFN1203M", "AGSPO6634",
                "aakfk3390d", "AALPL5521H", "AACFR9087B", "AAAPY1122C"),
  ifsc      = c("SBIN0004521", "PUNB0112200", "CNRBO001234", "UBIN0556789",
                "BARB0KOTAXX", "SBIN0007788", "HDFC0001234", "SBIN1003344")
)



library(dplyr)
conflicts_prefer(dplyr::filter)

vendor_master |>
  mutate(pan_ok  = str_detect(pan, pan_rx),
         ifsc_ok = str_detect(ifsc, ifsc_rx)) |>
  filter(!pan_ok | !ifsc_ok)

# A tibble: 4 × 6
  vendor_id vendor                   pan        ifsc        pan_ok ifsc_ok
  <chr>     <chr>                    <chr>      <chr>       <lgl>  <lgl>  
1 V003      Narmada Builders         AAFFN1203M CNRBO001234 TRUE   FALSE  
2 V004      Om Sai Caterers          AGSPO6634  UBIN0556789 FALSE  TRUE   
3 V005      Kaveri Suppliers         aakfk3390d BARB0KOTAXX FALSE  TRUE   
4 V008      Yamuna Cleaning Services AAAPY1122C SBIN1003344 TRUE   FALSE  


4 of the 8 vendors fail. Om Sai Caterers has a PAN with only nine characters. Kaveri Suppliers has a PAN in lower case. That one is probably correct, only untidily typed. Converting to upper case with str_to_upper() before the check, as advised in Section 19.10, would pass it. Narmada Builders has the letter O in place of the zero in its IFSC. Yamuna Cleaning Services has 1 where the zero should be.
The auditor’s next step is to ask the office for the PAN cards and cancelled cheques of these vendors. The office must also explain how payments were made to bank accounts with an invalid IFSC. Did they fail, or were they paid to some other account?

20.10.2 Dates in vouchers
Dates in Indian records are usually written day first, like 15/04/2024. The rebus constant DMY matches such dates. Let us check a few dates typed in a voucher register.

library(lubridate)

voucher_dates <- c("15/04/2024", "31/02/2024", "29/02/2023", "29/02/2024",
                   "4/7/2024", "2024/07/04", "31-12-2024")

tibble::tibble(date_text   = voucher_dates,
               shape_ok    = str_detect(voucher_dates, exactly(DMY)),
               parsed_date = dmy(voucher_dates, quiet = TRUE))

# A tibble: 7 × 3
  date_text  shape_ok parsed_date
  <chr>      <lgl>    <date>     
1 15/04/2024 TRUE     2024-04-15 
2 31/02/2024 TRUE     NA         
3 29/02/2023 TRUE     NA         
4 29/02/2024 TRUE     2024-02-29 
5 4/7/2024   FALSE    2024-07-04 
6 2024/07/04 FALSE    NA         
7 31-12-2024 TRUE     2024-12-31 


The regex checks only the shape of a date. It accepts 31/02/2024 and 29/02/2023, because 31 is a possible day and 02 a possible month. But there is no 31st of February, and 2023 was not a leap year. The function dmy() from lubridate, which we met in Chapter 16, knows the calendar. It returns NA for both. On the other hand, dmy() reads 4/7/2024 correctly, which the DMY pattern rejects for lack of leading zeros.






TipAudit tip



Use regex to find dates written in the wrong format, and a date parser like dmy() to find dates that do not exist. A voucher dated 31 February, or a bill dated after the date of its payment, is worth a closer look. Impossible dates are sometimes typing errors. Sometimes they are a sign that the document was prepared later, in a hurry.

title: 20  Readable Regular Expressions with rebus
text:
20.11 A suggested workflow


Write down the official format. Start from the rule that defines the identifier, such as PAN, IFSC or GSTIN, in plain words. For a PAN, it is five letters, then four digits, then one letter.

Build the pattern piece by piece. Join the parts with %R%, using ascii_upper(), ascii_digit(), char_class() and repeated(). Keep alternatives together with or().

Anchor the whole value. Wrap the pattern in exactly(). Otherwise a longer or shorter value may pass just because a part of it matches.

Print the pattern. Print the rebus object to see the regular expression it builds. Check that it means what you intended, for example that lower case letters are not allowed by mistake.

Test on known values. Try the pattern with str_detect() on a few valid and invalid samples before running it on the whole beneficiary or vendor list.

List the failures. Run the pattern over the column received from the auditee and pick out the records that fail. Each one is a data quality issue to be explained.

Check dates twice. Use DMY to find dates written in the wrong format, and dmy() to find dates that do not exist, like 31 February. Look closely at impossible dates in vouchers and bills.







ImportantRemember



A pattern checks only the shape of a value, not whether it is true. A date like 31/02/2024 passes DMY, and a GSTIN in the right format may have a wrong check character. Use dmy() for dates and gstin_valid() for GSTINs, and confirm doubtful cases from the records.

title: Part IV: Exploring and Sampling
text:
Once the data is in shape, look at it before testing it. Chart it, summarise it, and understand its spread and its oddities. A good chart often shows the finding before any test does.
This part covers charts in base R and in ggplot2, factors for categorical data, and descriptive statistics with a profile of a whole ledger. It then turns to probability and to audit sampling, including monetary unit sampling. It ends with the statistical tests that tell whether a difference between offices is real or chance.


21  Charts in Base R
Quick charts for a first look at the data.


22  Charts with ggplot2
The grammar of graphics, aesthetics and geoms, and a first look at the March rush.


23  Polishing Charts for Audit Reports
Scales, facets, labels and themes, for charts fit for an audit report.


24  Factors
Categorical data, kept in a sensible order.


25  Descriptive Statistics
Summarising data, and profiling a payment ledger.


26  Probability Distributions
The distributions behind audit sampling and testing.


27  Random Sampling
Random, systematic, stratified and monetary unit sampling.


28  Statistical Tests for Auditors
Deciding whether a difference is real or chance.

title: 21  Charts in Base R
text:
21.1 Our data, a bill register and a scheme
Suppose a Public Works Division gives us its bill register for the year. It has three thousand bills. Officers of the division may approve a bill up to ₹1 lakh. Anything above needs sanction from a higher authority. We want to know whether some bills were kept just below that limit on purpose. We also want to know whether spending rushed up in March, and whether one office pays much larger bills than the others.
A table of three thousand rows will not answer these questions. Totals and averages will not answer them either. A chart will. A histogram of the bill amounts shows a pile of bills just under ₹1 lakh at a glance. A line chart of monthly spending shows the March rush. A box plot puts the offices side by side. This is why we look at the data before we summarise it.
Charts also help us tell others what we found. A well drawn chart in an audit report says more than a table of numbers. It also helps us spot errors and odd values in the data.
In this chapter we learn the charts that come with base R, without any extra package. We will use plot(), barplot(), hist(), boxplot() and density plots, and arrange several charts on one page with par(). All the examples use audit data. At the end we use a histogram to find bills split to stay below the limit.
We will use two small datasets in this chapter.
The first, bills, is the bill register of a Public Works Division for the financial year 2024-25. The division has five sub-divisional offices. Each bill has a number, a date, the office, the head of expenditure and the amount in rupees. We have planted two irregularities in it. Our charts should bring both out.
The second, blocks, gives the number of beneficiaries and the expenditure of a state scheme in 40 blocks of a district. The scheme pays about ₹6,000 a year to each beneficiary. So the expenditure of a block should rise in step with its beneficiaries. One block does not follow this rule.
Code to create the bill register and the block dataset.seed(77)
offices <- c("Nandgaon", "Sonpur", "Bhimtal", "Kesarganj", "Rajnagar")
heads   <- c("Repairs", "Supplies", "Electricity", "Travel", "Office expenses")
fy_days <- seq(as.Date("2024-04-01"), as.Date("2025-03-31"), by = "day")

# Planted. Days in March are three times as likely to get a bill (a March rush)
day_wt <- ifelse(format(fy_days, "%m") == "03", 3, 1)

n <- 3000
bills <- data.frame(
  office    = sample(offices, n, TRUE),
  head      = sample(heads, n, TRUE, prob = c(3, 3, 2, 1, 2)),
  bill_date = sample(fy_days, n, TRUE, prob = day_wt),
  amount    = round(rlnorm(n, log(30000), 0.9))
)

# Planted. 60 repair bills of Kesarganj kept just below the limit of Rs 1 lakh
split_bills <- data.frame(
  office    = "Kesarganj",
  head      = "Repairs",
  bill_date = sample(fy_days, 60, TRUE),
  amount    = round(runif(60, 94000, 99999))
)

bills <- rbind(bills, split_bills)
bills <- bills[order(bills$bill_date), ]
rownames(bills) <- NULL
bills$bill_no <- sprintf("BL/24-25/%04d", seq_len(nrow(bills)))
fy_months <- month.abb[c(4:12, 1:3)]
bills$month <- factor(month.abb[as.integer(format(bills$bill_date, "%m"))],
                      levels = fy_months)
bills$quarter <- paste0("Q", (as.integer(bills$month) - 1) %/% 3 + 1)
bills <- bills[, c("bill_no", "bill_date", "month", "quarter", "office", "head", "amount")]

# Scheme data of 40 blocks, at about Rs 6,000 per beneficiary
blocks <- data.frame(
  block         = sprintf("Block %02d", 1:40),
  beneficiaries = round(runif(40, 800, 5000))
)
blocks$expenditure_lakh <- round(blocks$beneficiaries * 6000 * runif(40, 0.92, 1.08) / 1e5, 1)
# Planted. Block 27 spends far more than its beneficiaries justify
blocks$expenditure_lakh[27] <- round(blocks$expenditure_lakh[27] * 1.7, 1)
Let us look at the first few rows of each.
head(bills)

        bill_no  bill_date month quarter    office            head amount
1 BL/24-25/0001 2024-04-01   Apr      Q1    Sonpur     Electricity  85801
2 BL/24-25/0002 2024-04-01   Apr      Q1    Sonpur        Supplies  21666
3 BL/24-25/0003 2024-04-01   Apr      Q1 Kesarganj         Repairs  32067
4 BL/24-25/0004 2024-04-01   Apr      Q1    Sonpur Office expenses  98347
5 BL/24-25/0005 2024-04-01   Apr      Q1    Sonpur        Supplies  25745
6 BL/24-25/0006 2024-04-02   Apr      Q1  Rajnagar          Travel  27177

head(blocks)

     block beneficiaries expenditure_lakh
1 Block 01          4798            288.2
2 Block 02          3440            192.6
3 Block 03          2628            169.2
4 Block 04          1233             76.9
5 Block 05          3879            228.7
6 Block 06          1547             90.7
The register has 3,060 bills worth ₹14.3 crore in all.

title: 21  Charts in Base R
text:
21.2 Using plot()

The plot() function is very versatile. Its main use is to draw scatter plots. It can also draw line charts, box plots and other charts, depending on the data we give it. Its basic syntax is:
plot(x, y, ...)
The x and y arguments are the values for the x-axis and the y-axis. The ... can hold many optional arguments that change how the chart looks. The most common are listed here.


xlab is the label of the x-axis.

ylab is the label of the y-axis.

main is the main title of the chart.

xlim and ylim set the limits of the x-axis and the y-axis.

type is the type of chart. "p" draws points, "l" draws lines and "b" draws both.

col is the colour of the points or lines.

pch is the symbol used for the points.

cex is the size of the points and text.







Note



Here x and y are vectors, such as blocks$beneficiaries. In Chapter 22 we will give column names instead. The examples below make this clear.



21.2.1 A scatter plot
Let us plot the expenditure of each block against its number of beneficiaries.

plot(blocks$beneficiaries,
     blocks$expenditure_lakh,
     xlab = "Number of beneficiaries",
     ylab = "Expenditure (Rs lakh)",
     main = "Expenditure and beneficiaries of 40 blocks",
     pch = 19)






Figure 21.1: Expenditure of each block against its beneficiaries




The points lie close to a straight line, as they should. One point sits well above the line. It is Block 27. It spent ₹9,858 per beneficiary, against a median of ₹6,086 for all blocks.
We can mark that point in red with points(), and name it with text(). Both add to a chart that is already drawn.

plot(blocks$beneficiaries, blocks$expenditure_lakh,
     xlab = "Number of beneficiaries", ylab = "Expenditure (Rs lakh)",
     pch = 19, col = "grey50")
points(blocks$beneficiaries[odd], blocks$expenditure_lakh[odd],
       pch = 19, col = "red", cex = 1.5)
text(blocks$beneficiaries[odd], blocks$expenditure_lakh[odd],
     labels = blocks$block[odd], pos = 2)






Figure 21.2: The odd block marked in red




A scatter plot shows that two columns move together. It cannot prove that one causes the other. Here, though, the rule of the scheme tells us they should move together. So a point far from the line is a lead to follow up.

21.2.2 A line chart
Let us total the bills of each month with tapply(), in lakh. Then we draw the totals as a line.

monthly <- tapply(bills$amount, bills$month, sum) / 1e5
round(monthly, 1)

  Apr   May   Jun   Jul   Aug   Sep   Oct   Nov   Dec   Jan   Feb   Mar 
 96.3 102.4  98.0  93.1 102.7  97.4 108.4 111.4 127.5 113.2  77.7 302.3 

plot(1:12, monthly,
     type = "b",
     xlab = "Month of the financial year (1 = April)",
     ylab = "Amount (Rs lakh)",
     main = "Monthly total of bills, 2024-25")






Figure 21.3: Monthly total of bills




Here type = "b" draws both points and lines. With type = "l" we would get lines only. The total for March is ₹302.3 lakh. That is about 3 times the median of the other months. This is the March rush we planted.

21.2.3 A bar chart of counts
table() counts the bills under each head. barplot() draws the counts as bars.

barplot(table(bills$head),
        xlab = "Head of expenditure",
        ylab = "Number of bills",
        main = "Bills by head of expenditure")






Figure 21.4: Number of bills under each head





21.2.4 A box plot
When x is a factor and y is numeric, plot() draws one box plot for each level of the factor. Let us compare the bill amounts under each head.

plot(x = factor(bills$head),
     y = bills$amount,
     log = "y",
     main = "Bill amounts by head",
     xlab = "Head of expenditure",
     ylab = "Amount (Rs, log scale)",
     col = "darkgray")






Figure 21.5: Bill amounts under each head, on a log scale




Bill amounts are skewed. Most bills are small and a few are very large. On an ordinary scale the boxes would be squashed at the bottom. So we used log = "y". On a log scale, each step up the axis multiplies the amount, rather than adding to it. The boxes now have room to show their spread.

21.2.5 A density plot
A density plot is a smooth version of a histogram. We make it with density(), and draw it with plot().

plot(density(bills$amount / 1000),
     main = "Density of bill amounts",
     xlab = "Amount (Rs thousand)", ylab = "Density", col = "blue")






Figure 21.6: Density of bill amounts




The curve rises sharply near zero and has a long tail to the right. That is the usual shape of amounts in accounts.
Let us now learn the other chart functions of base R.

title: 21  Charts in Base R
text:
21.3 Bar plots using barplot()

As the name suggests, barplot() draws bar charts. Its basic syntax is barplot(height, ...). Here height is a vector giving the height of each bar. The other arguments can be seen with ?barplot.

21.3.1 A basic bar chart
We already have the monthly totals in monthly. The argument names.arg gives the label under each bar.

barplot(monthly,
        names.arg = levels(bills$month),
        main = "Monthly total of bills, 2024-25",
        xlab = "Month", ylab = "Amount (Rs lakh)",
        las = 2)






Figure 21.7: Monthly totals as bars




The argument las = 2 turns the labels on the x-axis so that they all fit.

21.3.2 A bar chart of summarised data
Let us find the average bill of each office with tapply(), and draw the averages as horizontal bars.

office_mean <- tapply(bills$amount, bills$office, mean) / 1000
round(office_mean, 1)

  Bhimtal Kesarganj  Nandgaon  Rajnagar    Sonpur 
     47.5      48.4      45.0      46.1      46.7 

old_par <- par(mar = c(5, 7, 4, 2))   # wider left margin for the names
barplot(height = office_mean,
        main = "Average bill by office",
        xlab = "Average bill (Rs thousand)",
        col = "steelblue",
        horiz = TRUE,
        las = 1,
        cex.names = 0.8)
par(old_par)






Figure 21.8: Average bill of each office




horiz = TRUE draws the bars sideways. las = 1 keeps the office names upright, and cex.names = 0.8 makes them a little smaller. The office names need more room on the left than R leaves by default. So we widened the left margin with par(mar = ), and restored it afterwards. We learn more about par() later in this chapter.
The averages are close. Kesarganj is a little ahead, at ₹48.4 thousand. An average alone does not show why. We will find out at the end of this chapter.

21.3.3 A grouped bar chart
Next, let us total the bills by head and by quarter. When tapply() gets two grouping columns in a list(), it gives a matrix. Each row is a head and each column a quarter.

head_qtr <- tapply(bills$amount, list(bills$head, bills$quarter), sum) / 1e5
round(head_qtr, 1)

                  Q1   Q2   Q3    Q4
Electricity     47.1 51.9 62.6  73.1
Office expenses 58.1 49.6 64.2  93.0
Repairs         92.4 82.7 99.9 144.3
Supplies        74.6 81.3 89.7 142.9
Travel          24.5 27.6 30.8  39.9



barplot(height = head_qtr,
        main = "Spending by head and quarter",
        xlab = "Quarter", ylab = "Amount (Rs lakh)",
        col = c("red", "green", "blue", "yellow", "purple"),
        beside = TRUE,
        legend.text = rownames(head_qtr),
        args.legend = list(x = "topleft", cex = 0.8))






Figure 21.9: Spending under each head, quarter by quarter




barplot() draws one group of bars for each column of the matrix. Inside a group, it draws one bar, in its own colour, for each row. So we get a group for each quarter, with one bar per head. The legend names the rows. Every head rises in the fourth quarter, because of the March rush.

21.3.4 A stacked bar chart
The same matrix with beside = FALSE stacks the rows inside each column. Now each bar is a quarter, and each coloured piece is a head.

barplot(head_qtr,
        main = "Spending by quarter and head",
        xlab = "Quarter", ylab = "Amount (Rs lakh)",
        col = c("red", "green", "blue", "yellow", "purple"),
        legend.text = rownames(head_qtr),
        args.legend = list(x = "topleft", cex = 0.8),
        beside = FALSE)






Figure 21.10: Spending in each quarter, made up of the heads




A stacked bar shows the total of each quarter, and how the heads make it up. A grouped bar is better for comparing one head across quarters.

21.3.5 A bar chart from a formula
We can also give barplot() a formula and a data frame. aggregate() makes the data frame of totals. Then amount ~ office means “amount for each office”.

office_total <- aggregate(amount ~ office, data = bills, FUN = sum)
office_total$amount <- office_total$amount / 1e5
barplot(amount ~ office, data = office_total,
        ylab = "Amount (Rs lakh)")






Figure 21.11: Total of bills of each office

title: 21  Charts in Base R
text:
21.4 Histograms using hist()

The hist() function draws a histogram. A histogram shows how the values of a numeric column are spread. The basic syntax is:
hist(x, breaks = "Sturges", freq = TRUE, main = NULL,
     xlab = NULL, ylab = "Frequency", ...)
The arguments are these.


x is the numeric vector to be plotted.

breaks sets the bins. By default R chooses the number of bins by the Sturges formula. We can give a different number of bins, or a vector of break points.

freq chooses what the y-axis shows. If TRUE, it shows the number of values in each bin. If FALSE, it shows the density.

main is the title of the histogram.

xlab and ylab are the labels of the axes.

... holds more arguments for the chart, such as col, border and xlim.

Let us draw a histogram of the bill amounts, in thousands of rupees.

hist(bills$amount / 1000, breaks = 50, col = "lightblue",
     xlab = "Amount (Rs thousand)", ylab = "Number of bills",
     main = "Histogram of bill amounts")






Figure 21.12: Histogram of bill amounts




Most bills are below ₹50 thousand. A few run to several lakh. A long tail on the right like this is called right skew.
Skewed amounts are easier to see on a log scale. log10() turns ₹10,000 into 4, ₹1 lakh into 5 and ₹10 lakh into 6. Let us draw the histogram of log10(amount) as a density, with freq = FALSE. Then we add a density curve on top of it with lines().

hist(log10(bills$amount),
     freq = FALSE,
     breaks = 40,
     col = "grey85",
     xlab = "log10 of amount (4 = Rs 10,000, 5 = Rs 1 lakh)",
     main = "Histogram, with density curve")
# add density curve
lines(density(log10(bills$amount)), col = "blue", lwd = 2)






Figure 21.13: Histogram of log10 of bill amounts, with a density curve




lines() adds a layer to the chart already drawn. The bars and the curve now have a smooth, bell-like shape. Look carefully at the bar just to the left of 5, that is, just below ₹1 lakh. It stands a little above the curve, while its neighbour on the right falls below it. The sign is faint here, among three thousand bills. We will come back to it.

title: 21  Charts in Base R
text:
21.5 Box plots using boxplot()

A box plot is also called a box and whiskers plot. It shows the spread of a numeric column through a few summary values. Figure 21.14 shows how to read one.







Figure 21.14: Understanding boxplots




The syntax is boxplot(x, ...). Here x is a numeric vector, or a list of numeric vectors. The ... holds more arguments to change how the chart looks.

boxplot(bills$amount / 1000, ylab = "Amount (Rs thousand)")






Figure 21.15: Box plot of all bill amounts




The points above the top whisker are values far from the middle of the data. Here there are 197 of them. That is about 6% of all bills. With skewed amounts many bills fall beyond the whisker, and most of them are genuine large bills. So a point beyond the whisker is a candidate to look at, not an error.
Box plots are most useful when drawn side by side for several groups. We can give a formula, such as amount ~ office, as we did for barplot(). Let us compare the offices.

boxplot(amount ~ office,
        data = bills,
        log = "y",
        col = "lightgray",
        xlab = "Office", ylab = "Amount (Rs, log scale)")






Figure 21.16: Bill amounts of each office, on a log scale




The thick line in each box is the median. Kesarganj has the highest median bill, ₹34,160, against ₹28,663 to ₹31,274 for the other offices. The difference is not large. A box plot shows the overall spread well, but it can hide a narrow pile of values. We need the histogram for that.






WarningCaution



A log scale cannot show zero or negative values. With log = "y", R leaves such values out of some charts with a warning. Other charts, like boxplot(), stop with an error. Real registers often have zero amounts (cancelled bills) or negative ones (reversals). Count and examine them separately before drawing a chart on a log scale.

title: 21  Charts in Base R
text:
21.6 Saving and exporting charts
Charts can be saved from the RStudio menu or through code. Both ways are explained near the end of Chapter 23, including the graphics devices used for base R charts.

title: 21  Charts in Base R
text:
21.7 Use of par()

One useful function of base R graphics is par(). It sets or reads the graphical parameters. In the following example, its argument mfrow = c(nr, nc) draws the next charts in a grid of nr rows and nc columns on the same page.
Here we use a famous built-in dataset, Anscombe’s quartet. It has four small datasets, created by the statistician Francis Anscombe in 1973 to show why we must look at data. Let us first look at their summary statistics.

data.frame(set  = 1:4,
           mean_x = sapply(1:4, \(i) mean(anscombe[[paste0("x", i)]])),
           mean_y = sapply(1:4, \(i) round(mean(anscombe[[paste0("y", i)]]), 2)),
           cor_xy = sapply(1:4, \(i) round(cor(anscombe[[paste0("x", i)]],
                                              anscombe[[paste0("y", i)]]), 3)))

  set mean_x mean_y cor_xy
1   1      9    7.5  0.816
2   2      9    7.5  0.816
3   3      9    7.5  0.816
4   4      9    7.5  0.817


The four datasets have the same means and practically the same correlation. Now let us draw them.

old_par <- par(mfrow = c(2, 2))
purrr::walk(1:4,
     ~plot(anscombe[[paste0('x', .x)]],
           anscombe[[paste0('y', .x)]],
           xlab = paste0('x', .x),
           ylab = paste0('y', .x),
           main = paste("Anscombe's Quartet Chart No.", .x))
     )
par(old_par)   # restore the earlier settings






Figure 21.17: Anscombe’s quartet, four datasets with the same summary statistics




The pictures are completely different. Only the first is a normal straight line relationship. The second is a curve. The third is a straight line spoiled by one outlier. In the fourth, a single point creates the whole correlation. Summary statistics alone would never tell us this. This is the strongest argument for always looking at the data.
par() returns the old settings. We saved them in old_par and restored them at the end. Otherwise all later charts would also be drawn four to a page.
The same idea is handy in audit. We can draw a histogram, a box plot, a monthly line and a bar chart of a new register on one page, and take in the whole picture at once.

old_par <- par(mfrow = c(2, 2))
hist(log10(bills$amount), breaks = 40, main = "Amounts (log10)", xlab = NULL)
boxplot(amount ~ quarter, data = bills, log = "y", main = "By quarter",
        xlab = NULL, ylab = NULL)
plot(1:12, monthly, type = "b", main = "Monthly total (Rs lakh)",
     xlab = "Month (1 = April)", ylab = NULL)
barplot(table(bills$office), main = "Bills by office", las = 2, cex.names = 0.7)
par(old_par)






Figure 21.18: A first look at the bill register, four charts on one page

title: 21  Charts in Base R
section: 21.8 Audit use case, payments just below a limit
text:
21.8 Audit use case, payments just below a limit
Officers of our division may approve a bill up to ₹1 lakh. Anything above needs a higher authority, or a tender. A common irregularity is to split a larger purchase into several bills, each just below the limit. A histogram of bill amounts can show this at a glance. Let us draw the bills between ₹50,000 and ₹1.5 lakh, in bins of ₹2,500.

near_limit <- bills$amount[bills$amount >= 50000 & bills$amount <= 150000]
hist(near_limit,
     breaks = seq(50000, 150000, by = 2500),
     col = "grey80", border = "white",
     xlab = "Amount of bill (Rs)", main = NULL)
abline(v = 100000, col = "red", lwd = 2)






Figure 21.19: Bills between Rs 50,000 and Rs 1.5 lakh, with the approval limit marked in red




The number of bills falls steadily as amounts rise, as expected. The exception is a sharp spike just below ₹1 lakh, and a drop just after it. The bins of ₹2,500 just under the limit hold far more bills than their neighbours. Such a spike is a strong lead for splitting of purchases.
The next step is to see whose bills these are. Let us take the bills from ₹95,000 up to the limit and count them by office and head.

just_below <- bills[bills$amount >= 95000 & bills$amount < 100000, ]
table(just_below$office, just_below$head)

           
            Electricity Office expenses Repairs Supplies Travel
  Bhimtal             2               2       2        0      0
  Kesarganj           1               3      54        3      0
  Nandgaon            1               0       0        2      0
  Rajnagar            1               0       0        2      1
  Sonpur              3               1       2        1      0


Of the 81 bills in this narrow range, 54 are repair bills of Kesarganj. The other offices have only a few each, spread over the heads. Let us draw them as bars to show the point in a report.

barplot(sort(table(just_below$office), decreasing = TRUE),
        col = c("firebrick", rep("grey70", 4)),
        ylab = "Number of bills", main = "Bills just below Rs 1 lakh")






Figure 21.20: Bills of Rs 95,000 up to the limit, by office




The auditor would now list the 54 repair bills of Kesarganj, sorted by date. Bills for the same work, to the same contractor, on nearby dates point to one job split into many. Ask the office for the estimates and the work orders. Then check who approved each bill and whether the combined value needed higher sanction. Put the chart, the list and the replies in the working papers. We test this pattern more formally in Chapter 31.






TipAudit tip



Choose the bins carefully. Too wide a bin hides the spike. Here we used bins of ₹2,500 and limited the chart to the range around the limit. Use abline() to mark the limit, so that the reader sees the point at once.








WarningCaution



By default, hist() counts a value that falls exactly on a break in the bin to its left. So a bill of exactly ₹1 lakh is counted in the bin just below the limit. Keep this in mind when the rule says “up to ₹1 lakh”, and check the bills exactly at the limit separately.

title: 21  Charts in Base R
text:
21.9 A suggested workflow


Look before you summarise. Draw a quick chart of any new data, like a bill register, before you work out totals. Anscombe’s quartet showed that summary statistics alone can hide very different patterns.

Check the spread of amounts with hist(). A histogram of amounts shows skew, outliers and unusual spikes. Try a few values of breaks, since bins that are too wide hide the pattern. Use log10() for skewed amounts.

Mark the limits with abline(). Draw the financial limit, say ₹1 lakh, on the chart. A spike just below the line is a lead for split purchases.

Compare groups with boxplot(). Use a formula like amount ~ office to compare the spread across offices or heads. Points beyond the whiskers are candidates to look at, not errors.

Count and total categories with barplot(). Count bills with table(), or total them with tapply(), and draw them as bars. Use beside = TRUE to compare groups side by side, or stacked bars to show the make-up of each total.

See trends with a line chart. Plot the monthly totals with type = "b". A rush in March stands out at once.

See relationships with plot(). A scatter plot of two columns shows whether they move together. Mark the odd points with points() and text(). It shows association, not cause.

Put related charts together with par(). Use par(mfrow = ) to see several charts on one page. Restore the old settings afterwards.

Follow up the leads. Take the bills in the unusual bin or group, and examine them by office, date and supporting documents.







ImportantRemember



A chart is the quickest way to see what the numbers hide. Look at the data before trusting any summary. But a spike or an outlier on a chart is only a lead. Confirm it from the original records before reporting.

title: 22  Charts with ggplot2
text:
22.1 Core concepts of grammar of graphics
An auditor often receives data with thousands of rows. Think of the bill register of a State scheme run in twelve districts, for a whole financial year. Somewhere in it, a district may have rushed its spending into March to avoid a lapse of funds. Another may have split its purchases into bills just below the limit of its financial powers. A third may have spent more than its budget. Each of these is hard to see in a table. Each is plain to see in a good chart.
Charts help the auditor twice. First, while analysing, a chart shows patterns, outliers and gaps that a summary table hides. Second, while reporting, a clear chart tells the reader in a few seconds what a paragraph of numbers cannot.
In Chapter 21 we drew charts with base R. In this chapter we learn ggplot2, the most widely used charting package in R. We will build every chart on a simulated bill register of a scheme, with a few irregularities planted in it. Step by step, we will learn
On the way, the charts will point us to the planted cases. At the end, an audit use case puts a number on one of them. In Chapter 23 we then learn to make these charts fit for an audit report, with scales, coordinate systems, facets, labels, themes and saving.
ggplot212 was developed by Hadley Wickham. It is based on the ideas of Leland Wilkinson in his book The Grammar of Graphics (2005).3 The grammar of graphics is a framework that describes a chart as a set of layers. Each layer does one job, and the layers together make the chart. Even the letters gg in ggplot2 stand for grammar of graphics.
Hadley Wickham explained his idea of a layered grammar in a paper titled A Layered Grammar of Graphics4 (2010).5 In the same paper, he put forward ggplot2 as an open source way of building such charts. Readers who want the theory in detail may read the paper. Over the next decade, the package grew6 into one of the most used packages in R.
Figure 22.17 shows how the parts of the two grammars relate. The parts on the left were put forward by Wilkinson. Those on the right were proposed by Wickham. TRANS has no match in ggplot2, because R itself does that job.
Figure 22.1: Layers in Grammar of Graphics mapped in GGPLOT2
So, to build a chart from data, we use seven main components.
Of these, the first three (data, aesthetics and geometries) must be given by us. The others are not less important. It is just that they have sensible defaults. For example, the default coordinate system is Cartesian. Let us start with the three essential components and build a chart with them.

title: 22  Charts with ggplot2
text:
Data. Every chart starts with data. It is also the first argument of the most important function in the package, ggplot(data = ).

Aesthetics. The function aes() gives a mapping from the columns of the data to the parts of the chart. For example, one column may go on the x axis, another on the y axis, and a third may decide the colour.

Geometries. The geom_*() functions, or geoms, decide the shape the data takes on the chart. They decide, for example, whether each row is drawn as a point, a bar or a line.

Statistics. A stat computes something from the data before drawing it, such as a count, a mean or a trend line.

Scales. A scale controls how values become positions, colours or sizes. For example, an axis may be shown on a logarithmic scale, or amounts may be shown in lakh.

Coordinate system. Most charts use the usual Cartesian system of x and y. A pie chart uses a polar system, and a map uses a map projection.

Facets. A facet splits one chart into small panels, one for each group in the data.

title: 22  Charts with ggplot2
section: 22.2 Our data, a bill register of a scheme
text:
22.2 Our data, a bill register of a scheme
We need data first. Let us create the bill register of an imaginary State scheme for the financial year 2024-25. The scheme runs in 12 districts, grouped into four divisions. Each bill belongs to one of four categories, which are Works, Supplies, Services and Vehicle hire. The West division hires no vehicles, as it has its own.
The rules of our scheme are simple. A district officer may pass a bill of up to ₹2 lakh. A bill above ₹2 lakh needs the sanction of a higher authority. Bills are normally paid after a few days of checking.
We have planted four irregularities in the data. We will not list them here. The charts in this chapter and in Chapter 23 will bring them out one by one. The code that creates the data is folded below. You may expand it once you are comfortable with dplyr.

library(tidyverse)


Code to create the bill register, the monthly expenditure and the budgetset.seed(2025)

district_list <- tibble(
  district = c("Amarpur", "Belapur", "Chandpur", "Devgarh", "Fatehpur", "Gopalganj",
               "Haripur", "Kishanpur", "Lalganj", "Madhopur", "Narsinghpur", "Rampur"),
  division = rep(c("North", "South", "East", "West"), each = 3),
  size     = round(runif(12, 0.6, 1.5), 2)   # bigger districts have more bills
)
fy_months <- seq(as.Date("2024-04-01"), by = "month", length.out = 12)
categories <- tibble(
  category = c("Works", "Supplies", "Services", "Vehicle hire"),
  lambda   = c(3, 4, 3, 2),                       # bills per month in a district
  median   = c(300000, 110000, 70000, 35000)      # typical bill amount
)
vendors <- list(
  "Works"        = c("Narmada Builders", "Shakti Constructions", "Jai Hind Infra",
                     "Pawan Contractors"),
  "Supplies"     = c("Bharat Stationers", "Kaveri Suppliers", "Om Sai Traders",
                     "Patel Hardware"),
  "Services"     = c("National Printers", "Rajdhani Computers", "Sagar Caterers"),
  "Vehicle hire" = c("Shree Ganesh Transport", "Annapurna Travels")
)

# Number of bills for each district, month and category
cells <- expand_grid(district_list, month_start = fy_months, categories) |>
  # Planted case 1. March rush in Fatehpur and Rampur
  mutate(rush   = district %in% c("Fatehpur", "Rampur") &
                  month_start == as.Date("2025-03-01"),
         lambda = if_else(division == "West" & category == "Vehicle hire", 0, lambda),
         n      = rpois(n(), lambda * size * if_else(rush, 2, 1)))

bills <- cells |>
  uncount(n) |>
  mutate(
    bill_date   = month_start + sample(0:27, n(), replace = TRUE),
    amount      = round(rlnorm(n(), log(median), 0.55) * if_else(rush, 2.5, 1), -1),
    vendor      = map_chr(category, \(k) sample(vendors[[k]], 1)),
    days_to_pay = 3 + rnbinom(n(), mu = 15, size = 3)
  )

# Planted case 2. Supplies split into bills just below Rs 2 lakh in Devgarh
split_bills <- tibble(
  district = "Devgarh", division = "South", category = "Supplies",
  vendor = "Shubham Enterprises",
  bill_date = as.Date("2024-06-03") + sort(sample(0:270, 28)),
  amount = round(runif(28, 190000, 199900), -1),
  days_to_pay = 3 + rnbinom(28, mu = 15, size = 3)
)

# Planted case 3. Large works bills paid within a day in Lalganj
fast_bills <- tibble(
  district = "Lalganj", division = "East", category = "Works",
  vendor = "Vikas Constructions",
  bill_date = as.Date("2024-08-05") + sort(sample(0:200, 6)),
  amount = round(runif(6, 650000, 900000), -1),
  days_to_pay = c(0, 1, 0, 1, 1, 0)
)

bills <- bind_rows(bills, split_bills, fast_bills) |>
  mutate(month_start = floor_date(bill_date, "month"),
         month   = factor(format(month_start, "%b"), levels = format(fy_months, "%b")),
         quarter = (as.integer(month) - 1) %/% 3 + 1) |>
  arrange(bill_date) |>
  mutate(bill_no = sprintf("B-%04d", row_number())) |>
  select(bill_no, district, division, category, vendor, bill_date, month_start,
         month, quarter, amount, days_to_pay)

# Monthly expenditure statement, built from the bills
spend <- bills |>
  summarise(vouchers = n(), exp = sum(amount),
            .by = c(district, division, month_start, month, category)) |>
  arrange(district, month, category)

# Budget estimate of each district for the year
budget <- spend |>
  summarise(amt_exp = sum(exp), .by = district) |>
  mutate(util = runif(12, 0.6, 0.98),
         # Planted case 4. Devgarh and Lalganj spent more than their budget
         util = replace(util, district %in% c("Devgarh", "Lalganj"), c(1.18, 1.27)),
         amt_be = round(amt_exp / util, -5)) |>
  select(district, amt_be)

# Small helpers for amounts in prose
lakh  <- function(x) round(x / 1e5, 1)
crore <- function(x) round(x / 1e7, 2)
