title: 32  Duplicate Detection
text:
32.1 Prerequisites
Duplicate detection is one of the oldest and most useful checks in audit. It is simple to understand. It is also simple to run. Yet it often gives the quickest results in a fraud or forensic audit.
A duplicate payment means money has gone out twice for the same thing. Sometimes it is an honest mistake. Sometimes it is not. In either case, it is a loss to the organisation, and the auditor must find it.
Duplicates may point to many kinds of problems. A few common ones are:
In this chapter we will learn how to find such duplicates in R. We will start with the simplest case, where two records are exactly the same. We will then move to cases where records are almost the same. These are harder to find, and they are usually the more interesting ones for an auditor.
We will use three packages in this chapter. tidyverse gives us dplyr and stringr. janitor gives us a very handy function get_dupes(). stringdist will help us find names which are similar but not identical. Later in the chapter, we will also use fullmetaphone to find names which sound alike. Its installation is explained in Chapter 33.
library(tidyverse)
library(janitor)
library(stringdist)

title: 32  Duplicate Detection
text:
32.2 Our sample data
To learn the tests, we need some data where we already know the answers. So let us create a small payment register of an imaginary office for the financial year 2024-25. It has about 170 payments made to 14 vendors. We have deliberately planted a few duplicates in it. Our job in this chapter is to find all of them using R.
The code to create the data is given below. New readers need not worry about this code right now. You may expand it later, once you are comfortable with dplyr.

Code to create the sample payment registerset.seed(2025)

# Vendor master
vendors <- tibble(
  vendor_id   = sprintf("V%03d", 1:14),
  vendor_name = c("Sharma Traders", "Gupta Enterprises", "Bharat Stationers",
                  "Kaveri Suppliers", "Laxmi Electricals", "National Printers",
                  "Om Sai Caterers", "Patel Hardware", "Rajdhani Computers",
                  "Shree Ganesh Transport", "Ashok Estates", "Verma & Sons",
                  "Sharma Trader's", "Guptha Enterprises")
)

# 150 ordinary payments
n <- 150
payments <- tibble(
  vendor_id    = sample(vendors$vendor_id[c(1:10, 12)], n, replace = TRUE),
  invoice_no   = paste0("INV-", sample(1000:9999, n)),
  invoice_date = as.Date("2024-04-01") + sample(0:330, n, replace = TRUE),
  amount       = round(runif(n, 2000, 200000))
)

# Monthly office rent. Same amount every month, but genuine.
rent <- tibble(
  vendor_id    = "V011",
  invoice_no   = paste0("AE/RENT/", 1:12),
  invoice_date = seq(as.Date("2024-04-01"), by = "month", length.out = 12),
  amount       = 45000
)

# Planted case 1. Invoices paid twice (one of them thrice).
paid_again <- payments[c(12, 47, 47, 101), ]

# Planted case 2. Same invoice keyed in again with a slightly different number.
retyped <- payments[c(23, 88), ] |>
  mutate(invoice_no = c(str_remove(invoice_no[1], "-"),
                        str_to_lower(invoice_no[2])))

# Planted case 3. Same bill raised again with a suffix "A", two days later.
suffixed <- payments[64, ] |>
  mutate(invoice_no   = paste0(invoice_no, "A"),
         invoice_date = invoice_date + 2)

# Planted case 4. Same invoice paid to a look-alike vendor.
lookalike <- payments |>
  filter(vendor_id %in% c("V001", "V002")) |>
  slice(c(2, 5)) |>
  mutate(vendor_id = if_else(vendor_id == "V001", "V013", "V014"))

payments <- bind_rows(payments, rent, paid_again, retyped, suffixed, lookalike) |>
  mutate(payment_date = invoice_date + sample(7:45, n(), replace = TRUE)) |>
  arrange(payment_date) |>
  mutate(voucher_no = sprintf("PV-%04d", row_number())) |>
  left_join(vendors, by = "vendor_id") |>
  select(voucher_no, payment_date, vendor_id, vendor_name,
         invoice_no, invoice_date, amount)

# Planted case 5. Two rows repeated in the data extract itself.
payments <- bind_rows(payments, payments[c(30, 90), ]) |>
  arrange(voucher_no)


Let us have a look at the first few rows.

head(payments)

# A tibble: 6 × 7
  voucher_no payment_date vendor_id vendor_name   invoice_no invoice_date amount
  <chr>      <date>       <chr>     <chr>         <chr>      <date>        <dbl>
1 PV-0001    2024-04-18   V011      Ashok Estates AE/RENT/1  2024-04-01    45000
2 PV-0002    2024-04-21   V005      Laxmi Electr… INV-6900   2024-04-01   169386
3 PV-0003    2024-05-02   V009      Rajdhani Com… INV-5628   2024-04-20   171411
4 PV-0004    2024-05-07   V008      Patel Hardwa… INV-4836   2024-04-27    43171
5 PV-0005    2024-05-11   V009      Rajdhani Com… INV-2321   2024-04-19    97584
6 PV-0006    2024-05-13   V004      Kaveri Suppl… INV-9114   2024-04-27     2354


Each row is one payment. The columns are:


voucher_no is the payment voucher number, given by the office.

payment_date is the date on which payment was made.

vendor_id and vendor_name tell us who was paid.

invoice_no and invoice_date come from the bill submitted by the vendor.

amount is the amount paid, in rupees.

title: 32  Duplicate Detection
section: 32.3 What do we mean by a duplicate?
text:
32.3 What do we mean by a duplicate?
This question looks simple. But it is the most important step of the whole exercise. Two records are “duplicates” only with respect to some columns, which we choose. These chosen columns are called the key.
Consider two payments to Sharma Traders. Both are for ₹ 25,000. Are they duplicates? We cannot say yet. If they also have the same invoice number, they almost certainly are. If the invoice numbers differ and the payments are a month apart, they are probably two genuine supplies.
So, before running any test, the auditor must decide the key. Forensic auditors commonly use the kinds of tests summarised in Table 32.1.


Table 32.1: Types of duplicate tests









Test
What matches
What differs
Typical finding



Exact duplicate
Every column
Nothing
Same row repeated in data, or keyed in twice


Same-Same-Same
All key columns, say vendor, invoice number and amount
Other columns like voucher number and date
Same invoice paid twice


Same-Same-Different
Two key columns, say vendor and amount
The third key column, say invoice number
Same bill re-submitted with a new or altered number


Fuzzy duplicate
Values are similar, not equal
Spelling, case, punctuation
Look-alike vendors, retyped invoice numbers






The names Same-Same-Same and Same-Same-Different are commonly used in forensic analytics literature. They are easy to remember. Three key columns are compared. The name tells us which of the three should match and which should not.

title: 32  Duplicate Detection
text:
32.4 Exact duplicates
Let us begin with the easiest case. Are there rows which are the same in every column?
Base R has a function duplicated(), which we met in Chapter 4. It returns TRUE for every row which has already appeared earlier in the data. So summing it up gives the number of extra copies.

sum(duplicated(payments))

[1] 2


There are two such rows. But duplicated() marks only the second copy as TRUE. The first copy is marked FALSE. An auditor usually wants to see both copies side by side. For this, get_dupes() from janitor is much more convenient. If we do not give it any column names, it uses all columns.

payments |>
  get_dupes()

# A tibble: 4 × 8
  voucher_no payment_date vendor_id vendor_name   invoice_no invoice_date amount
  <chr>      <date>       <chr>     <chr>         <chr>      <date>        <dbl>
1 PV-0030    2024-07-08   V007      Om Sai Cater… INV-2410   2024-06-07    41810
2 PV-0030    2024-07-08   V007      Om Sai Cater… INV-2410   2024-06-07    41810
3 PV-0090    2024-10-20   V001      Sharma Trade… INV-7755   2024-09-29   103923
4 PV-0090    2024-10-20   V001      Sharma Trade… INV-7755   2024-09-29   103923
# ℹ 1 more variable: dupe_count <int>


The output shows each duplicate row along with a new column dupe_count. This column tells us how many times that row appears.
Note that even the voucher numbers are the same here. A real office would never issue the same voucher number twice. So these are not two payments. These are the same payment appearing twice in our data. This usually happens when data is exported from a system, or when two files are merged carelessly.






TipAudit tip



Always check exact duplicates first, and before any other analysis. If the data itself has repeated rows, every total, average and count you calculate will be wrong. Ask the data owner why the rows are repeated. Do not just delete them silently. The answer may itself be an audit finding about the quality of the IT system.


Once we are satisfied with the reason, we may remove the repeated rows using dplyr::distinct(). It keeps only the first copy of each row.

payments <- payments |>
  distinct()

nrow(payments)

[1] 171

title: 32  Duplicate Detection
text:
32.5 Same-Same-Same test
Now let us look for the real problem. Has any invoice been paid more than once?
For this, our key will be three columns. These are vendor_id, invoice_no and amount. If all three match, the same bill has been paid again. Voucher numbers and payment dates will be different, of course, because these are two separate payments.
We just have to pass the key columns to get_dupes().

sss <- payments |>
  get_dupes(vendor_id, invoice_no, amount)

sss

# A tibble: 7 × 8
  vendor_id invoice_no amount dupe_count voucher_no payment_date vendor_name    
  <chr>     <chr>       <dbl>      <int> <chr>      <date>       <chr>          
1 V006      INV-3315    50572          3 PV-0069    2024-09-03   National Print…
2 V006      INV-3315    50572          3 PV-0071    2024-09-05   National Print…
3 V006      INV-3315    50572          3 PV-0079    2024-09-22   National Print…
4 V005      INV-2863   135555          2 PV-0087    2024-10-16   Laxmi Electric…
5 V005      INV-2863   135555          2 PV-0088    2024-10-19   Laxmi Electric…
6 V005      INV-4296   172125          2 PV-0032    2024-07-10   Laxmi Electric…
7 V005      INV-4296   172125          2 PV-0035    2024-07-15   Laxmi Electric…
# ℹ 1 more variable: invoice_date <date>


We see three invoices here. One invoice of National Printers has been paid three times. Two invoices of Laxmi Electricals have been paid twice each. Look at the payment_date column. In one case the second payment was made only two days after the first. In real life, such cases need a closer look at the approval process.

32.5.1 How much money is involved?
An audit observation is incomplete without the money value. In each group, one payment was correct and the rest were extra. So the excess payment is the amount multiplied by one less than the number of times it was paid.

sss |>
  summarise(
    times_paid = n(),
    amount = first(amount),
    excess_paid = (n() - 1) * first(amount),
    .by = c(vendor_id, invoice_no)
  )

# A tibble: 3 × 5
  vendor_id invoice_no times_paid amount excess_paid
  <chr>     <chr>           <int>  <dbl>       <dbl>
1 V006      INV-3315            3  50572      101144
2 V005      INV-2863            2 135555      135555
3 V005      INV-4296            2 172125      172125


We may add a further summarise() to get the grand total. That total is the figure which goes into the audit observation.

sss |>
  summarise(excess_paid = (n() - 1) * first(amount), .by = c(vendor_id, invoice_no)) |>
  summarise(total_excess = sum(excess_paid))

# A tibble: 1 × 1
  total_excess
         <dbl>
1       408824


So, in our small data, ₹ 4,08,824 has been paid in excess on just three invoices.






NoteChoosing the key wisely



Why did we not use invoice_date in the key? We could have. But dates are often entered differently by different clerks, so adding more columns to the key can make us miss duplicates. On the other hand, too few columns produce too many false alarms. Start with a small key. Then add columns if the output is too long to examine.

title: 32  Duplicate Detection
text:
32.6 Same-Same-Different test
A clever fraudster knows that most accounting software rejects an invoice number already entered for a vendor. So they change the invoice number a little. They may add a suffix, or change one digit. The Same-Same-Same test above will not catch this.
This is where the Same-Same-Different test helps. Here we look for records where the vendor and the amount are the same, but the invoice number is different.
In dplyr, we can do this with filter() and its .by argument, which we learnt in Chapter 13. Inside each group of vendor and amount, we keep the group only if it has more than one distinct invoice number. The function n_distinct() counts the distinct values.

ssd <- payments |>
  filter(n_distinct(invoice_no) > 1, .by = c(vendor_id, amount)) |>
  arrange(vendor_id, amount, invoice_date)

ssd |>
  select(voucher_no, vendor_name, invoice_no, invoice_date, amount)

# A tibble: 18 × 5
   voucher_no vendor_name        invoice_no invoice_date amount
   <chr>      <chr>              <chr>      <date>        <dbl>
 1 PV-0139    Gupta Enterprises  INV-9665   2025-01-10    29117
 2 PV-0155    Gupta Enterprises  INV9665    2025-01-10    29117
 3 PV-0160    Rajdhani Computers INV-8850   2025-02-15    93149
 4 PV-0171    Rajdhani Computers INV-8850A  2025-02-17    93149
 5 PV-0066    Rajdhani Computers inv-3601   2024-08-14   127872
 6 PV-0077    Rajdhani Computers INV-3601   2024-08-14   127872
 7 PV-0001    Ashok Estates      AE/RENT/1  2024-04-01    45000
 8 PV-0008    Ashok Estates      AE/RENT/2  2024-05-01    45000
 9 PV-0034    Ashok Estates      AE/RENT/3  2024-06-01    45000
10 PV-0047    Ashok Estates      AE/RENT/4  2024-07-01    45000
11 PV-0058    Ashok Estates      AE/RENT/5  2024-08-01    45000
12 PV-0078    Ashok Estates      AE/RENT/6  2024-09-01    45000
13 PV-0099    Ashok Estates      AE/RENT/7  2024-10-01    45000
14 PV-0116    Ashok Estates      AE/RENT/8  2024-11-01    45000
15 PV-0133    Ashok Estates      AE/RENT/9  2024-12-01    45000
16 PV-0152    Ashok Estates      AE/RENT/10 2025-01-01    45000
17 PV-0149    Ashok Estates      AE/RENT/11 2025-02-01    45000
18 PV-0169    Ashok Estates      AE/RENT/12 2025-03-01    45000


Let us read this output carefully, group by group.


Gupta Enterprises, ₹ 29,117. Invoice numbers are INV-9665 and INV9665. Only the hyphen is missing. This is clearly the same invoice entered again.

Rajdhani Computers, ₹ 93,149. Invoice numbers are INV-8850 and INV-8850A, dated two days apart. Adding a suffix like “A” is a classic way to get a bill paid twice. This needs to be examined with the original documents.

Rajdhani Computers, ₹ 1,27,872. Invoice numbers are inv-3601 and INV-3601. Only the case differs. Again the same invoice.

Ashok Estates, ₹ 45,000. Twelve invoices, one for each month. This is the monthly rent of the office building. It is not a duplicate. The same amount is genuinely paid every month.

So the test has found the real problems. But it has also raised one false alarm. This is normal. Every duplicate test produces some false alarms. The auditor’s job is to reduce them sensibly and then examine the rest.

32.6.1 Reducing false alarms with a date window
Rent, salary, annual maintenance charges and similar payments repeat by their very nature. But they repeat after a gap, usually a month or more. A bill re-submitted for double payment usually comes within a few days or weeks of the original.
So let us also calculate how many days have passed since the previous invoice of the same vendor and amount. The function lag() gives us the previous value within each group.

ssd <- ssd |>
  mutate(days_since_previous = as.numeric(invoice_date - lag(invoice_date)),
         .by = c(vendor_id, amount))

ssd |>
  select(vendor_name, invoice_no, invoice_date, amount, days_since_previous)

# A tibble: 18 × 5
   vendor_name        invoice_no invoice_date amount days_since_previous
   <chr>              <chr>      <date>        <dbl>               <dbl>
 1 Gupta Enterprises  INV-9665   2025-01-10    29117                  NA
 2 Gupta Enterprises  INV9665    2025-01-10    29117                   0
 3 Rajdhani Computers INV-8850   2025-02-15    93149                  NA
 4 Rajdhani Computers INV-8850A  2025-02-17    93149                   2
 5 Rajdhani Computers inv-3601   2024-08-14   127872                  NA
 6 Rajdhani Computers INV-3601   2024-08-14   127872                   0
 7 Ashok Estates      AE/RENT/1  2024-04-01    45000                  NA
 8 Ashok Estates      AE/RENT/2  2024-05-01    45000                  30
 9 Ashok Estates      AE/RENT/3  2024-06-01    45000                  31
10 Ashok Estates      AE/RENT/4  2024-07-01    45000                  30
11 Ashok Estates      AE/RENT/5  2024-08-01    45000                  31
12 Ashok Estates      AE/RENT/6  2024-09-01    45000                  31
13 Ashok Estates      AE/RENT/7  2024-10-01    45000                  30
14 Ashok Estates      AE/RENT/8  2024-11-01    45000                  31
15 Ashok Estates      AE/RENT/9  2024-12-01    45000                  30
16 Ashok Estates      AE/RENT/10 2025-01-01    45000                  31
17 Ashok Estates      AE/RENT/11 2025-02-01    45000                  31
18 Ashok Estates      AE/RENT/12 2025-03-01    45000                  28


For rent, the gap is around 30 days each time. For the suspicious groups, the gap is zero or two days. Now we keep only those groups where some invoice came within, say, 15 days of the previous one.

ssd |>
  filter(any(days_since_previous <= 15, na.rm = TRUE), .by = c(vendor_id, amount)) |>
  select(voucher_no, vendor_name, invoice_no, invoice_date, amount)

# A tibble: 6 × 5
  voucher_no vendor_name        invoice_no invoice_date amount
  <chr>      <chr>              <chr>      <date>        <dbl>
1 PV-0139    Gupta Enterprises  INV-9665   2025-01-10    29117
2 PV-0155    Gupta Enterprises  INV9665    2025-01-10    29117
3 PV-0160    Rajdhani Computers INV-8850   2025-02-15    93149
4 PV-0171    Rajdhani Computers INV-8850A  2025-02-17    93149
5 PV-0066    Rajdhani Computers inv-3601   2024-08-14   127872
6 PV-0077    Rajdhani Computers INV-3601   2024-08-14   127872


The rent payments are gone. Only the three suspicious groups remain.






WarningCaution



The window of 15 days is only an example. Choose it according to the business. A fortnightly payment would need a shorter window. A fraudster who knows about this test may also wait for a few weeks before re-submitting the bill. So treat the date window as a way to rank cases for examination, not as a final rule.



32.6.2 Other combinations
The Same-Same-Different idea works with any combination of columns. We only have to decide which two should match and which one should differ. For example, let us look for the same invoice number and amount, but paid to different vendors.

payments |>
  filter(n_distinct(vendor_id) > 1, .by = c(invoice_no, amount)) |>
  arrange(invoice_no) |>
  select(voucher_no, vendor_id, vendor_name, invoice_no, amount)

# A tibble: 4 × 5
  voucher_no vendor_id vendor_name        invoice_no amount
  <chr>      <chr>     <chr>              <chr>       <dbl>
1 PV-0111    V002      Gupta Enterprises  INV-8297    29819
2 PV-0121    V014      Guptha Enterprises INV-8297    29819
3 PV-0097    V013      Sharma Trader's    INV-8564    93897
4 PV-0100    V001      Sharma Traders     INV-8564    93897


This is an interesting result. An invoice of Sharma Traders has also been paid to Sharma Trader’s. An invoice of Gupta Enterprises has also been paid to Guptha Enterprises. These look-alike names have different vendor codes. This is a serious red flag. We will come back to it in Section 32.8.
A few other useful combinations are given in Table 32.2.


Table 32.2: Some other Same-Same-Different combinations









Same
Same
Different
What it may reveal

title: 32  Duplicate Detection
section: 32.7 Hidden duplicates, and why cleaning matters
text:
32.7 Hidden duplicates, and why cleaning matters
Look again at the groups found by the Same-Same-Different test. INV-9665 and INV9665 are the same invoice. So are inv-3601 and INV-3601. But the Same-Same-Same test missed them, because to a computer these strings are different.
This teaches us an important lesson. Clean the key columns before testing for duplicates. For invoice numbers, a simple cleaning would be to

convert everything to upper case, and
remove spaces, hyphens, slashes and other punctuation.

We learnt the required stringr functions in Chapter 18. The regular expression [^A-Z0-9] means “any character which is not a capital letter or a digit”. Removing all such characters leaves only letters and digits.

payments <- payments |>
  mutate(invoice_clean = invoice_no |>
           str_to_upper() |>
           str_remove_all("[^A-Z0-9]"))

payments |>
  get_dupes(vendor_id, invoice_clean, amount) |>
  select(vendor_id, invoice_no, invoice_clean, amount, dupe_count, voucher_no)

# A tibble: 11 × 6
   vendor_id invoice_no invoice_clean amount dupe_count voucher_no
   <chr>     <chr>      <chr>          <dbl>      <int> <chr>

title: 32  Duplicate Detection
text:
32.8 Fuzzy duplicates in names
Our last test found two invoices paid to look-alike vendors. Such vendors are often the root of the problem. A fictitious vendor is created with a name very close to a genuine one. Bills of the genuine vendor are then paid again, to the fictitious one. A casual reader of the payment register will not notice the difference.
Cleaning alone cannot catch these. Sharma Traders and Sharma Trader’s differ by an apostrophe. Gupta and Guptha differ by one letter. We need a way to measure how similar two names are. Chapter 33, which follows this chapter, explains several such measures in detail. Here we will use the Jaro-Winkler distance. It is 0 for identical strings and close to 1 for completely different ones.
The idea is simple. We compare every vendor name in the vendor master with every other vendor name. Then we look at the pairs with the smallest distance.
Step-1: Make all possible pairs of vendors. We do this by joining the vendors table with itself. But we do not want a vendor paired with itself. We also do not want each pair twice, once as (A, B) and again as (B, A). So we join each vendor only with those vendors whose ID is greater than its own. This is an inequality join, which we learnt in Section 14.5. The suffix argument tells R how to name the columns coming from the two copies of the table.

vendor_pairs <- vendors |>
  inner_join(vendors, by = join_by(vendor_id < vendor_id), suffix = c("_1", "_2"))

nrow(vendor_pairs)

[1] 91


With 14 vendors, we get 13 + 12 + … + 1 = 91 pairs.






TipWhy not cross_join()?



Another way is to make every combination using cross_join(), and then keep the required pairs with filter(vendor_id_1 < vendor_id_2). The result is the same. But cross_join() first builds the full table of n × n rows, and then throws away more than half of it. The inequality join builds only the pairs we need. In a test with 6,000 vendors, the inequality join took less than a second, while cross_join() and filter() took about 11 seconds and needed more than 1 GB of memory along the way.


Step-2: Calculate the distance between the two names in each pair. We convert both names to lower case first, as the measure is case sensitive.

vendor_pairs <- vendor_pairs |>
  mutate(jw_distance = stringdist(tolower(vendor_name_1),
                                  tolower(vendor_name_2),
                                  method = "jw"))

Step-3: Sort the pairs by distance and look at the closest ones.

vendor_pairs |>
  arrange(jw_distance) |>
  head(5)

# A tibble: 5 × 5
  vendor_id_1 vendor_name_1     vendor_id_2 vendor_name_2      jw_distance
  <chr>       <chr>             <chr>       <chr>                    <dbl>
1 V002        Gupta Enterprises V014        Guptha Enterprises      0.0185
2 V001        Sharma Traders    V013        Sharma Trader's         0.0222
3 V003        Bharat Stationers V009        Rajdhani Computers      0.292 
4 V001        Sharma Traders    V007        Om Sai Caterers         0.306 
5 V002        Gupta Enterprises V004        Kaveri Suppliers        0.306 


The first two pairs stand out clearly. Their distance is about 0.02. The next pair is already at about 0.29, and those names have nothing in common. So, in this data, a cut-off of say 0.1 separates suspicious pairs from the rest.

vendor_pairs |>
  filter(jw_distance < 0.1)

# A tibble: 2 × 5
  vendor_id_1 vendor_name_1     vendor_id_2 vendor_name_2      jw_distance
  <chr>       <chr>             <chr>       <chr>                    <dbl>
1 V001        Sharma Traders    V013        Sharma Trader's         0.0222
2 V002        Gupta Enterprises V014        Guptha Enterprises      0.0185








NoteHow to choose the cut-off?



There is no fixed rule. Sort the pairs by distance and read down the list. You will usually find a point after which the pairs stop looking alike. Use that point as the cut-off for this data. With large vendor masters, also compare other fields like PAN, GSTIN, bank account, address and mobile number. Two vendors with different names but the same bank account are even more suspicious than look-alike names.



32.8.1 Trying other similarity measures
Jaro-Winkler is not the only choice. Chapter 33 explains several other measures. These include Levenshtein distance, Q-grams and Soundex. All of them are available in the same stringdist() function. We only change the method argument. Let us calculate a few of them on our vendor pairs and compare.

vendor_pairs |>
  mutate(
    name_1  = tolower(vendor_name_1),
    name_2  = tolower(vendor_name_2),
    lv      = stringdist(name_1, name_2, method = "lv"),
    jw      = stringdist(name_1, name_2, method = "jw"),
    qgram_3 = stringdist(name_1, name_2, method = "qgram", q = 3),
    soundex = stringdist(name_1, name_2, method = "soundex")
  ) |>
  arrange(jw) |>
  select(vendor_name_1, vendor_name_2, lv, jw, qgram_3, soundex) |>
  head(5)

# A tibble: 5 × 6
  vendor_name_1     vendor_name_2         lv     jw qgram_3 soundex
  <chr>             <chr>              <dbl>  <dbl>   <dbl>   <dbl>
1 Gupta Enterprises Guptha Enterprises     1 0.0185       5       0
2 Sharma Traders    Sharma Trader's        1 0.0222       3       0
3 Bharat Stationers Rajdhani Computers    14 0.292       29       1
4 Sharma Traders    Om Sai Caterers       11 0.306       23       1
5 Gupta Enterprises Kaveri Suppliers      14 0.306       29       1


All four measures pick out the same two pairs. But each one speaks in its own language. Let us read them one by one.


Levenshtein (lv) counts the number of single-character edits. Both look-alike pairs need just one edit. Other pairs need 11 or more. But this is a count, so it depends on the length of the names. One edit in a five-letter name is a big change. One edit in a thirty-letter name is a small one. So the same cut-off does not suit short and long names alike.

Jaro-Winkler (jw) is always between 0 and 1, whatever the length of the names. This makes it easier to choose a single cut-off. It also gives more weight to the beginning of the string, where people usually make fewer mistakes.

Q-gram (qgram_3) counts the groups of three consecutive letters which are present in one name but not in the other. Notice that Gupta and Guptha score 5, though only one letter differs. A single extra letter breaks several three-letter groups at once.

Soundex (soundex) checks whether two strings sound alike in English. It gives only a yes or no answer. 0 means they sound the same and 1 means they do not. It caught both pairs, because Gupta and Guptha are pronounced the same way.







WarningCaution with Soundex on long names



Soundex looks only at the first letter and the next few consonant sounds of a string. It ignores everything after that. So long names which merely begin alike will also be called a match.

stringdist("sharma traders",
           c("sharma transport", "sharma tours", "shree traders"),
           method = "soundex")

[1] 0 0 1


All three vendors starting with “Sharma Tr…” are treated as the same. Soundex works best on single words like surnames. For full names, use it along with another measure, not alone.



32.8.2 A better phonetic measure, Double Metaphone
Double Metaphone is a more refined way to check whether two names sound alike. It gives two codes for each name, a primary and a secondary code. Comparing these codes gives three levels of match. These are strong, normal and weak, as Chapter 33 explains. The package fullmetaphone keeps the full code, while other packages keep only the first four characters. Full codes matter here, because firm names are long.
Let us calculate the codes for all our vendors. double_metaphone() returns a data frame with two columns, primary and secondary. We attach these to the vendor master.

library(fullmetaphone)

vendor_codes <- vendors |>
  bind_cols(double_metaphone(vendors$vendor_name))

vendor_codes

# A tibble: 14 × 4
   vendor_id vendor_name            primary      secondary   
   <chr>     <chr>                  <chr>        <chr>       
 1 V001      Sharma Traders         XRMTRTRS     XRMTRTRS    
 2 V002      Gupta Enterprises      KPTNTRPRSS   KPTNTRPRSS  
 3 V003      Bharat Stationers      PRTSTXNRS    PRTSTXNRS   
 4 V004      Kaveri Suppliers       KFRSPLRS     KFRSPLRS    
 5 V005      Laxmi Electricals      LKSMLKTRKLS  LKSMLKTRKLS 
 6 V006      National Printers      NXNLPRNTRS   NXNLPRNTRS  
 7 V007      Om Sai Caterers        AMSKTRRS     AMSKTRRS    
 8 V008      Patel Hardware         PTLRTR       PTLRTR      
 9 V009      Rajdhani Computers     RJTNKMPTRS   RJTNKMPTRS  
10 V010      Shree Ganesh Transport XRKNXTRNSPRT XRKNXTRNSPRT
11 V011      Ashok Estates          AXKSTTS      AXKSTTS     
12 V012      Verma & Sons           FRMSNS       FRMSNS      
13 V013      Sharma Trader's        XRMTRTRS     XRMTRTRS    
14 V014      Guptha Enterprises     KP0NTRPRSS   KPTNTRPRSS  


Now we make pairs exactly as before, and compare the codes of each pair.

vendor_codes |>
  inner_join(vendor_codes, by = join_by(vendor_id < vendor_id), suffix = c("_1", "_2")) |>
  mutate(match_level = case_when(
    primary_1 == primary_2 ~ "strong",
    primary_1 == secondary_2 | secondary_1 == primary_2 ~ "normal",
    secondary_1 == secondary_2 ~ "weak",
    TRUE ~ "none"
  )) |>
  filter(match_level != "none") |>
  select(vendor_name_1, vendor_name_2, match_level)

# A tibble: 2 × 3
  vendor_name_1     vendor_name_2      match_level
  <chr>             <chr>              <chr>      
1 Sharma Traders    Sharma Trader's    strong     
2 Gupta Enterprises Guptha Enterprises normal     


Only our two look-alike pairs are matched. Sharma Traders and Sharma Trader’s have exactly the same primary code, so it is a strong match. Guptha is coded as KP0..., because “th” may be spoken like the “th” in “think”. But its secondary code is KPT..., the same as the primary code of Gupta. So it is a normal match. Unlike Soundex, the full codes did not match any other firm.
Table 32.3 sums up when each measure is useful in audit work.


Table 32.3: Choosing a string similarity measure









Measure
How to calculate
Result
Best suited for



Levenshtein
stringdist(method = "lv")
0 upwards, counts edits
Codes of fixed length, like PAN, GSTIN or invoice numbers


Jaro-Winkler
stringdist(method = "jw")
0 to 1
Names of persons and firms, with one common cut-off


Q-gram
stringdist(method = "qgram")
0 upwards
Longer text like addresses, where words may be rearranged


Soundex
stringdist(method = "soundex")
0 or 1
Single words that sound alike, like Geeta and Gita



Double Metaphone
double_metaphone()
Strong, normal, weak or no match
Full names of persons and firms that sound alike












TipAudit tip



A pair flagged by two different measures is a stronger lead than a pair flagged by only one. For example, a pair with a low Jaro-Winkler distance and a strong Double Metaphone match deserves a closer look first. One measure checks spelling, the other checks sound. Together they catch both typing mistakes and deliberate look-alike names.


Comparing every name with every other name creates a very large table when the master is big. A master of 10,000 vendors gives about five crore pairs. In such cases, compare names only within smaller groups, say within the same state or the same first letter. This is called blocking.

title: 32  Duplicate Detection
section: 32.9 Duplicates across more than one ID
text:
32.9 Duplicates across more than one ID
Sometimes duplicates are hidden even better. A beneficiary may register twice with a different mobile number but the same bank account. Then again with a different bank account but the same Aadhaar or PAN. No single column shows a duplicate. But together, the records form a chain.
Such chains can be found using graph theory. We discuss this with a complete example in Section 52.2.

title: 32  Duplicate Detection
text:
32.10 A suggested workflow
Let us put everything together. For any payment, claim or beneficiary data, an auditor may follow these steps.


Understand the data. Know what each column means and which columns identify a transaction.

Check exact duplicates. Find repeated rows with get_dupes(). Find out why they exist, then remove them with distinct().

Clean the key columns. Fix case, spaces, punctuation and leading zeros.

Run the Same-Same-Same test on the cleaned key. Quantify the excess payment.

Run Same-Same-Different tests on suitable combinations. Use date windows and business knowledge to reduce false alarms.

Look for fuzzy duplicates in master data like vendors, employees and beneficiaries.

Verify with documents. Analytics only points to the cases. The finding is confirmed only after examining the original bills, approvals and bank records.







ImportantRemember



A duplicate found in data is a lead, not a finding. There may be a genuine reason, such as a part payment, a cancelled and re-issued cheque, or a credit note. Always examine the supporting records before reporting.

title: 33  String Similarity and Fuzzy Matching
text:
33.1 Why does an auditor need string similarity?
Comparing two numbers is easy. We can subtract one from the other, or use any of several statistical measures. Comparing two pieces of text is not so simple. Is Geeta the same as Gita? Is M/s Sharma Traders the same as Sharma Trader’s? Is Mohd. Iqbal the same person as Mohammad Iqbal? A computer, checking for exact equality, will say “no” to all three.
String similarity methods solve this problem. They take two strings and return a score that tells how alike they are. A good method should give a high score to Geeta and Gita, but not to Apple and Microsoft. Matching strings in this approximate way is often called fuzzy matching.
Over several decades, many methods have been developed for this. They have different strengths and weaknesses. They fall into three broad groups.
Names and addresses are typed by different people, at different times, in different systems. So the same person or firm is rarely written the same way everywhere. Exact matching misses such cases. Fuzzy matching finds them. Typical audit uses include these.
crumbs: 33  String Similarity and Fuzzy Matching

title: 33  String Similarity and Fuzzy Matching
text:
Duplicate beneficiaries or vendors, registered twice with slightly different names, as we saw in Section 32.8.

Conflict of interest. Matching the names of vendors’ proprietors, partners or directors against the list of employees.

Ineligible beneficiaries. Matching a list of beneficiaries against a list of deceased persons, government employees or income-tax payers, when there is no common ID.

Ghost employees. Matching the pay roll against attendance or posting records.

Linking two databases that were never designed to be linked, such as a scheme database and a land record.

33.2 Prerequisites
We will mainly use the stringdist package. For phonetic codes, we also use phonics and fullmetaphone.

library(tidyverse)
library(stringdist)

title: 33  String Similarity and Fuzzy Matching
text:
33.4 Distance and similarity
stringdist() returns a distance. Zero means the strings are identical, and larger numbers mean more different. Its companion stringsim() returns a similarity between 0 and 1. One means identical, and zero means completely different. The two carry the same information, scaled differently.

stringdist("helo", "hello", method = "lv")

[1] 1

stringsim("helo", "hello", method = "lv")

[1] 0.8


Both functions are vectorised. They compare the first element of one vector with the first of the other, the second with the second, and so on. Their main arguments are these.


a and b are the two strings, or vectors of strings, to be compared.

method is the method to use. The default is osa, explained below. Others include lv, dl, hamming, lcs, qgram, cosine, jaccard, jw and soundex.

q is the size of the letter groups, for the token-based methods.

p is the Winkler prefix factor, for the jw method.

Similarity is often easier to work with, because it is on the same 0 to 1 scale for every method, whatever the length of the strings.
crumbs: 33  String Similarity and Fuzzy Matching

title: 33  String Similarity and Fuzzy Matching
text:
33.5 Edit-based methods
Edit-based methods count the smallest number of changes needed to turn one string into another. They match strings based on a simple model of typing errors.

33.5.1 Levenshtein distance
It is named after Vladimir Levenshtein, who considered this distance in 1965. The Levenshtein distance between two words is the minimum number of single-character edits, that is, insertions, deletions or substitutions, required to change one word into the other. It is often simply called the edit distance.
For the two words helo and hello, there is a missing letter l. To change helo into hello, we need to insert just that one letter. So the distance is 1, as we saw above.

33.5.2 Optimal String Alignment and Damerau-Levenshtein
Consider atharv and its typo ahtarv. The letters th have been swapped to ht. Such swaps, called transpositions, are among the most common typing errors. Levenshtein counts a swap as two substitutions. Optimal String Alignment (osa) and Damerau-Levenshtein (dl) count it as a single edit.

c(lv  = stringdist("atharv", "ahtarv", method = "lv"),
  osa = stringdist("atharv", "ahtarv", method = "osa"),
  dl  = stringdist("atharv", "ahtarv", method = "dl"))

 lv osa  dl 
  2   1   1 


This is why osa is the default method of stringdist(). For most typing errors, osa and dl give the same answer.

33.5.3 Hamming distance
This distance is computed by placing one string over the other, and counting the positions where the letters differ. It was designed for strings of the same length, such as codes. For strings of different lengths, stringdist() returns Inf.

stringdist(c("ABCPS1234K", "ABCPS1234K"),
           c("ABCPS1243K", "ABCPS123K"), method = "hamming")

[1]   2 Inf


The first pair, two PAN-like codes with two digits swapped, differs in 2 positions. The second pair has different lengths, so the distance is infinite. Hamming distance is useful for fixed-length identifiers like PAN, IFSC, vehicle numbers or account numbers of a known length.

33.5.4 Longest common subsequence
The lcs method looks for the longest subsequence, that is, letters appearing in the same order, though not necessarily next to each other, that both strings share. The distance is the number of letters left out of it, in both strings together.

33.5.5 Jaro and Jaro-Winkler
The Jaro method gives a high score to two strings if

they contain the same characters, not too far from each other, and
the matching characters appear in the same order.

To be exact, two characters count as matching only if they are no further apart than one less than half the length of the longer string. So if the longer string has 6 letters, a letter of the first string must be found within 2 positions of the same place in the second.
Jaro-Winkler (jw) adds a bonus when the strings begin alike, controlled by the argument p, usually set to 0.1. The idea is that people rarely make mistakes in the first few letters of a name. Without p, the jw method gives the plain Jaro distance.

c(jaro          = stringdist("martha", "marhta", method = "jw"),
  jaro_winkler  = stringdist("martha", "marhta", method = "jw", p = 0.1))

        jaro jaro_winkler 
  0.05555556   0.03888889 


Jaro-Winkler distance always lies between 0 and 1, whatever the length of the strings. This makes it easy to use one cut-off for all names, which is why it is very popular for matching names.
crumbs: 33  String Similarity and Fuzzy Matching

title: 33  String Similarity and Fuzzy Matching
text:
33.6 Token-based methods
Token-based methods break each string into small pieces and compare the sets of pieces.

33.6.1 Q-grams
A q-gram is a group of q consecutive characters. To illustrate, take q = 3. Groups of three letters are also called trigrams. For atharv and its possible typo ahtarv, the trigrams are as follows.

For atharv, {ath, tha, har, arv}

For ahtarv, {aht, hta, tar, arv}


Only one trigram, arv, is common to both. Two measures can be built from these sets.

The q-gram distance (qgram) counts the trigrams that are present in one string but not in the other. Here 3 of each string’s 4 trigrams are unmatched, so the distance is 6.
The Jaccard distance (jaccard) divides the number of shared trigrams by the number of distinct trigrams in the two strings together. Together, there are 7 distinct trigrams, and only 1 is shared. So the Jaccard similarity is 1/7, about 14%, and the Jaccard distance is 6/7.


c(qgram   = stringdist("atharv", "ahtarv", method = "qgram", q = 3),
  jaccard = stringdist("atharv", "ahtarv", method = "jaccard", q = 3),
  jaccard_similarity = stringsim("atharv", "ahtarv", method = "jaccard", q = 3))

             qgram            jaccard jaccard_similarity 
         6.0000000          0.8571429          0.1428571 


We can see that q-grams are not very effective for transpositions. A single swap of two letters breaks several trigrams at once. The cosine method (cosine) is a close cousin, which compares how often each q-gram occurs.

33.6.2 Word order
Token-based methods have one big advantage. They are not much affected by the order of words. In Indian records, the same person may be written as Rajesh Kumar Sharma in one place and Sharma Rajesh Kumar in another.

pair <- c("rajesh kumar sharma", "sharma rajesh kumar")

c(osa     = stringsim(pair[1], pair[2], method = "osa"),
  jw      = stringsim(pair[1], pair[2], method = "jw", p = 0.1),
  qgram_2 = stringsim(pair[1], pair[2], method = "qgram", q = 2),
  cosine  = stringsim(pair[1], pair[2], method = "cosine", q = 2))

      osa        jw   qgram_2    cosine 
0.2631579 0.8421053 0.8888889 0.9166667 


OSA, a pure edit-based measure, sees these as very different. Jaro-Winkler is in between. The token-based measures see them as nearly the same. Another simple trick, which works with any method, is to sort the words of each name before comparing.

sort_words <- function(x) {
  map_chr(str_split(x, " "), \(w) paste(sort(w), collapse = " "))
}

sort_words(pair)

[1] "kumar rajesh sharma" "kumar rajesh sharma"


After sorting, both names become kumar rajesh sharma, and every method sees them as identical.
crumbs: 33  String Similarity and Fuzzy Matching

title: 33  String Similarity and Fuzzy Matching
text:
33.7 Phonetic methods
Phonetic matching methods compare strings by how they sound. Consider Geeta and Gita. They sound alike, so one person may write Geeta and another Gita. Neither is a misspelling of the other. They simply sound the same.

33.7.1 Soundex
Created by Robert Russell and Margaret King Odell in 1918, this method was meant to match names and surnames based on the basic rules of English pronunciation. Similar-sounding names get the same code. The code keeps the first letter, followed by three digits for the next few consonant sounds. stringdist() gives 0 when two strings have the same Soundex code, and 1 otherwise.

stringdist(c("geeta", "susheel", "ram"), c("gita", "sushil", "rama"), method = "soundex")

[1] 0 0 0


Because Soundex looks at only the first few sounds, long names that merely begin alike also match. We saw this problem with firm names in Section 32.8.

33.7.2 Metaphone
Developed by Lawrence Philips in 1990, Metaphone is more accurate than Soundex, because it takes groups of letters into account, such as ph sounding like f. Its disadvantage shows up with names that are not English, as it is based on the rules of English pronunciation. The phonics package calculates it.

library(phonics)

metaphone(c("geeta", "gita", "susheel", "sushil", "laxmi", "lakshmi"))

[1] "JT"   "JT"   "SXL"  "SXL"  "LKSM" "LKXM"


Geeta and Gita get the same code, and so do Susheel and Sushil. But Laxmi and Lakshmi do not. Metaphone codes x as KS and sh as X, so the two names get LKSM and LKXM. Such variations, very common in Indian names, are better handled during cleaning, for example by replacing ksh with x in both lists before matching.
metaphone() works on single words. It cannot handle spaces or other special characters, so we apply it to cleaned single words, or to each word of a name separately.

33.7.3 Double Metaphone
Following Metaphone, Philips also designed the Double Metaphone. As its name suggests, it returns two codes, a primary and a secondary one, so there are more chances to match. At the same time, it means a higher chance of a false match. There are three matching levels.

Primary code against primary code is the strongest match.
Secondary code against primary code is a normal match.
Secondary code against secondary code is the weakest match.

Philips later refined it further, as Metaphone 3. That algorithm is, however, proprietary and not open-source.
Double Metaphone can be calculated with the function DoubleMetaphone() from the PGRdup package. The function is vectorised. It returns a list of two vectors, primary and alternate.

suppressPackageStartupMessages(library(PGRdup))

DoubleMetaphone(c("geeta", "gita", "susheel", "sushil"))

$primary
[1] "JT"  "JT"  "SXL" "SXL"

$alternate
[1] "KT"  "KT"  "SXL" "SXL"








WarningPGRdup keeps only four characters



DoubleMetaphone() of PGRdup cuts every code to its first four characters. This was the default in the original design of the algorithm. It works well for short single names like the ones above. But longer names, and names of firms, get the same code merely because they begin alike.

DoubleMetaphone(c("Bhattacharya", "Bhattacharjee", "Sharma Traders", "Sharma Transport"))$primary

[1] "PTKR" "PTKR" "XRMT" "XRMT"


Both surnames get PTKR. Both firms get XRMT. In audit work, where we compare full names of beneficiaries or vendors, this can produce many false matches.



33.7.4 Full length Double Metaphone with fullmetaphone

To overcome this limitation, Atharv Tyagi and the author have developed an R package, fullmetaphone. It follows the rules of the reference implementation of Double Metaphone. It keeps codes of up to 32 characters instead of four. Until it is available on CRAN, it can be installed from GitHub.

# install.packages("remotes")
remotes::install_github("anilyayavar/dblmetaphone")

Its main function is double_metaphone(). It takes one name or a whole vector of names, and returns a data frame with columns primary and secondary. The package also has metaphone(), for the older single-code algorithm, and sounds_like(), which tells whether two names sound alike.

library(fullmetaphone)


Attaching package: 'fullmetaphone'


The following object is masked from 'package:phonics':

    metaphone

double_metaphone("Guptha")

  primary secondary
1     KP0       KPT

double_metaphone(c("Bhattacharya", "Bhattacharjee", "Sharma Traders", "Sharma Transport"))

     primary  secondary
1       PTKR       PTKR
2      PTKRJ      PTKRJ
3   XRMTRTRS   XRMTRTRS
4 XRMTRNSPRT XRMTRNSPRT


Now the four names get four different primary codes. For short names, the codes are the same as those from PGRdup.
Let us apply the three matching levels to a few pairs of names. We write a small function, so that we can use it again later.

dm_match <- function(a, b) {
  dm_a <- double_metaphone(a)
  dm_b <- double_metaphone(b)
  case_when(
    dm_a$primary == dm_b$primary ~ "strong",
    dm_a$secondary == dm_b$primary | dm_a$primary == dm_b$secondary ~ "normal",
    dm_a$secondary == dm_b$secondary ~ "weak",
    TRUE ~ "no match"
  )
}

nameset1 <- c("Geeta", "Susheel", "Ram", "Dr. Suchitra")
nameset2 <- c("Gita", "Sushil", "Rama", "Suchitra")

tibble(nameset1, nameset2,
       raw     = dm_match(nameset1, nameset2),
       cleaned = dm_match(clean_name(nameset1), clean_name(nameset2)))

# A tibble: 4 × 4
  nameset1     nameset2 raw      cleaned
  <chr>        <chr>    <chr>    <chr>  
1 Geeta        Gita     strong   strong 
2 Susheel      Sushil   strong   strong 
3 Ram          Rama     strong   strong 
4 Dr. Suchitra Suchitra no match strong 


On the raw names, Dr. Suchitra does not match Suchitra. The title “Dr.” changes the beginning of the code, and phonetic codes depend heavily on how a name begins. After cleaning with our clean_name() function, the title is gone and the two match. This shows, once again, why cleaning comes first.

title: 33  String Similarity and Fuzzy Matching
text:
33.8 Comparing the methods
Let us now put all the methods side by side, on pairs of names that show typical Indian variations. We use similarities, so that all methods are on the same 0 to 1 scale.

pairs <- tribble(
  ~name_1,                ~name_2,                 ~variation,
  "geeta",                "gita",                  "Spelling (ee/i)",
  "lakshmi devi",         "laxmi devi",            "Spelling (ksh/x)",
  "atharv",               "ahtarv",                "Typing (swap)",
  "suresh chandra",       "suresh chander",        "Spelling (ending)",
  "rajesh kumar sharma",  "sharma rajesh kumar",   "Word order",
  "r k gupta",            "ram kishan gupta",      "Initials",
  "anil kumar",           "sunil kumar",           "Different person"
)

pairs |>
  mutate(osa    = stringsim(name_1, name_2, method = "osa"),
         jw     = stringsim(name_1, name_2, method = "jw", p = 0.1),
         qgram  = stringsim(name_1, name_2, method = "qgram", q = 2),
         dmeta  = dm_match(name_1, name_2)) |>
  mutate(across(where(is.double), \(x) round(x, 2))) |>
  knitr::kable()

Some lessons stand out from this table.


No single method wins everywhere. Jaro-Winkler handles spelling and typing well. Q-grams handle word order. The phonetic code handles Geeta and Gita, but not Lakshmi and Laxmi, which need a cleaning rule.

Initials are hard for every method. R K Gupta and Ram Kishan Gupta may well be the same person, but no method sees them as very similar. Matching on the surname, and checking initials separately, works better.

Similar is not the same. Anil Kumar and Sunil Kumar get high scores from all the lexical methods, yet they are different people. Here the phonetic code correctly says “no match”, which shows the value of using two kinds of method together. A high score is a lead, not proof.

section: 33.9 Matching two lists, an audit use case
text:
33.9 Matching two lists, an audit use case
So far we have compared names in pairs. In audit, we usually have two lists, and want to find which names in one list resemble names in the other. Let us take a common example, a check for conflict of interest. We have a list of employees of an office, and a list of proprietors of firms that supplied goods to it. Both lists are made up. Click on the code below to see how they were created.

Code to create the employee and proprietor listsemployees <- tibble(
  emp_id   = c("E01", "E02", "E03", "E04", "E05", "E06", "E07"),
  emp_name = c("Rakesh Kumar Verma", "Smt. Sunita Devi", "Mohd. Iqbal Khan",
               "Pradeep Singh", "Kavita Sharma", "Anand Prakash", "Neha Gupta")
)

proprietors <- tibble(
  firm      = c("Verma Enterprises", "Sunrise Traders", "Iqbal & Sons",
                "Singh Suppliers", "Kavya Stationers", "Gupta Agencies"),
  proprietor = c("Rakesh Kr. Verma", "Arvind Mehta", "Mohammad Iqbal Khan",
                 "Pradip Singh", "Kavya Sharma", "Neeraj Gupta")
)
employees

# A tibble: 7 × 2
  emp_id emp_name          
  <chr>  <chr>             
1 E01    Rakesh Kumar Verma
2 E02    Smt. Sunita Devi  
3 E03    Mohd. Iqbal Khan  
4 E04    Pradeep Singh     
5 E05    Kavita Sharma     
6 E06    Anand Prakash     
7 E07    Neha Gupta        

Code to create the employee and proprietor listsproprietors

# A tibble: 6 × 2
  firm              proprietor         
  <chr>             <chr>              
1 Verma Enterprises Rakesh Kr. Verma   
2 Sunrise Traders   Arvind Mehta       
3 Iqbal & Sons      Mohammad Iqbal Khan
4 Singh Suppliers   Pradip Singh       
5 Kavya Stationers  Kavya Sharma       
6 Gupta Agencies    Neeraj Gupta       



33.9.1 Method 1, compare every pair
With small lists, we can simply compare every employee with every proprietor. cross_join(), which we used in Section 32.8, makes all the pairs. We compare the cleaned names, keep the pairs above a chosen similarity, and add the Double Metaphone match level as a second opinion.

candidates <- employees |>
  cross_join(proprietors) |>
  mutate(jw = stringsim(clean_name(emp_name), clean_name(proprietor),
                        method = "jw", p = 0.1),
         sound = dm_match(clean_name(emp_name), clean_name(proprietor))) |>
  filter(jw >= 0.85) |>
  arrange(desc(jw))

candidates |>
  mutate(jw = round(jw, 2)) |>
  select(emp_name, proprietor, firm, jw, sound)

# A tibble: 5 × 5
  emp_name           proprietor          firm                 jw sound   
  <chr>              <chr>               <chr>             <dbl> <chr>   
1 Mohd. Iqbal Khan   Mohammad Iqbal Khan Iqbal & Sons       1    strong  
2 Kavita Sharma      Kavya Sharma        Kavya Stationers   0.94 no match
3 Rakesh Kumar Verma Rakesh Kr. Verma    Verma Enterprises  0.92 no match
4 Pradeep Singh      Pradip Singh        Singh Suppliers    0.92 strong  
5 Neha Gupta         Neeraj Gupta        Gupta Agencies     0.91 no match


Let us read the result.


Rakesh Kumar Verma and Rakesh Kr. Verma are almost certainly the same person, written with a short form. The phonetic code misses this pair, because Kr sounds nothing like Kumar. Adding a rule to our cleaning function, to expand kr to kumar, would fix it. So a “no match” from one method does not prove that two names are different.

Mohd. Iqbal Khan and Mohammad Iqbal Khan become identical after cleaning, since our clean_name() function expands Mohd.

Pradeep Singh and Pradip Singh are very close, and sound the same. A strong lead.

Kavita Sharma and Kavya Sharma, and Neha Gupta and Neeraj Gupta, are close in spelling, but are probably different people. Note that the phonetic code does not match them. Such pairs show why every match must be checked against other details.

33.9.2 Method 2, amatch()

stringdist has a ready function for finding, for each string, the closest match in another list. amatch(x, table, maxDist) returns, for each element of x, the position of the closest element in table, if it is within maxDist. Otherwise it returns NA.

pos <- amatch(clean_name(employees$emp_name), clean_name(proprietors$proprietor),
              method = "jw", p = 0.1, maxDist = 0.15)

employees |>
  mutate(matched_proprietor = proprietors$proprietor[pos],
         matched_firm       = proprietors$firm[pos])

# A tibble: 7 × 4
  emp_id emp_name           matched_proprietor  matched_firm     
  <chr>  <chr>              <chr>               <chr>            
1 E01    Rakesh Kumar Verma Rakesh Kr. Verma    Verma Enterprises
2 E02    Smt. Sunita Devi   <NA>                <NA>             
3 E03    Mohd. Iqbal Khan   Mohammad Iqbal Khan Iqbal & Sons     
4 E04    Pradeep Singh      Pradip Singh        Singh Suppliers  
5 E05    Kavita Sharma      Kavya Sharma        Kavya Stationers 
6 E06    Anand Prakash      <NA>                <NA>             
7 E07    Neha Gupta         Neeraj Gupta        Gupta Agencies   


A Jaro-Winkler distance of 0.15 is the same as a similarity of 0.85, the cut-off we used above. amatch() is fast and convenient, but it returns only the single closest match for each name. When there may be more than one candidate, the pairwise method is safer.






TipAudit tip



A name match alone is weak evidence, especially for common names. For every candidate pair, compare a second detail, such as father’s name, date of birth, address, mobile number, PAN or bank account. In a conflict-of-interest check, a matching bank account or address between an employee and a vendor is often stronger evidence than the name itself.

title: 33  String Similarity and Fuzzy Matching
text:
33.10 Choosing a cut-off
Every fuzzy match needs a cut-off, and every cut-off is a trade-off.

A strict cut-off, say a Jaro-Winkler similarity of 0.95, finds few false matches, but misses many true ones.
A loose cut-off, say 0.80, finds most true matches, but also many false ones, which must then be checked by hand.

A practical approach is to start loose, sort the pairs by score, and read down the list. You will usually see that above a certain score most pairs are real, and below another score most are not. Set the cut-off between the two, keeping in mind how many pairs your team can actually check.
crumbs: 33  String Similarity and Fuzzy Matching

title: 33  String Similarity and Fuzzy Matching
text:
33.11 Large lists
Comparing every pair becomes slow when the lists are large. Two lists of 10,000 names each give ten crore pairs. Three ideas help.


Blocking. Compare names only within smaller groups that must match anyway, such as the same district, the same year of birth, or the same first letter of the surname. Blocks can also be formed by phonetic codes.

Inequality joins. When comparing a list with itself, compare each pair only once, as we did with inner_join(..., join_by(id < id)) in Section 32.8.

stringdistmatrix(). It calculates all distances between two vectors in one call, and uses several processor cores. The argument nthread controls how many.







WarningPrivacy



Names, addresses and identity numbers are personal data. Do fuzzy matching only on secure systems approved for such data. Never paste such lists into online tools or AI chatbots.
crumbs: 33  String Similarity and Fuzzy Matching

title: 33  String Similarity and Fuzzy Matching
text:
33.12 A suggested workflow


Define the question. Which two lists, or which one list, and what would a match mean?

Clean the names. Case, punctuation, titles, common short forms and, where useful, word order.

Choose a method suited to the kind of variation you expect, and a second method as a check.

Block if the lists are large.

Compare and score, with stringsim(), cross_join() or amatch().

Choose a cut-off by reading down the sorted list of pairs.

Confirm each candidate with a second identifier, like date of birth, address or bank account.

Report the original names, with the evidence for each match.







ImportantRemember



Fuzzy matching finds names that look or sound alike. It cannot tell whether they belong to the same person. Two different people can have very similar names, and one person can be written in very different ways. Treat every match as a question to be answered from other evidence.

title: 34  Record Linkage
text:
34.1 Why a simple join is not enough
Some of the most important audit findings come not from one data set, but from putting two together.
In each case, we have to find the same person in two lists. If both lists carried a reliable common number, such as an Aadhaar number seeded in both, this would be a simple join, which we learnt in Chapter 14. But very often they do not. The death register has no pension ID. The scheme lists were made by different departments, at different times, by different data entry operators. The same person is written as Kamla Devi in one and Smt. Kamala Devi in the other, with an age that differs by a year and a village spelt two ways.
Record linkage is the craft of finding records which belong to the same person (or firm, or property) when there is no common key, using several imperfect details together. It is also called record matching, entity resolution or, when done within one list, deduplication. In this chapter we learn it from the beginning, step by step, on a realistic example.
Prerequisites
We use the string similarity measures of Chapter 33, especially Jaro-Winkler similarity, and Double Metaphone phonetic codes. Readers new to them may read that chapter first.
Let us start with a tiny example, three pensioners and three death records.
pension_list <- tibble(
  ben_id        = c("P1", "P2", "P3"),
  name          = c("Kamla Devi", "Ramesh Yadav", "Sita Ram Verma"),
  relation_name = c("Mohan Lal", "Jagdish Yadav", "Bhagwan Verma"),
  village       = c("Amarpur", "Chandanpura", "Daulatpur"),
  age_2024      = c(72, 81, 68)
)
death_register <- tibble(
  reg_no        = c("D101", "D102", "D103"),
  name          = c("Smt. Kamala Devi", "Ramesh Yadav", "Sitaram Verma"),
  relation_name = c("Mohan Lal", "Rakesh Yadav", "Bhagwan Varma"),
  village       = c("Amarpur", "Chandanpura", "Daulatpur"),
  age_at_death  = c(73, 45, 68)
)
An exact join on name and village finds only one pair.
pension_list |>
  inner_join(death_register, by = c("name", "village"), suffix = c("_pension", "_death")) |>
  select(name, village, relation_name_pension, relation_name_death, age_2024, age_at_death)

# A tibble: 1 × 6
  name   village relation_name_pension relation_name_death age_2024 age_at_death
  <chr>  <chr>   <chr>                 <chr>                  <dbl>        <dbl>
1 Rames… Chanda… Jagdish Yadav         Rakesh Yadav              81           45
And that one pair is wrong! Ramesh Yadav of Chandanpura in the death register is a different person. His father’s name is Rakesh, not Jagdish, and he died at 45, while our pensioner is 81. Meanwhile the join has missed both true pairs. Kamla Devi and Smt. Kamala Devi, with the same husband, village and nearly the same age, are surely the same person. So are Sita Ram Verma and Sitaram Verma.
Two lessons follow, and the rest of the chapter builds on them.

title: 34  Record Linkage
text:
Names alone are not enough. Common names repeat, especially within a village. We must use several details together: name, father’s or husband’s name, age, village.

Each detail must be compared with tolerance, allowing for spelling variations, titles, and small differences in age.

title: 34  Record Linkage
text:
34.2 The steps of record linkage
Every record linkage, however large, follows the same seven steps. We will go through each with our example.


Table 34.1: The seven steps of record linkage








Step
What we do
Why



1. Standardise
Clean each field in the same way in both lists
Remove differences that do not matter, like titles and punctuation


2. Block
Choose which pairs of records to compare
Comparing every record with every other is too slow


3. Compare
Measure how closely each field agrees, for each pair
Allow for spelling and age differences


4. Weigh
Turn the agreements into a total score of evidence
Agreement on a rare detail counts more than on a common one


5. Decide
Link, review by hand, or reject each pair, by its score
Not every pair can be decided by the data alone


6. One-to-one
Keep the best partner for each record
A person can die only once


7. Check
Verify the links, and measure the quality
Every link becomes an audit observation

section: 34.3 Our data, pensioners and the death register
text:
34.3 Our data, pensioners and the death register
We have the list of 3,000 beneficiaries of an old-age pension scheme in a development block, all being paid ₹1,000 a month (₹1,500 for those aged 80 or more) as on 31 March 2025. We also have the death register of the same block for April 2022 to December 2024, with 1,212 entries. The audit question is: are any of the pensioners in the death register, and still being paid?
The two lists were prepared independently. The pension list records the date of birth. The death register, as is common, records only the age at death, often as told by a relative, and so often rounded to a multiple of five. Names are written with variations, and some death records have no father’s or husband’s name.
The code below creates the data. It is long, because it imitates the many ways in which real records differ. New readers may skip it. What matters is that, unknown to the auditor, 150 of the pensioners died during the period, and their death records carry the kinds of variation described above. We also planted a dozen traps: deaths of other persons who share the name and village of a living pensioner. Since the data are simulated, we keep the true answer in a separate table, truth, only to measure how well our linkage works at the end. In a real audit there is no such table.

Code to create the pension list and death registerset.seed(2024)

variants <- c("Lakshmi" = "Laxmi", "Kamla" = "Kamala", "Bimla" = "Vimla", "Shanti" = "Santi",

              "Prasad" = "Parsad", "Yadav" = "Yadaw", "Kushwaha" = "Kushwah",

              "Chhote" = "Chote", "Shakuntala" = "Sakuntala", "Pushpa" = "Puspa",
              "Gayatri" = "Gaytri", "Urmila" = "Urmilla", "Tiwari" = "Tiwary")
typo <- function(x) {   # drop one letter from the middle
  map_chr(x, \(s) {
    pos <- 2 + sample.int(max(1, nchar(s) - 3), 1)
    paste0(substr(s, 1, pos - 1), substr(s, pos + 1, nchar(s)))
  })
}
apply_variant <- function(x) {
  map_chr(x, \(s) {
    hits <- names(variants)[str_detect(s, fixed(names(variants)))]
    if (length(hits) == 0) return(s)
    h <- sample(hits, 1)
    str_replace(s, fixed(h), variants[[h]])
  })
}
messy <- function(x, p_variant, p_typo) {
  v <- runif(length(x)) < p_variant
  x[v] <- apply_variant(x[v])
  t <- runif(length(x)) < p_typo
  x[t] <- typo(x[t])
  x
}

# Planted. 150 pensioners died, but are still on the pension list
dead <- pensioners |>
  slice_sample(n = 150) |>
  mutate(date_of_death = as.Date("2022-04-01") + sample(0:1004, n(), TRUE),
         true_age = floor(as.numeric(date_of_death - dob) / 365.25))

  mutate(

    reg_relation = messy(relation_name, 0.4, 0.15),
    reg_relation = if_else(runif(n()) < 0.08, NA_character_, reg_relation),
    reg_age = true_age + sample(c(0, 0, 0, 0, 1, -1, 1, 2, -2), n(), TRUE),
    reg_age = if_else(runif(n()) < 0.15, 5 * round(true_age / 5), reg_age),  # age rounded
    reg_village = messy(village, 0, 0.12)
  )

# Deaths of other persons in the block

  gender      = sample(c("M", "F"), n_other, TRUE),

title: 34  Record Linkage
34  Record Linkage
text:
34.5 Step 2. Block
How many pairs could we compare?

nrow(pen) * nrow(dth)

[1] 3636000


That is more than 36 lakh pairs, for a single block. For a district, or a State, comparing every pair becomes impossible. But we do not need to. A pensioner of Amarpur is very unlikely to appear in the death register under Pipariya. So we compare only pairs which share a blocking key, here the same village and the same gender. A blocking key is a cheap test which every true pair is expected to pass.

pairs_village <- pen |>
  inner_join(dth, by = c("village_cmp", "gender"), relationship = "many-to-many") |>
  select(ben_id, reg_no)
nrow(pairs_village)

[1] 44856


Blocking has reduced the work about 80 times. But it has a cost. If a true pair fails the blocking test, it is never compared, and so never found. Here, a death record whose village is misspelt, say Chandanpur for Chandanpura, would never be compared with the right pensioner.
The usual remedy is to block twice, with two different keys, and combine the pairs. Our second key is the phonetic code of the first word of the name, with gender. A misspelt village is now caught through the name, and a misspelt name through the village. Only a record with both wrong slips through.

pairs_name <- pen |>
  inner_join(dth, by = c("name_code", "gender"), relationship = "many-to-many") |>
  select(ben_id, reg_no)

pairs <- bind_rows(pairs_village, pairs_name) |> distinct()
c(village_block = nrow(pairs_village), name_block = nrow(pairs_name), combined = nrow(pairs))

village_block    name_block      combined 
        44856         53807         97146 


We now have 97,146 pairs to compare instead of 36 lakh. Since our data are simulated, we can peek at how many of the 150 true pairs survived. The village block alone kept 132, the name block alone 133, and the two together 147. Two keys are clearly better than one.






Note



Good blocking keys are fields that are rarely wrong and split the data into many small groups: village or PIN code, year of birth, gender, or a phonetic code of the surname. A key that is often wrong loses true pairs, and a key with few values, like gender alone, saves little work.

title: 34  Record Linkage
text:
34.6 Step 3. Compare
For each pair, we now compare the fields one by one.


Name, father’s or husband’s name and village, with Jaro-Winkler similarity (Chapter 33), which gives 1 for identical strings and less for different ones.

Age. The pension list has the date of birth, and the death register the age at death. From the date of birth and the date of death we can work out what the pensioner’s age would have been at that death, and compare it with the recorded age.


compared <- pairs |>
  left_join(pen |> select(ben_id, name_p = name_cmp, rel_p = rel_cmp,
                          village_p = village_cmp, dob), by = "ben_id") |>
  left_join(dth |> select(reg_no, name_d = name_cmp, rel_d = rel_cmp,
                          village_d = village_cmp, age_at_death, date_of_death), by = "reg_no") |>
  mutate(name_sim    = stringsim(name_p, name_d, method = "jw", p = 0.1),
         rel_sim     = stringsim(rel_p, rel_d, method = "jw", p = 0.1),
         village_sim = stringsim(village_p, village_d, method = "jw", p = 0.1),
         age_gap     = abs(floor(as.numeric(date_of_death - dob) / 365.25) - age_at_death))

# a few pairs whose names are close but not identical
compared |>
  filter(name_sim > 0.9, name_sim < 1, !is.na(rel_sim)) |>
  select(name_p, name_d, rel_p, rel_d, name_sim, rel_sim, village_sim, age_gap) |>
  mutate(across(ends_with("sim"), \(x) round(x, 2))) |>
  arrange(age_gap) |>
  slice(c(1:3, n() - 2:0))   # three with close ages, three far apart

# A tibble: 6 × 8
  name_p         name_d         rel_p rel_d name_sim rel_sim village_sim age_gap
  <chr>          <chr>          <chr> <chr>    <dbl>   <dbl>       <dbl>   <dbl>
1 radhamishra    radhamisra     gang… gang…     0.98    1           1          0
2 surendrajatav  surenderjatav  dine… dine…     0.94    0.98        1          0
3 shakuntalasahu shakuntalaver… ramp… mahe…     0.9     0.5         1          0
4 gayatridevi    gayatriyadav   prem… kish…     0.91    0.44        0.66      62
5 mahendrakori   mahendralodhi  mang… sure…     0.92    0.52        0.48      63
6 gayatridevi    gayatriyadav   raje… kish…     0.91    0.54        0.67      63


The first two, with the same age and nearly the same father’s name, look like the same person written differently (Misra for Mishra, Surender for Surendra). The third has the same first name and age, but a different surname and father, so is probably someone else. The last three, decades apart in age, are clearly different people, despite their similar names. No single field decides; we need to weigh them together.
Similarities are numbers between 0 and 1. To weigh them in the next step, it is simpler to sort each comparison into a few levels.


Table 34.2: Comparison levels










Field
Agree

Disagree
Far apart



Name

0.90 to 0.95
below 0.90



Father’s or husband’s name
