title: 37  Simple Linear Regression
text:
37.9 Using lm for predictions
The output of lm() is actually a list. It contains much more information than we saw above. Let us see what it contains.

names(lin_reg1) |>
  as.data.frame() |>
  setNames('Objects')

         Objects
1   coefficients
2      residuals
3        effects
4           rank
5  fitted.values
6         assign
7             qr
8    df.residual
9        xlevels
10          call
11         terms
12         model


We may extract any of these as needed. For example,

lin_reg1$coefficients

(Intercept)       staff 
 15.5084352   0.3477244 


The package broom gives all this information as a tidy data frame. Its function augment() gives the fitted value, residual, leverage (.hat), Cook’s distance (.cooksd) and standardised residual (.std.resid) for every row. If we pass the original data as data =, it keeps all the other columns too, like office_id. Let us sort the offices by their standardised residual, which we will explain in Section 37.10.

augment(lin_reg1, data = bdo) |>
  select(office_id, terrain, staff, office_exp, .fitted, .resid, .std.resid, .hat, .cooksd) |>
  arrange(desc(.std.resid)) |>
  head()

# A tibble: 6 × 9
  office_id terrain staff office_exp .fitted .resid .std.resid    .hat .cooksd
  <chr>     <fct>   <dbl>      <dbl>   <dbl>  <dbl>      <dbl>   <dbl>   <dbl>
1 BDO-088   Plain      27       32.7    24.9   7.82       2.71 0.0101   0.0374
2 BDO-086   Hilly      37       34.5    28.4   6.14       2.13 0.0108   0.0246
3 BDO-035   Hilly      34       32.6    27.3   5.27       1.83 0.00882  0.0148
4 BDO-081   Hilly      25       29.4    24.2   5.22       1.81 0.0119   0.0197
5 BDO-062   Hilly      28       30.5    25.2   5.22       1.81 0.00938  0.0155
6 BDO-105   Hilly      34       32.2    27.3   4.83       1.67 0.00882  0.0124


The planted office BDO-088 is at the top. It spent ₹7.82 lakh more than offices of its size usually do. But where is the other planted office, BDO-027? It is only at number 35 when all the offices are sorted this way. We will find out why in Section 38.6. Notice also that the other five offices at the top are all in the hills. Our model does not know about terrain yet. We will add it in Chapter 38.
Let us also visualise the predicted values against the actual values and residuals, in Figure 37.11.


















Figure 37.11: Predicted vs. actual values (left) and residuals (right)


To predict for new data, we use the base R function predict(). The new data must be a data frame with a column of the same name as the predictor. Suppose three new block offices are being opened, with 15, 30 and 45 staff. Let us predict their yearly office expenses, which can help to check the budget estimates they send.

new_vals <- data.frame(staff = c(15, 30, 45))
predict(lin_reg1, new_vals)

       1        2        3 
20.72430 25.94017 31.15603 


A prediction is never exact. We can ask predict() for a prediction interval, the range in which the expenses of a new office are likely to fall, 95 times out of 100.

predict(lin_reg1, new_vals, interval = "prediction")

       fit      lwr      upr
1 20.72430 14.89517 26.55343
2 25.94017 20.17468 31.70566
3 31.15603 25.34891 36.96315


So an office with 30 staff will most likely spend between about ₹20.2 lakh and ₹31.7 lakh a year. An office of that size which spends well beyond this range deserves a question.






WarningCaution



Predict only within the range of the data used to build the model. Our block offices have from 13 to 54 staff. The model knows nothing about an office with 300 staff, and its prediction there may be nonsense. Predicting outside the range is called extrapolation. In audit, a model built on block offices should not be used to judge a district headquarters office.

title: 37  Simple Linear Regression
section: 37.10 Audit use case, offices that spend more than their staff explains
text:
37.10 Audit use case, offices that spend more than their staff explains
Let us now put this chapter’s tools to one audit question. Which block offices spend much more than their staff strength explains? augment() already gives us the residual of every office. To judge how unusual each residual is, we use the standardised residual (.std.resid). It is the residual divided by its standard error, so all offices are on one scale. Under our assumptions, a value above 2 happens by chance in only about 1 office in 40. Let us keep such offices and show their excess in lakh.

leads1 <- augment(lin_reg1, data = bdo) |>
  mutate(excess = office_exp - .fitted) |>
  filter(.std.resid > 2) |>
  arrange(desc(.std.resid)) |>
  select(office_id, district, terrain, staff, office_exp, .fitted, excess, .std.resid)
leads1

# A tibble: 2 × 8
  office_id district terrain staff office_exp .fitted excess .std.resid
  <chr>     <chr>    <fct>   <dbl>      <dbl>   <dbl>  <dbl>      <dbl>
1 BDO-088   Firozpur Plain      27       32.7    24.9   7.82       2.71
2 BDO-086   Chamba   Hilly      37       34.5    28.4   6.14       2.13


Only 2 offices cross this line. Together they spent about ₹14.0 lakh more than offices of their size usually do. The first, BDO-088 in Firozpur, is one of the two offices we planted. The second, BDO-086 in Chamba, is in a hilly block.
What would the auditor do with these leads? For BDO-088, we would call for the bills of its largest heads of expense, like vehicle hire, and check them with the log books. For BDO-086, we would first ask whether the terrain itself explains the excess. Vehicle hire costs more in the hills, and our model knows nothing about terrain. We would record the model, the leads and the replies in the working papers.






WarningCaution



A model with one driver is only a first screen. This one missed the other planted office, BDO-027, and it points to offices in the hills which may be innocent. Chapter 38 adds beneficiaries and terrain to the model. In Section 38.6 both planted offices then stand out clearly.
crumbs: Part VI: Modelling and Risk Scoring

title: 37  Simple Linear Regression
text:
37.11 A suggested workflow
For a simple regression in audit, we may follow these steps.


Understand the drivers. Decide, from knowledge of the business, which variable should explain the amount under audit. Regression only confirms or rejects relationships which make sense.

Visualise first. Draw a scatter plot to see whether the relationship looks linear, and to spot obvious errors.

Fit a simple model with lm(), and read its summary().

Check influence. Look at Cook’s distance and leverage. Investigate and correct data entry errors before going further.

Check the assumptions with plot() or check_model().

Measure the fit. Use R-squared, the residual standard error, MAE or RMSE to judge how far the expected values miss.

Flag the residuals. Use augment() and pick the units with large standardised residuals. Quantify the excess in rupees. If many leads share a feature, like terrain, add it to the model first (Chapter 38).

Verify with records. Examine the documents of the flagged units before drawing any conclusion.







ImportantRemember



A regression model shows association, not cause. A large residual means only that a unit does not fit the pattern of the others. It is a lead, not a finding. A model with one predictor knows only one driver. It may miss an irregular unit and point to an innocent one. Always examine the records before reporting.

title: 37  Simple Linear Regression
text:
37.12 Where next
Chapter 38 adds more predictors to the model, including categories like terrain and interactions. It finds both planted block offices, and it looks for ghost employees in the salary bills of sub-divisional offices.

title: 38  Multiple Regression in Audit
text:
38.1 Prerequisites
In Chapter 37 we explained the office expenses of block offices by one driver, their staff strength. That model found one of the two offices we had planted. It missed the other. It also pointed to several offices in the hills which may have done nothing wrong. One driver is rarely enough. The expenses of an office also depend on the beneficiaries it serves and on the terrain it covers.
An auditor meets this in most data. The cost of a road depends on its width, the terrain, the lead and the price of bitumen. The salary bill of an office depends on its staff and on the class of its city, which fixes the house rent allowance. Multiple regression lets us use all these drivers together. It gives a fairer expected amount for every unit. The units which spend more than expected then stand out more clearly, and innocent units drop away.
We end the chapter with the question we posed at the start of Chapter 37. Which offices spend much more on salary than their staff strength explains? That is where ghost employees hide.
In this chapter we will learn to
We use the same packages as in Chapter 37, and three more. car calculates the variance inflation factor. GGally draws correlation plots and moderndive draws parallel slopes.
library(tidyverse)
library(broom)
library(performance)
library(car)
library(GGally)
library(moderndive)

title: 38  Multiple Regression in Audit
text:
38.2 The block office data
We continue with the office expenses of block offices, described in Section 37.2. For each office we know its district and terrain, its staff in position and sanctioned posts, the floor area of its building, the population of its block and the beneficiaries it serves. We also know its office expenses for 2023-24, in ₹ lakh. Two offices have expenses inflated by ₹11 lakh each, as if vehicle hire was paid for vehicles never used. The code below creates exactly the same data as before.

Code to create the block office dataset.seed(4012)
n <- 120
district_terrain <- c(Etawah = "Plain", Sitapur = "Plain", Firozpur = "Plain",
                      Almora = "Hilly", Chamba = "Hilly",
                      Bastar = "Tribal", Mayurbhanj = "Tribal")
bdo <- tibble(
  office_id = sprintf("BDO-%03d", 1:n),
  district  = sample(names(district_terrain), n, replace = TRUE,
                     prob = c(0.17, 0.17, 0.16, 0.13, 0.12, 0.13, 0.12))
) |>
  mutate(
    terrain = factor(district_terrain[district], levels = c("Plain", "Hilly", "Tribal")),
    # offices in the hills and tribal areas are smaller
    staff = round(case_when(terrain == "Plain" ~ runif(n, 22, 55),
                            terrain == "Hilly" ~ runif(n, 12, 38),
                            TRUE               ~ runif(n, 16, 44))),
    sanctioned    = round(staff / runif(n, 0.80, 0.95)),
    # bigger offices have bigger buildings
    area_sqm      = round(120 + 11 * staff + rnorm(n, 0, 45)),
    population    = round(runif(n, 60, 200) * if_else(terrain == "Plain", 1.2, 0.8)),
    beneficiaries = round(population * runif(n, 0.25, 0.35), 1),
    # office expenses in lakh, driven by staff, beneficiaries and terrain
    office_exp = round(5 + 0.45 * staff + 0.12 * beneficiaries +
                       c(Plain = 0, Hilly = 6, Tribal = 3.5)[as.character(terrain)] +
                       rnorm(n, 0, 1.6), 2)
  )

# Planted cases. Vehicle hire of Rs 11 lakh paid without any vehicle used
planted <- c("BDO-027", "BDO-088")
bdo <- bdo |>
  mutate(office_exp = if_else(office_id %in% planted, office_exp + 11, office_exp))


We will compare our new models with the model of staff alone, lin_reg1, from Chapter 37. So let us fit it again.

lin_reg1 <- lm(office_exp ~ staff, data = bdo)

title: 38  Multiple Regression in Audit
text:
38.3 Multiple linear regression
In multiple linear regression, several independent variables together explain the dependent variable. The regression equation becomes
\[
y = \beta_0 + \beta_1x_1 + \beta_2x_2 + \beta_3x_3 + ... + \epsilon
\tag{38.1}\]
where \(x_1\), \(x_2\), \(x_3\) …, \(x_n\) are the \(n\) independent variables and \(y\) is the dependent variable as usual.
With two predictors, this equation is no longer a line but a flat plane in three dimensions. With more predictors, it is a hyperplane, which we cannot draw. So we usually look at the predictors one at a time, or use correlation plots.
As we noted in Chapter 37, there is one more assumption now. The independent variables should not be strongly related to each other, that is, there should be no multi-collinearity. Let us build an example. We just add the predictors to the formula using the + operator.
Example 2. Staff strength alone explained about 60% of the variation in office expenses. Let us try to explain office expenses using staff strength staff, floor area of the building area_sqm and the number of beneficiaries beneficiaries together. First, let us visualise each relationship separately, in Figure 38.1.
























Figure 38.1: Relationship between each predictor and office expenses


Let us also visualise the correlation between all these variables. See Figure 38.2.







Figure 38.2: Correlation between the variables in Example 2




Notice that two of the predictors are strongly correlated with each other too. Staff strength and floor area have a correlation of 0.93. Offices with more staff need bigger buildings. Keep this in mind. Now let us build the model.

data2 <- bdo[, c("office_exp", "staff", "area_sqm", "beneficiaries")]
lin_reg2 <- lm(office_exp ~ .,
               data = data2)
summary(lin_reg2)


Call:
lm(formula = office_exp ~ ., data = data2)

Residuals:
   Min     1Q Median     3Q    Max 
-6.447 -1.860  0.174  1.697  7.215 

Coefficients:
               Estimate Std. Error t value Pr(>|t|)    
(Intercept)   14.278375   1.263300  11.302  < 2e-16 ***
staff          0.343135   0.068615   5.001 2.05e-06 ***
area_sqm      -0.002411   0.006299  -0.383 0.702572    
beneficiaries  0.065658   0.017518   3.748 0.000279 ***
---
Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1

Residual standard error: 2.762 on 116 degrees of freedom
Multiple R-squared:  0.6407,    Adjusted R-squared:  0.6314 
F-statistic: 68.96 on 3 and 116 DF,  p-value: < 2.2e-16


In the formula, we used . instead of naming all the variables. The . is a shorthand for “all other columns of the data”. There is now one slope for each predictor and one intercept. The equation can be written as Equation 38.2.
\[
\text{Office expenses} = 14.2784 + 0.3431 \cdot \text{Staff} - 0.002411 \cdot \text{Area} + 0.0657 \cdot \text{Beneficiaries}
\tag{38.2}\]
Interpretation. The slopes of staff and beneficiaries are positive, so office expenses rise with both. Each slope is read keeping the other variables constant. For example, if two offices have the same floor area and the same number of beneficiaries, the one with 1 more employee spends ₹0.343 lakh more a year. Similarly, 1,000 more beneficiaries add ₹0.066 lakh, for the same staff and floor area. “Keeping other variables constant” is important. If the other variables also change, the effect on expenses is different.
Results. The model explains about 64% of the variation in office expenses (Multiple R-squared), against 60% with staff alone. Adjusted R-squared is a little lower, at 63%, after the penalty for three predictors. The F-test p-value is very small, so at least one slope is not zero.
Look at area_sqm, however. On its own, floor area is clearly related to office expenses (Figure 38.1, middle). In this model, its slope is -0.0024, slightly negative, as if a bigger building cost less to run. Its p-value is 0.70, not significant at all. This is because area_sqm carries almost the same information as staff. Once staff is in the model, area has little new to say, and its slope is left to chance. We could remove area_sqm and re-run the model. We will come back to this when we discuss multi-collinearity.

title: 38  Multiple Regression in Audit
section: 38.4 Including categorical or factor variables in lm
text:
38.4 Including categorical or factor variables in lm

So far, both our response variable and our predictors were numeric. But what if a predictor is categorical, like the terrain of a block, the city class of an office, or the type of a contract?
In such a case, we should make sure that the categorical variable is of type factor before building the model. We learnt about factors in Chapter 24. The first level of the factor matters, as we will see. We created terrain with the levels in the order Plain, Hilly, Tribal.
Example 3. Let us try to explain office_exp by terrain alone. Offices in the hills and tribal areas need more vehicle hire to cover the same block, so we would expect them to spend more. terrain is already a factor, so we need not convert it. Before moving on, let us visualise the relationship. Box plots are best suited here.







Figure 38.3: Office expenses by terrain




Now let us build the model.

lm_fact <- lm(office_exp ~ terrain, data = bdo)
summary(lm_fact)


Call:
lm(formula = office_exp ~ terrain, data = bdo)

Residuals:
    Min      1Q  Median      3Q     Max 
-9.6503 -3.3458  0.0324  3.3282 11.1032 

Coefficients:
              Estimate Std. Error t value Pr(>|t|)    
(Intercept)    27.3068     0.5985  45.622   <2e-16 ***
terrainHilly   -1.6142     0.9792  -1.648    0.102    
terrainTribal  -1.4965     1.0307  -1.452    0.149    
---
Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1

Residual standard error: 4.519 on 117 degrees of freedom
Multiple R-squared:  0.02967,   Adjusted R-squared:  0.01308 
F-statistic: 1.789 on 2 and 117 DF,  p-value: 0.1718


We now got one intercept and two slopes for a single predictor terrain. What happened?
Interpretation. R converts a factor into dummy variables. A dummy variable is 1 when a row belongs to a category and 0 otherwise. Being numeric, the dummies can be used in linear regression as before. The first level of the factor is taken as the baseline. It gets no dummy of its own. terrain has three levels, so it is encoded as two dummy variables. To see this, we can use the contrasts() function.

contrasts(bdo$terrain)

       Hilly Tribal
Plain      0      0
Hilly      1      0
Tribal     0      1


We can also see the actual numbers that went into the model with model.matrix(). Let us look at the first office of each terrain.

first_rows <- match(levels(bdo$terrain), bdo$terrain)
model.matrix(office_exp ~ terrain, data = bdo)[first_rows, ]

  (Intercept) terrainHilly terrainTribal
2           1            0             0
7           1            1             0
1           1            0             1


When the office is in the hills, terrainHilly is 1 and terrainTribal is 0, and the other way round for a tribal area. When both are 0, the office is in the plains, the baseline. That is why there is no separate coefficient for Plain. Now we can write the regression equation as Equation 38.3.
\[
\text{Office expenses} = 27.307 - 1.614 \cdot \text{terrainHilly} - 1.496 \cdot \text{terrainTribal}
\tag{38.3}\]
Reading this equation is now easy. For an office in the hills, the predicted expense is 27.307 - 1.614, or 25.693. When both dummy variables are zero, the predicted expense is just the intercept. So the intercept is the prediction for the baseline level, Plain, and each slope is the difference from the baseline. If we remove the intercept by adding - 1 to the formula, R gives us one coefficient for each level directly.

lm_fact0 <- lm(office_exp ~ terrain -1, data = bdo)
summary(lm_fact0)


Call:
lm(formula = office_exp ~ terrain - 1, data = bdo)

Residuals:
    Min      1Q  Median      3Q     Max 
-9.6503 -3.3458  0.0324  3.3282 11.1032 

Coefficients:
              Estimate Std. Error t value Pr(>|t|)    
terrainPlain   27.3068     0.5985   45.62   <2e-16 ***
terrainHilly   25.6926     0.7750   33.15   <2e-16 ***
terrainTribal  25.8103     0.8391   30.76   <2e-16 ***
---
Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1

Residual standard error: 4.519 on 117 degrees of freedom
Multiple R-squared:  0.9724,    Adjusted R-squared:  0.9717 
F-statistic:  1376 on 3 and 117 DF,  p-value: < 2.2e-16


Results. Compare these coefficients with Figure 38.3. They are nothing but the mean office expenses of each terrain, which is logical. The equation without intercept is Equation 38.4.
\[
\text{Office expenses} = 27.307 \cdot \text{terrainPlain} + 25.693 \cdot \text{terrainHilly} + 25.810 \cdot \text{terrainTribal}
\tag{38.4}\]
Since these coefficients are not slopes in the true sense, we will call them intercepts in the next examples.
There is a surprise here. Offices in the hills and tribal areas seem to spend less than offices in the plains, not more. And the p-values of the two slopes in lm_fact, 0.10 and 0.15, say that terrain makes no real difference at all. Should we conclude that terrain does not matter? Not yet. We will find the answer in the next section.






WarningCaution



Look at the R-squared of the two models. With an intercept it is 0.030. Without an intercept it jumps to 0.972. The fit has not improved at all, since the predictions are exactly the same. Without an intercept, R measures R-squared against zero instead of against the mean, which makes it look much larger. So use - 1 to read the coefficients easily, but compare models using the version with an intercept.



38.4.1 Parallel slopes regression
To understand how a categorical predictor works together with a numeric one, let us build a model step by step.
Example 4. Let us explain office expenses office_exp by staff strength staff and terrain terrain together. Let us visualise the variables first. From Figure 38.4 it is clear that office expenses rise linearly with staff, in all three terrains. Notice also that the offices in the hills and tribal areas are generally smaller.

ggplot(bdo, aes(staff, office_exp)) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = FALSE, formula = "y ~ x") +
  facet_wrap(.~ terrain) +
  labs(x = "Staff in position", y = "Office expenses (₹ lakh)") +
  theme_bw()






Figure 38.4: Office expenses vs. staff, for each terrain




Step 1. Let us first use only the numeric variable staff to explain office expenses, and look at the coefficients. This is the same model as Example 1 of Chapter 37.

par_slop1 <- lm(office_exp ~ staff, data = bdo)
coef(par_slop1)

(Intercept)       staff 
 15.5084352   0.3477244 


We got one intercept and one slope. We can see the line in Figure 38.5 (left).
Step 2. Now let us explain office expenses by terrain only. We also add - 1 to the formula, which removes the common intercept and gives one intercept for each terrain. This is the model lm_fact0 of Example 3. If a variable is not yet a factor, like a year stored as a number, we can convert it inside the formula with factor(). Now see the coefficients.

par_slop2 <- lm(office_exp ~ factor(terrain) - 1, data = bdo)
coef(par_slop2)

 factor(terrain)Plain  factor(terrain)Hilly factor(terrain)Tribal 
             27.30684              25.69265              25.81034 


We got one intercept for each terrain. As Figure 38.5 (right) shows, these are nothing but the mean expenses for each terrain. The three means are close to each other.


















Figure 38.5: Office expenses vs. staff (left) and terrain (right)


Step 3. Now we build the complete model with both variables together, and look at the coefficients.

par_slop <- lm(office_exp ~ staff + terrain - 1, data = bdo)
coef(par_slop)

        staff  terrainPlain  terrainHilly terrainTribal 
    0.4416366    11.1599895    15.3011985    12.0282383 


There is one slope for the numeric variable and a separate intercept for each terrain. If we draw these, we get three parallel lines with the same slope. See Figure 38.6.







Figure 38.6: Parallel slopes




This is also clear from the equation, Equation 38.5.
\[
\text{Office expenses} = 0.4416 \cdot \text{Staff} + 11.1600 \cdot \text{Plain} + 15.3012 \cdot \text{Hilly} + 12.0282 \cdot \text{Tribal}
\tag{38.5}\]
For any office, one of the three dummy variables is 1 and the others are 0. The one with 1 acts as the intercept, but the slope stays the same. In other words, whatever the terrain, office expenses change with staff at the same rate.
Notice something interesting. In Step 2, the three terrains had almost the same mean expenses. But now, for the same staff strength, an office in the hills spends about ₹4.1 lakh a year more than an office in the plains. An office in a tribal area spends about ₹0.9 lakh more. The difference was hidden because offices in the hills are smaller on average (23.5 staff against 36.6 in the plains). This is the power of multiple regression. It separates the effect of one variable from another. It also answers the surprise of Example 3. Terrain does matter, once we compare offices of the same size.
But is it right to force the same slope on all terrains? Perhaps each extra employee in the hills costs more, because each one travels more. How do we allow for that? The answer is interaction, discussed next.

38.4.2 Extending multiple linear regression by including interactions

The parallel slopes model forced a common slope on each category. That is not always the best option.
Example 4, continued. In the same example, we can allow an interaction between the two predictors using the operator : in the formula.

new_model <- lm(office_exp ~ staff + terrain + staff:terrain - 1, data = bdo)
coef(new_model)

              staff        terrainPlain        terrainHilly       terrainTribal 
         0.41006413         12.31432196         13.90042255         11.71979650 
 staff:terrainHilly staff:terrainTribal 
         0.09110541          0.04145620 


Notice the two extra coefficients. Each is the change in slope when we move from the baseline terrain, Plain, to Hilly or to Tribal. So the model now has a different slope for each terrain. See Figure 38.7.







Figure 38.7: Changing slopes with interaction




Let us see the summary.

summary(new_model)


Call:
lm(formula = office_exp ~ staff + terrain + staff:terrain - 1, 
    data = bdo)

Residuals:
    Min      1Q  Median      3Q     Max 
-6.1826 -1.5569  0.1208  1.5467  9.3339 

Coefficients:
                    Estimate Std. Error t value Pr(>|t|)    
staff                0.41006    0.03737  10.972  < 2e-16 ***
terrainPlain        12.31432    1.40597   8.759 2.12e-14 ***
terrainHilly        13.90042    1.37275  10.126  < 2e-16 ***
terrainTribal       11.71980    1.78908   6.551 1.72e-09 ***
staff:terrainHilly   0.09111    0.06685   1.363    0.176    
staff:terrainTribal  0.04146    0.06680   0.621    0.536    
---
Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1

Residual standard error: 2.499 on 114 degrees of freedom
Multiple R-squared:  0.9918,    Adjusted R-squared:  0.9914 
F-statistic:  2294 on 6 and 114 DF,  p-value: < 2.2e-16


We may write the equation now (Equation 38.6).
\[
\begin{aligned}
\text{Office expenses} = {} & 0.4101 \cdot \text{Staff} + 12.3143 \cdot \text{Plain} + 13.9004 \cdot \text{Hilly} + 11.7198 \cdot \text{Tribal} \\
& + 0.0911 \cdot \text{Staff} \cdot \text{Hilly} + 0.0415 \cdot \text{Staff} \cdot \text{Tribal}
\end{aligned}
\tag{38.6}\]
So for offices in the hills, the slope of staff is \(0.4101 + 0.0911\), or 0.5012. But look at the p-values of the two interaction terms, 0.18 and 0.54. They are far above 0.05. So the data does not give us any real evidence that the slopes differ between the terrains. The three lines in Figure 38.7 are nearly parallel too. Here the simpler parallel slopes model is good enough. Always check whether an interaction is significant before reading meaning into it. We will see an interaction which does matter in Section 38.9.
We can add as many interactions as we like using :. When there are many, we can use another shorthand, *. So x*z means x + z + x:z, and x*z*w means x + z + w + x:z + x:w + z:w + x:z:w. It does not change the model, but saves a lot of typing.

title: 38  Multiple Regression in Audit
section: 38.5 Multi-collinearity and the variance inflation factor (VIF)
text:
38.5 Multi-collinearity and the variance inflation factor (VIF)
Multi-collinearity means that the predictor variables are strongly related to each other. This creates a problem. When two predictors move together, the model cannot tell which of them is really affecting \(y\). The coefficient estimates become unstable. A small change in the data can change them a lot, sometimes even flip their sign. Their standard errors become large, so useful variables may look insignificant. We saw this with area_sqm in Example 2.
Note that multi-collinearity does not spoil the predictions of the model much. It spoils our ability to interpret the individual coefficients. For an auditor, who usually wants to explain a finding, that matters.
There are many ways to detect multi-collinearity. One is to use correlation plots, as in Figure 38.2. Another is the Variance Inflation Factor or VIF. To find the VIF of a predictor, we regress it on all the other predictors and note the \(R^2\) of that regression. The VIF score thus tells us how well a predictor is explained by the other predictors.
\[
{VIF} = \frac{1}{1-R^2}
\tag{38.7}\]
So the closer this \(R^2\) is to \(1\), the higher the \({VIF}\).


\(VIF\) starts at \(1\) and has no upper limit.

\({VIF} = 1\) means the predictor is not related to the other predictors at all.

\({VIF}\) above \(5\) is commonly taken to indicate a problem, and above \(10\) a serious one.

In R, we do not have to calculate \({VIF}\) by hand. The function vif() from the package car does it. Let us first check our model of Example 2.

car::vif(lin_reg2)

        staff      area_sqm beneficiaries 
     7.507741      7.599050      1.109000 


The VIFs of staff and area_sqm are 7.5 and 7.6, both above 5. That confirms what we suspected. The VIF of beneficiaries is close to 1, so it brings its own information. Now let us try a model where office expenses are explained by all the numeric columns of our data. Sanctioned posts move with staff in position, and beneficiaries move with the population of the block. We again use the shorthand . for all other variables.

bdo_num <- bdo |>
  select(office_exp, staff, sanctioned, area_sqm, population, beneficiaries)
mod <- lm(office_exp ~ . , data = bdo_num)
car::vif(mod)

        staff    sanctioned      area_sqm    population beneficiaries 
    46.598673     39.612223      7.630437     16.333157     16.109711 


Four predictors here have a VIF above 10. Such a model would be hard to interpret. In practice, we would keep only one predictor from each related pair, the one which makes more business sense. For office expenses, staff in position matters more than sanctioned posts, because vacant posts spend nothing.






TipAudit tip



Many indicators in government data come in related pairs. Sanctioned posts and staff in position, population and beneficiaries, budget and expenditure, length and cost of a road. Putting both members of a pair in one model rarely helps. Pick the one closer to the actual cause of the expenditure. Chapter 43 shows another way, which combines related indicators into one.

title: 38  Multiple Regression in Audit
section: 38.6 Audit use case, block offices with inflated expenses
text:
38.6 Audit use case, block offices with inflated expenses
Let us now return to the two block offices we planted. We have learnt a good deal about their data. Office expenses rise with staff and with beneficiaries. Offices in the hills and tribal areas spend more for the same size. Floor area, sanctioned posts and population add little once staff and beneficiaries are in the model. So the model which makes business sense uses staff, beneficiaries and terrain.

bdo_final <- lm(office_exp ~ staff + beneficiaries + terrain, data = bdo)
summary(bdo_final)


Call:
lm(formula = office_exp ~ staff + beneficiaries + terrain, data = bdo)

Residuals:
    Min      1Q  Median      3Q     Max 
-5.4439 -1.0171  0.0541  1.1266  9.4715 

Coefficients:
              Estimate Std. Error t value Pr(>|t|)    
(Intercept)    6.86558    1.04020   6.600 1.32e-09 ***
staff          0.42329    0.02250  18.812  < 2e-16 ***
beneficiaries  0.10770    0.01459   7.380 2.68e-11 ***
terrainHilly   5.38553    0.56025   9.613  < 2e-16 ***
terrainTribal  2.62761    0.54161   4.851 3.88e-06 ***
---
Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1

Residual standard error: 2.066 on 115 degrees of freedom
Multiple R-squared:  0.8005,    Adjusted R-squared:  0.7936 
F-statistic: 115.4 on 4 and 115 DF,  p-value: < 2.2e-16


All the predictors are significant, and the model explains 80% of the variation in office expenses, against 60% with staff alone. The residual standard error has come down from ₹2.90 lakh to ₹2.07 lakh. Now let us find the offices which spend more than expected, with augment().

augment(bdo_final, data = bdo) |>
  mutate(excess = office_exp - .fitted) |>
  arrange(desc(.std.resid)) |>
  select(office_id, district, staff, beneficiaries, office_exp, .fitted, excess, .std.resid) |>
  head(5)

# A tibble: 5 × 8
  office_id district   staff beneficiaries office_exp .fitted excess .std.resid
  <chr>     <chr>      <dbl>         <dbl>      <dbl>   <dbl>  <dbl>      <dbl>
1 BDO-088   Firozpur      27          46         32.7    23.2   9.47       4.65
2 BDO-027   Sitapur       26          18.9       26.4    19.9   6.47       3.24
3 BDO-074   Mayurbhanj    40          37.1       33.6    30.4   3.19       1.58
4 BDO-115   Etawah        34          33         28.0    24.8   3.15       1.54
5 BDO-010   Firozpur      46          37         33.4    30.3   3.06       1.51


Two offices, BDO-088 and BDO-027, have standardised residuals above 3. They are exactly the two offices we planted. Together they spent about ₹15.9 lakh more than expected. No other office comes close.
Why did BDO-027 hide in the model of staff alone, in Chapter 37? Let us compare it under both models.

bind_rows(
  augment(lin_reg1, data = bdo) |> mutate(model = "Staff only"),
  augment(bdo_final, data = bdo) |> mutate(model = "Staff, beneficiaries, terrain")
) |>
  filter(office_id == "BDO-027") |>
  select(model, staff, beneficiaries, office_exp, .fitted, .std.resid)

# A tibble: 2 × 6
  model                        staff beneficiaries office_exp .fitted .std.resid
  <chr>                        <dbl>         <dbl>      <dbl>   <dbl>      <dbl>
1 Staff only                      26          18.9       26.4    24.5      0.635
2 Staff, beneficiaries, terra…    26          18.9       26.4    19.9      3.24 


BDO-027 serves only 18.9 thousand beneficiaries, against an average of 38.0 thousand. An office of its size with so few beneficiaries should spend less than the average. The model with staff alone did not know this. It expected the expenses of an average office of that size, and the inflated bill looked normal against it. Once beneficiaries are in the model, the expected expenses fall, and the inflation stands out.






WarningCaution



A model that leaves out an important driver does more than fit badly. It can hide an irregularity, as it hid BDO-027, or point to innocent offices, as it pointed to the offices in the hills. Before trusting the residuals, make sure the model includes every driver which the business suggests.


What would the auditor do next? For each of the two offices, we would call for the vehicle hire bills, the log books of the vehicles and the sanction for hiring them. Bills without matching log book entries, or log books written up in one hand at the end of the year, are common signs of payments for vehicles never used. We would ask the office to explain the excess in writing, and record the model, the flagged offices and the replies in the working papers.

title: 38  Multiple Regression in Audit
section: 38.7 A complete example, cost of rural road works
text:
38.7 A complete example, cost of rural road works
Example 5. Let us now go through the whole process on a different audit dataset. A state builds rural roads under a scheme. We have 90 road works completed in five financial years, 2019-20 to 2023-24. For each work we know


cost_lakh, the cost per kilometre, in ₹ lakh,

width_m, the width of the carriageway in metres,

hilly_pct, the percentage of the road length in hilly terrain,

lead_km, the distance from the quarry, from which stone is carried,

rain_cm, the average annual rainfall of the area, in centimetres,

bitumen_k, the rate of bitumen in the year of the work, in ₹ thousand per tonne, and

year_no, the year of the work, from 1 for 2019-20 to 5 for 2023-24.

The cost of a road should depend on its width, the terrain, the lead and the price of bitumen. The auditor would like a model of the expected cost per kilometre. Works which cost far more than expected can then be picked for detailed examination of their estimates and measurement books.

Code to create the road works dataset.seed(2411)
n <- 90
roads <- tibble(
  work_id   = sprintf("RW-%03d", 1:n),
  fin_year  = sample(2019:2023, n, replace = TRUE),
  width_m   = sample(c(3, 3.75, 5.5), n, replace = TRUE, prob = c(0.4, 0.4, 0.2)),
  hilly_pct = round(100 * rbeta(n, 0.7, 1.8)),
  lead_km   = round(runif(n, 5, 60)),
  rain_cm   = round(runif(n, 60, 250))
) |>
  mutate(
    # bitumen rate rises every year
    bitumen_k = round(38 + 3.5 * (fin_year - 2019) + rnorm(n, 0, 1.5), 1),
    year_no   = fin_year - 2018,
    # rainfall has no effect on cost in this data
    cost_lakh = round(20 + 9 * width_m + 0.22 * hilly_pct + 0.12 * lead_km +
                      0.8 * bitumen_k + rnorm(n, 0, 8), 1)
  )
# Keep only the response and the predictors, for the model
road_vars <- roads |>
  select(cost_lakh, width_m, hilly_pct, lead_km, rain_cm, bitumen_k, year_no)



# See the first 6 rows
head(road_vars)

# A tibble: 6 × 7
  cost_lakh width_m hilly_pct lead_km rain_cm bitumen_k year_no
      <dbl>   <dbl>     <dbl>   <dbl>   <dbl>     <dbl>   <dbl>
1     104.     3.75        35      24      91      47         4
2      95.4    3           15      13     102      42.3       3
3     132.     5.5         72      35     240      50.1       4
4     100.     3.75        59      21     164      37.7       1
5     102.     5.5          2      24     200      49.6       4

# Build a model
ex1 <- lm(cost_lakh ~ . , data = road_vars)

Multiple R-squared is about 68%. But look at bitumen_k. Its slope is -0.087, which would mean that roads get cheaper as bitumen gets costlier. Its p-value is 0.88. Something is not right. Let us see some diagnostic plots (Figure 38.8).

performance::check_model(ex1)






Figure 38.8: Diagnostic plots




We can notice high collinearity between bitumen_k and year_no in Figure 38.8. It is clearly visible in Figure 38.9. The rate of bitumen rose every year, so the two move together.

road_vars %>%
  ggplot(aes(year_no, bitumen_k)) +
  geom_point()+
  geom_smooth(method = 'lm', formula = 'y~x') +
  labs(x = "Year of work (1 is 2019-20)", y = "Bitumen rate (₹ thousand per tonne)") +

Figure 38.9: Are the year and the bitumen rate correlated?




This can also be seen in the correlation plots in Figure 38.10.







Figure 38.10: Correlation plots




Let us see the VIF of the predictors.

car::vif(ex1)

  width_m hilly_pct   lead_km   rain_cm bitumen_k   year_no 
 1.071049  1.089254  1.146704  1.192879 14.623986 14.823085 


Both bitumen_k and year_no have a VIF above 5. The other predictors have a VIF close to 1. So let us remove one of the pair. The bitumen rate is the actual cause of the change in cost, while the year only stands in for it. So we remove year_no and re-run the model.

ex2 <- lm(cost_lakh ~ width_m + hilly_pct + lead_km + rain_cm + bitumen_k, data = road_vars)
summary(ex2)


Call:

    bitumen_k, data = road_vars)

(Intercept) 24.84885    9.18404   2.706 0.008254 ** 
width_m      8.56951    0.99032   8.653 2.96e-13 ***
hilly_pct    0.24861    0.03214   7.734 2.06e-11 ***

Multiple R-squared has dropped a little, to 67.3%. That is expected, since R-squared never rises when we remove a variable. But look at what we gained. The slope of bitumen_k is now 0.659, positive as it should be. Its standard error has fallen from 0.598 to 0.162. Its estimate is now much more precise. Let us also remove rain_cm, whose coefficient is not significant.

ex3 <- lm(cost_lakh ~ width_m + hilly_pct + lead_km + bitumen_k, data = road_vars)
summary(ex3)


Call:

    data = road_vars)

Residuals:

-21.8051  -5.5384  -0.2481   4.1768  20.7802 

Coefficients:

(Intercept) 28.22990    7.98257   3.536 0.000660 ***
width_m      8.49810    0.98320   8.643 2.85e-13 ***
hilly_pct    0.24337    0.03129   7.777 1.59e-11 ***
lead_km      0.14085    0.05517   2.553 0.012471 *  
bitumen_k    0.63868    0.15915   4.013 0.000129 ***
---
Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1

Residual standard error: 7.675 on 85 degrees of freedom
Multiple R-squared:  0.6708,    Adjusted R-squared:  0.6553 
F-statistic:  43.3 on 4 and 85 DF,  p-value: < 2.2e-16


Multiple R-squared falls slightly again, to 67.1%. But adjusted R-squared stays almost the same (0.6535 before, 0.6553 now). So rain_cm was adding nothing useful, and the simpler model with four predictors does as well as the one with five. All of its coefficients are significant. When two models explain the data about equally well, we prefer the simpler one.
Now the model reads sensibly. A road 1 metre wider costs about ₹8.5 lakh more per kilometre. Each 10 percentage points of hilly length add about ₹2.4 lakh per kilometre. A rise of ₹1,000 per tonne in the bitumen rate adds about ₹0.64 lakh per kilometre. The auditor can compare these with the schedule of rates. If the model says that terrain or lead adds much more than the rates allow, the estimates deserve a look.
Let us visualise one of the main relationships through a scatter plot.

road_vars %>%
  ggplot(aes(hilly_pct, cost_lakh)) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_smooth(method = 'lm', formula = 'y ~ x', se = FALSE) +
  labs(x = "Hilly length (%)", y = "Cost per km (₹ lakh)") +
  theme_bw()






Figure 38.11: Ascertaining linear relationship




The relationship between hilly length and cost is real, but the points are widely scattered around the line. That is because width, lead and the bitumen rate also vary from work to work. Only the model with all of them together explains about two thirds of the variation. The rest is due to things this data does not have, like soil, culverts and the quality of the contractor’s work.

title: 38  Multiple Regression in Audit
text:
38.8 Simpson’s paradox
Edward Hugh Simpson, a statistician and former cryptanalyst at Bletchley Park, described this phenomenon in a paper in 1951. It is a classic example of how a regression that leaves out an important variable can mislead. The paradox arises when a trend seen in each subgroup of the data reverses or disappears when the subgroups are combined. We saw a mild form of it in Example 4, where terrain seemed not to matter until we compared offices of the same size.
Example 6. A health department runs 60 hospitals of three types. There are primary health centres (PHCs), community health centres (CHCs) and district hospitals. For each we know the number of patients treated in the year (patients, in thousand) and the cost per patient (cost_pp, in ₹). Does a hospital that treats more patients spend less per patient? Let us try to establish a relationship between the two. See the plots in Figure 38.12.

Code to create the hospital dataset.seed(77)
hosp_types <- c("PHC", "CHC", "District hospital")
hosp <- tibble(type = factor(rep(hosp_types, each = 20), levels = hosp_types)) |>
  mutate(
    patients = round(case_when(type == "PHC" ~ runif(n(), 5, 15),
                               type == "CHC" ~ runif(n(), 18, 35),
                               TRUE          ~ runif(n(), 40, 80)), 1),
    # within each type, cost per patient falls as the number of patients grows
    base    = c(PHC = 950, CHC = 1700, "District hospital" = 3300)[as.character(type)],
    centre  = c(PHC = 10, CHC = 26, "District hospital" = 60)[as.character(type)],
    cost_pp = round(base - 18 * (patients - centre) + rnorm(n(), 0, 80))
  ) |>
  select(type, patients, cost_pp)




















Figure 38.12: Regression having variable hidden (left) and exposed (right)


In the left plot, the relationship is positive. Hospitals treating more patients seem to spend more per patient. But when the hidden variable type is exposed (right), we see a negative relationship within each type. A busier PHC costs less per patient than a quieter PHC, and the same holds for CHCs and district hospitals. Let us confirm this with two models.

coef(lm(cost_pp ~ patients, data = hosp))

(Intercept)    patients 
  638.36759    41.53393 

coef(lm(cost_pp ~ patients + type, data = hosp))

          (Intercept)              patients               typeCHC 
           1126.86491             -19.10646            1086.58582 
typeDistrict hospital 
           3296.68779 


Without type, the slope of patients is 41.53. Once type is in the model, it becomes -19.11. The sign has flipped. Type of hospital is a confounding variable here. District hospitals treat more patients and treat costlier cases. An auditor who compared all hospitals together might wrongly conclude that busy hospitals are wasteful. So before finalising a model, we must make sure that we are not missing an important variable. To avoid being misled by Simpson’s paradox, we should


Identify confounding variables. Think about what else could affect both variables under study.

Consider all levels. Analyse the data at the subgroup level and at the combined level, and compare.

Use statistical techniques such as multiple regression, as we just did, to control for confounding variables.

Report transparently. Clearly state the method, assumptions and limitations of the analysis so that others can evaluate the findings.







TipAudit tip



Simpson’s paradox is common in audit data. A scheme may show a falling rejection rate in every district, yet a rising rate for the state as a whole, because the mix of districts has changed. Before reporting a trend on combined data, always check it within the main subgroups, like districts, years, or types of contract.

title: 38  Multiple Regression in Audit
section: 38.9 Audit use case, offices that spend more than expected
text:
38.9 Audit use case, offices that spend more than expected
We have used regression on audit data throughout this chapter. Let us now put it all together on the question with which we started. Salary expenditure of an office should depend mainly on its staff strength. If an office spends far more than its staff strength explains, it may have ghost employees on its pay roll, or other irregular payments. Regression gives us an expected expenditure for every office. The residual is then the unexplained part. Large positive residuals are our leads.

38.9.1 Our sample data
We create the data of 90 sub-divisional offices (SDOs) of an imaginary department. For each office we have its staff strength, the class of the city where it is located, and its monthly salary expenditure in ₹ lakh. House rent allowance (HRA) is 30%, 20% and 10% of pay in X, Y and Z class cities respectively. So, for the same staff, an office in an X class city spends more.
We have planted a few cases.

Three offices have salary expenditure inflated by 16%, as if ghost employees were added.
In one office, the staff strength was keyed in with an extra zero.

As before, new readers may skip the code which creates the data.

Code to create the sample office dataset.seed(2026)
n <- 90
offices <- tibble(
  office_id  = sprintf("SDO-%02d", 1:n),
  city_class = factor(sample(c("X", "Y", "Z"), n, replace = TRUE,
                             prob = c(0.2, 0.4, 0.4)),
                      levels = c("Z", "Y", "X")),
  staff      = sample(8:60, n, replace = TRUE)
) |>
  mutate(hra    = c(Z = 0.10, Y = 0.20, X = 0.30)[as.character(city_class)],
         # about ₹0.85 lakh basic cost per employee, plus HRA, plus noise
         salary = round(staff * 0.85 * (1 + hra) + rnorm(n, 0, 1.2), 2)) |>
  select(-hra)

# Planted case 1. Ghost employees, salary inflated by 16%
ghost <- c("SDO-17", "SDO-44", "SDO-63")
offices <- offices |>
  mutate(salary = if_else(office_id %in% ghost, round(salary * 1.16, 2), salary))

# Planted case 2. Staff strength keyed in with an extra zero
offices <- offices |>
  mutate(staff = if_else(office_id == "SDO-81", staff * 10L, staff))



head(offices)

# A tibble: 6 × 4
  office_id city_class staff salary
  <chr>     <fct>      <int>  <dbl>
1 SDO-01    Z             11   9.67
2 SDO-02    Z             36  33.8 
3 SDO-03    Y             15  14.3 
4 SDO-04    Y             45  46.3 
5 SDO-05    Z             23  23.6 
6 SDO-06    Y             13  14.1 



38.9.2 First model, and a surprise
Let us fit a model of salary on staff strength and city class.

off_m1 <- lm(salary ~ staff + city_class, data = offices)
summary(off_m1)


Call:
lm(formula = salary ~ staff + city_class, data = offices)

Residuals:
     Min       1Q   Median       3Q      Max 
-28.4279  -9.3392  -0.3861  10.1467  25.8925 

Coefficients:
            Estimate Std. Error t value Pr(>|t|)    
(Intercept) 32.16193    2.45813  13.084  < 2e-16 ***
staff        0.09919    0.02362   4.199 6.51e-05 ***
city_classY -0.52788    3.18400  -0.166    0.869    
city_classX  1.53420    4.00355   0.383    0.703    
---
Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1

Residual standard error: 13.54 on 86 degrees of freedom
Multiple R-squared:  0.1708,    Adjusted R-squared:  0.1419 
F-statistic: 5.906 on 3 and 86 DF,  p-value: 0.001031


Something is wrong. Salary expenditure must surely rise steeply with staff strength. Yet the slope of staff is only 0.099 lakh per employee, and R-squared is only 17%. Let us look at the influence of each office, using augment() and Cook’s distance.

augment(off_m1, data = offices) |>
  arrange(desc(.cooksd)) |>
  select(office_id, staff, salary, .fitted, .hat, .cooksd) |>
  head(4)

# A tibble: 4 × 6
  office_id staff salary .fitted   .hat  .cooksd
  <chr>     <int>  <dbl>   <dbl>  <dbl>    <dbl>
1 SDO-81      600  62.7     91.1 0.948  384.    
2 SDO-80        9   7.93    34.6 0.0607   0.0667
3 SDO-84       60  65.5     39.6 0.0609   0.0632
4 SDO-08       58  64.3     39.4 0.0606   0.0580


One office, SDO-81, has a Cook’s distance of 384, where the rest are below 0.1. Its staff strength is shown as 600, while no other office has more than 60. Its leverage (.hat) is close to 1, the maximum possible. This single wrong entry has pulled the whole line towards itself. Figure 38.13 shows this.

ggplot(offices, aes(staff, salary)) +
  geom_point(aes(color = office_id == "SDO-81"), show.legend = FALSE) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", formula = "y ~ x", se = FALSE) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c("grey40", "red")) +
  labs(x = "Staff strength (as recorded)", y = "Monthly salary (₹ lakh)") +
  theme_bw()






Figure 38.13: One wrong entry (red) pulls the whole line










TipAudit tip



Always check Cook’s distance and leverage before reading the residuals. A single data entry error with an extreme value can spoil the whole model. It then makes genuine outliers look normal, and normal offices look odd. Such an entry is itself an audit finding about the quality of the data.


On checking the records, suppose we find that the office actually has 60 staff. We should correct the entry. Here we simply keep it aside and re-fit.

38.9.3 A better model
HRA is a percentage of pay. So each extra employee in an X class city costs more than an extra employee in a Z class city. In other words, the slope of staff should be different for each city class. This is exactly what an interaction does. Let us fit both the parallel slopes model and the interaction model on the clean data, and compare them.

clean <- offices |> filter(office_id != "SDO-81")

off_m2 <- lm(salary ~ staff + city_class, data = clean)
off_m3 <- lm(salary ~ staff * city_class, data = clean)
summary(off_m3)


Call:
lm(formula = salary ~ staff * city_class, data = clean)

Residuals:
    Min      1Q  Median      3Q     Max 
-2.6904 -1.0081 -0.0339  0.6564  6.1181 

Coefficients:
                  Estimate Std. Error t value Pr(>|t|)    
(Intercept)        0.32799    0.70731   0.464  0.64406    
staff              0.93692    0.01751  53.514  < 2e-16 ***
city_classY        0.17978    0.96590   0.186  0.85280    
city_classX       -1.18493    1.06279  -1.115  0.26810    
staff:city_classY  0.07495    0.02482   3.019  0.00337 ** 
staff:city_classX  0.18740    0.02749   6.816 1.39e-09 ***
---
Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1

Residual standard error: 1.42 on 83 degrees of freedom
Multiple R-squared:  0.9909,    Adjusted R-squared:  0.9903 
F-statistic:  1798 on 5 and 83 DF,  p-value: < 2.2e-16


Both interaction terms are significant. For every extra employee, the expected salary goes up by 0.94 lakh in a Z class city, and by 1.12 lakh in an X class city. R-squared is now 99.1%.
To check formally whether the interaction model is better, we can compare the two models with anova(). It tests whether the extra terms reduce the residuals by more than chance would.

anova(off_m2, off_m3)

Analysis of Variance Table

Model 1: salary ~ staff + city_class
Model 2: salary ~ staff * city_class
  Res.Df    RSS Df Sum of Sq     F    Pr(>F)    
1     85 261.20                                 
2     83 167.46  2    93.736 23.23 9.733e-09 ***
---
Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1


The p-value is very small, so the interaction model is clearly better. Its residual standard error is 1.42 lakh, against 1.75 lakh for the parallel slopes model. The more accurate our expected values are, the easier it is to spot offices which do not fit.

38.9.4 Finding the offices
Now let us look at the residuals. Raw residuals are in lakh. To judge how unusual each one is, we use the standardised residual (.std.resid). It is the residual divided by its standard error, so it is on a common scale. Under our assumptions, values beyond 3 are very rare, about 3 in 1,000. Let us also calculate the excess expenditure in rupees.

flagged <- augment(off_m3, data = clean) |>
  mutate(excess = salary - .fitted) |>
  arrange(desc(.std.resid)) |>
  select(office_id, staff, city_class, salary, .fitted, excess, .std.resid)

head(flagged, 5)

# A tibble: 5 × 7
  office_id staff city_class salary .fitted excess .std.resid
  <chr>     <int> <fct>       <dbl>   <dbl>  <dbl>      <dbl>
1 SDO-63       41 Z            44.9    38.7   6.12       4.37
2 SDO-44       28 Z            31.4    26.6   4.79       3.45
3 SDO-79       28 Y            31.3    28.8   2.42       1.73
4 SDO-17       27 Z            27.7    25.6   2.10       1.51
5 SDO-88       30 X            34.8    32.9   1.89       1.37


Two offices, SDO-63 and SDO-44, have standardised residuals above 3. Together they spend about ₹10.9 lakh a month, or about ₹1.3 crore a year, more than expected. Both are planted ghost employee cases. They are clearly our first leads.
The third planted office, SDO-17, has a standardised residual of only 1.51. Its excess of ₹2.1 lakh is within the normal variation between offices. Regression cannot separate it from genuine offices. Let us see all of this in Figure 38.14.

augment(off_m3, data = clean) |>
  ggplot(aes(.fitted, .std.resid)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = c(-3, 3), linetype = 2, color = "red") +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, color = "grey50") +
  geom_point(aes(color = office_id %in% ghost)) +
  geom_text(data = \(d) filter(d, abs(.std.resid) > 3 | office_id %in% ghost),
            aes(label = office_id), vjust = -0.8, size = 3) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c("grey40", "red"),
                     labels = c("Other offices", "Planted cases")) +
  labs(x = "Expected salary (₹ lakh)", y = "Standardised residual", color = NULL) +
  theme_bw() +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")






Figure 38.14: Standardised residuals of offices. Offices beyond 3 are leads.










WarningCaution



Regression finds only those deviations which are large compared to the normal variation between offices. A small office with a few ghost employees, like SDO-17, can hide in that variation. So a clean result from regression does not prove that there is no fraud. For individual offices, it must be followed by other tests, like matching the pay roll with the attendance and bank account data (see Chapter 32).








NoteWhat about large negative residuals?



Offices which spend much less than expected may also deserve a look. The reason may be vacant posts, salary not paid on time, or expenditure booked under the wrong head. Here no office has a standardised residual below -3.



38.9.5 What the auditor does next
The model has given us 2 leads and one data quality finding. None of them is yet an audit finding. For each lead, we would

obtain the pay roll of the office for a few months, and count the employees actually paid against the staff strength reported,
match the employees paid with the attendance register, the service books and the bank accounts into which pay was credited, looking for the same account shared by two employees, or employees who never mark attendance,
ask the office to explain the excess of about ₹10.9 lakh a month, in writing, and
record the model, the residuals and the replies in the working papers, so that the selection of these offices can be justified later.

The keying error in the staff strength of SDO-81 should be reported as a weakness in the data, because the same figure may be used elsewhere, for example to sanction posts or to allot funds.

title: 38  Multiple Regression in Audit
text:
38.10 Uses of regression in audit
We have seen that regression analysis is a powerful tool for an auditor. It may be used, among other things, for the following.


Detection of anomalies and outliers. As in our office examples, regression gives the expected value of an amount based on its drivers. Large residuals point to transactions or units which do not fit, and these may be errors, irregularities or fraud.

Analytical procedures. The auditor can estimate what an expenditure should be, say fuel cost from vehicle kilometres, or electricity charges from the connected load, and compare it with what was booked.

Risk assessment. Units with large unexplained deviations can be ranked and taken up first in the audit plan. This helps the auditor use limited time and staff well.

Benchmarking. Regression can compare the performance of an organisation with similar ones, after adjusting for size and other factors. Deviations from the expected relationship highlight areas that deserve a closer look. The cost of road works per kilometre, adjusted for width, terrain and lead, is one example.

title: 38  Multiple Regression in Audit
text:
38.11 A suggested workflow
For any regression analysis in audit, we may follow these steps.


Understand the drivers. Decide, from knowledge of the business, which variables should explain the amount under audit. Regression only confirms or rejects relationships which make sense.

Visualise first. Draw scatter plots and box plots to see whether the relationships look linear, and to spot obvious errors.

Fit a simple model with lm(), and read its summary().

Check influence. Look at Cook’s distance and leverage. Investigate and correct data entry errors before going further.

Check the assumptions with plot() or check_model(). Check multi-collinearity with vif() when there are several predictors, and keep only one predictor from each related pair.

Improve the model. Add factors and interactions that make business sense. Watch for hidden variables which can reverse a trend. Compare models with adjusted R-squared or anova().

Flag the residuals. Use augment() and pick the units with large standardised residuals. Quantify the excess in rupees.

Verify with records. Examine the documents of the flagged units before drawing any conclusion.







ImportantRemember



A regression model shows association, not cause. A large residual means only that a unit does not fit the pattern of the others. It is a lead, not a finding. There may be a genuine reason which the model does not know about. Always examine the records before reporting.
crumbs: Part VI: Modelling and Risk Scoring

title: 38  Multiple Regression in Audit
text:
38.12 Where next
Linear regression predicts a number. When the audit question has a yes or no answer, like whether a claim is irregular, we use logistic regression, in Chapter 39. When many indicators are related to each other, Chapter 43 shows how to combine them before modelling.

title: 39  Logistic Regression for Risk Scoring
text:
39.1 From a straight line to an S-curve
In Chapter 37 and Chapter 38 we used linear regression to predict a number, like the expected expenditure of an office. Many audit questions, though, have a yes or no answer. Was this refund claim irregular? Will this contract overrun? Is this beneficiary ineligible? We cannot examine every case, so we would like to know, before examining them, which cases are most likely to be a “yes”.
Logistic regression answers exactly this. It learns from cases whose outcome is already known, like claims examined in last year’s audit, how the chance of a “yes” depends on the features of a case. It then gives every new case a risk score, the estimated probability of a “yes”. Examining the highest-scoring cases first finds far more irregularities for the same effort than picking cases at random.
Logistic regression is the workhorse of risk scoring in tax departments, banks and insurers. For auditors it has one more virtue. Its results can be explained in plain words, “claims of merchant exporters had about twice the odds of being irregular”, which matters when a selection has to be justified.
Prerequisites
Why not use linear regression for a yes/no outcome, coding “yes” as 1 and “no” as 0? Because a straight line goes on rising, or falling, for ever. For large enough values it predicts “probabilities” above 1 or below 0, which make no sense.
Logistic regression instead fits an S-shaped curve, which always stays between 0 and 1. It rises slowly at first, then steeply, and then flattens out as it approaches 1.
tibble(x = seq(-6, 6, by = 0.1)) |>
  ggplot(aes(x, plogis(x))) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = c(0, 1), linetype = "dashed", colour = "grey50") +
  labs(x = "Combined risk from all features (log-odds)", y = "Probability of 'yes'") +
  theme_minimal()



The logistic curve stays between 0 and 1
To understand the output, we need one idea, the odds. The odds of an event are the chance that it happens divided by the chance that it does not.
Logistic regression is a linear regression, not on the probability itself, but on the logarithm of the odds (the log-odds). We need not work with log-odds directly. What matters is how to read the result. Each coefficient, converted with exp(), becomes an odds ratio, the number by which the odds are multiplied when that feature increases by one unit. An odds ratio of 2 doubles the odds, 1 leaves them unchanged, and 0.5 halves them.

A probability of 0.5 is odds of 0.5/0.5 = 1, often said “1 to 1” or “evens”.
A probability of 0.2 is odds of 0.2/0.8 = 0.25, or “1 to 4”.
A probability of 0.8 is odds of 0.8/0.2 = 4, or “4 to 1”.

section: 39.2 Our data, last year’s refund audit
text:
39.2 Our data, last year’s refund audit
Exporters can claim a refund of the GST paid on their inputs. Refunds are a known risk area, because fake input tax credit, claimed on invoices from suppliers who never paid the tax, can be turned into cash. Last year, the audit party examined 2,000 refund claims in detail, and recorded whether each was found irregular. For each claim we know


exporter_type, a manufacturer or a merchant exporter (who buys goods and exports them without manufacturing),

reg_months, how many months the claimant had been registered under GST,

amount_lakh, the refund claimed, in ₹ lakh,

nonfiler_pct, the percentage of the claimant’s input tax credit which came from suppliers who had not filed their own returns,

irregular, the outcome of the audit.


Code to create the refund claimsmake_claims <- function(n, prefix) {
  tibble(
    claim_id      = sprintf("%s-%04d", prefix, 1:n),
    exporter_type = sample(c("Manufacturer", "Merchant"), n, TRUE, prob = c(0.65, 0.35)),
    reg_months    = pmax(1, round(rexp(n, 1 / 40))),
    amount_lakh   = round(rlnorm(n, log(8), 1), 2),
    nonfiler_pct  = round(100 * rbeta(n, 0.6, 6), 1)
  ) |>
    # The true risk, unknown to the auditor: higher for merchants, for claimants
    # registered less than a year ago, for larger claims, and above all for
    # credit from non-filing suppliers
    mutate(true_logodds = -4.3 + 1.1 * (exporter_type == "Merchant") +
             1.5 * (reg_months < 12) + 0.3 * log(amount_lakh) + 0.08 * nonfiler_pct,
           irregular = runif(n) < plogis(true_logodds)) |>
    select(-true_logodds)
}
set.seed(2028)

title: 39  Logistic Regression for Risk Scoring
text:
39.4 Training and test data
A model always fits the data it learnt from better than new data, just as a student does best on questions already seen. To judge honestly how well it will work on new claims, we keep part of the data aside. The model learns from 70% of the claims, the training set, and is judged on the remaining 30%, the test set, which it has never seen.

set.seed(7)
train_rows <- sample(nrow(past), size = 0.7 * nrow(past))
train <- past[train_rows, ]
test  <- past[-train_rows, ]
c(train = nrow(train), test = nrow(test))

train  test 
 1400   600

title: 39  Logistic Regression for Risk Scoring
text:
39.5 Fitting the model
Logistic regression is fitted with glm(), the function for generalised linear models. The formula is written as in lm(). The argument family = binomial makes it a logistic regression. Since amounts are skewed, we use the logarithm of the amount, as is usual for money.

model1 <- glm(irregular ~ exporter_type + reg_months + log(amount_lakh) + nonfiler_pct,
              family = binomial, data = train)
summary(model1)


Call:
glm(formula = irregular ~ exporter_type + reg_months + log(amount_lakh) + 
    nonfiler_pct, family = binomial, data = train)

Coefficients:
                       Estimate Std. Error z value Pr(>|z|)    
(Intercept)           -3.208706   0.271141 -11.834  < 2e-16 ***
exporter_typeMerchant  1.241768   0.174881   7.101 1.24e-12 ***
reg_months            -0.014396   0.002945  -4.888 1.02e-06 ***
log(amount_lakh)       0.206591   0.089481   2.309    0.021 *  
nonfiler_pct           0.082169   0.007209  11.399  < 2e-16 ***
---
Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1

(Dispersion parameter for binomial family taken to be 1)

    Null deviance: 1155.47  on 1399  degrees of freedom
Residual deviance:  933.44  on 1395  degrees of freedom
AIC: 943.44

Number of Fisher Scoring iterations: 6


The output looks like that of lm(). Every feature has a small p-value, so each is related to the risk. But the coefficients are in log-odds, which are hard to read. broom::tidy() with exponentiate = TRUE converts them into odds ratios, with confidence intervals.

or1 <- tidy(model1, exponentiate = TRUE, conf.int = TRUE)
or1 |> mutate(across(where(is.numeric), \(x) round(x, 3)))

# A tibble: 5 × 7
  term                  estimate std.error statistic p.value conf.low conf.high
  <chr>                    <dbl>     <dbl>     <dbl>   <dbl>    <dbl>     <dbl>
1 (Intercept)              0.04      0.271    -11.8    0        0.023     0.068
2 exporter_typeMerchant    3.46      0.175      7.10   0        2.46      4.90 
3 reg_months               0.986     0.003     -4.89   0        0.98      0.991
4 log(amount_lakh)         1.23      0.089      2.31   0.021    1.03      1.47 
5 nonfiler_pct             1.09      0.007     11.4    0        1.07      1.10 


Read them like this.


Exporter type. Merchant exporters have 3.5 times the odds of an irregular claim, compared with manufacturers with the same other features. The comparison is with the first category, Manufacturer, just as with factors in lm().

Credit from non-filers. Each extra percentage point multiplies the odds by 1.086. That looks small, but it is per point. Ten more points multiply the odds by 1.08610, or 2.3.

Amount. Since we used the logarithm, the odds ratio applies to each multiplication of the amount by e (about 2.7). Larger claims are somewhat riskier.

Months registered. An odds ratio of 0.986 per month, slightly below 1. Older registrations are slightly less risky.







Caution



Odds ratios describe association, not cause. Being a merchant exporter does not make a claim irregular. Merchant exporters have simply been riskier in this data, perhaps because fake invoices are easier to use when nothing is manufactured. The model tells us where to look, not who is guilty.

39  Logistic Regression for Risk Scoring

title: 39  Logistic Regression for Risk Scoring
text:
39.7 How good is the model?

39.7.1 The accuracy trap
The obvious way to use a probability is to call a claim “irregular” if its score is above 0.5. Let us count how that works on the test set, in a confusion matrix.

table(predicted_irregular = test$score > 0.5, actually_irregular = test$irregular)

                   actually_irregular
predicted_irregular FALSE TRUE
              FALSE   486   87
              TRUE      9   18


The model is right for 84% of the claims. That sounds good, until we notice that calling every claim regular would be right for 82.5%, since most claims are regular. Worse, it catches only 18 of the 105 irregular claims, 17%. When “yes” cases are rare, as irregularities usually are, accuracy is a misleading measure. Two other measures matter to an auditor.


Recall (or sensitivity), the share of irregular claims that the selection catches. Low recall means irregularities slip through.

Precision, the share of selected claims that turn out irregular. Low precision means examining many clean claims.

A lower cut-off catches more irregular claims, at the cost of examining more clean ones.

evaluate_cutoff <- function(cutoff) {
  picked <- test$score > cutoff
  tibble(cutoff,
         selected  = sum(picked),
         caught    = sum(picked & test$irregular),
         recall    = round(mean(picked[test$irregular]), 2),
         precision = round(mean(test$irregular[picked]), 2))
}
map(c(0.5, 0.3, 0.2, 0.1), evaluate_cutoff) |> list_rbind()

# A tibble: 4 × 5
  cutoff selected caught recall precision
   <dbl>    <int>  <int>  <dbl>     <dbl>
1    0.5       27     18   0.17      0.67
2    0.3       77     38   0.36      0.49
3    0.2      149     62   0.59      0.42
4    0.1      290     86   0.82      0.3 


There is no single right cut-off. It depends on how many claims the audit party can examine, and on the cost of missing an irregular claim compared with examining a clean one.

39.7.2 Ranking: the ROC curve and AUC
In audit we rarely need a yes/no prediction at all. We need a good ranking, so that we can examine claims from the top down as far as our resources allow. The standard measure of ranking quality is the AUC, the area under the ROC curve. It has a simple meaning. Pick one irregular claim and one regular claim at random. The AUC is the probability that the model gives the irregular one the higher score. An AUC of 0.5 is no better than tossing a coin, and 1 is a perfect ranking. In practice, 0.7 to 0.8 is useful, and above 0.8 is good.
The AUC can be calculated from ranks, in the same way as the Wilcoxon test of Section 28.8.

auc <- function(score, actual) {
  r  <- rank(score)
  n1 <- sum(actual)
  n0 <- sum(!actual)
  (sum(r[actual]) - n1 * (n1 + 1) / 2) / (n1 * n0)
}
auc1 <- auc(test$score, test$irregular)
auc1

[1] 0.7983261


The AUC on the test set is 0.80. The ROC curve itself shows, for every possible cut-off, the share of irregular claims caught against the share of regular claims wrongly selected.

roc_points <- function(score, actual) {
  ord <- order(score, decreasing = TRUE)
  tibble(false_alarm_rate = c(0, cumsum(!actual[ord]) / sum(!actual)),
         catch_rate       = c(0, cumsum(actual[ord]) / sum(actual)))
}
roc_points(test$score, test$irregular) |>
  ggplot(aes(false_alarm_rate, catch_rate)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1) +
  geom_abline(linetype = "dashed", colour = "grey50") +
  labs(x = "Share of regular claims selected (false alarms)",
       y = "Share of irregular claims caught",
       subtitle = paste("AUC =", sprintf("%.2f", auc1), "; the dashed line is random selection")) +
  coord_equal() +
  theme_minimal()



ROC curve of the refund risk model on the test set



The further the curve bows towards the top-left corner, the better. The dashed diagonal is what random selection would achieve.

39.7.3 The gains table, in audit language
The most useful view for planning is the gains table. Sort the claims by score, divide them into ten equal groups (deciles), and count how many irregular claims each group holds.

gains <- test |>
  mutate(decile = ntile(desc(score), 10)) |>
  summarise(claims = n(), irregular = sum(irregular), .by = decile) |>
  arrange(decile) |>
  mutate(cum_claims_pct = round(100 * cumsum(claims) / sum(claims)),
         cum_caught_pct = round(100 * cumsum(irregular) / sum(irregular)))
gains

# A tibble: 10 × 5
   decile claims irregular cum_claims_pct cum_caught_pct
    <int>  <int>     <int>          <dbl>          <dbl>
 1      1     60        30             10             29
 2      2     60        23             20             50
 3      3     60        21             30             70
 4      4     60         8             40             78
 5      5     60         6             50             84
 6      6     60         9             60             92
 7      7     60         3             70             95
 8      8     60         2             80             97
 9      9     60         2             90             99
10     10     60         1            100            100


Examining the top 20% of claims by score would have caught 50% of the irregular ones, and the top 30%, 70%. Random selection of 20% of claims would catch only about 20%. That is the value of the model, stated in terms any audit manager understands.

title: 39  Logistic Regression for Risk Scoring
text:
39.8 Making better features
Remember the registration table. The risk was high for claimants registered for less than a year, and much lower after that. But model1 uses reg_months as a straight-line effect, a small change in risk for every month. It cannot capture a jump at one year. A simple feature that says whether the claimant is a new registrant matches the pattern better.

train <- train |> mutate(new_registrant = reg_months < 12)
test  <- test  |> mutate(new_registrant = reg_months < 12)

model2 <- glm(irregular ~ exporter_type + new_registrant + log(amount_lakh) + nonfiler_pct,
              family = binomial, data = train)
or2 <- tidy(model2, exponentiate = TRUE, conf.int = TRUE)
or2 |> mutate(across(where(is.numeric), \(x) round(x, 3)))

# A tibble: 5 × 7
  term                  estimate std.error statistic p.value conf.low conf.high
  <chr>                    <dbl>     <dbl>     <dbl>   <dbl>    <dbl>     <dbl>
1 (Intercept)              0.012     0.295    -15.0    0        0.007     0.021
2 exporter_typeMerchant    3.74      0.182      7.26   0        2.63      5.38 
3 new_registrantTRUE       5.49      0.184      9.26   0        3.84      7.91 
4 log(amount_lakh)         1.22      0.091      2.14   0.032    1.02      1.46 
5 nonfiler_pct             1.09      0.008     11.9    0        1.08      1.11 

test <- test |> mutate(score2 = predict(model2, newdata = test, type = "response"))
auc2 <- auc(test$score2, test$irregular)
c(model1 = round(auc1, 3), model2 = round(auc2, 3))

model1 model2 
 0.798  0.825 


New registrants have 5.5 times the odds of an irregular claim, and the AUC on the test set improves from 0.798 to 0.825.
With only about 100 irregular claims in the test set, a small difference in AUC could be the luck of one particular split. A simple check is to repeat the split many times, and see how often the new model wins. (Repeating the split in a systematic way is called cross-validation.)

auc_gain <- map_dbl(1:40, \(i) {
  set.seed(i)
  rows <- sample(nrow(past), size = 0.7 * nrow(past))
  tr <- past[rows, ] |> mutate(new_registrant = reg_months < 12)
  te <- past[-rows, ] |> mutate(new_registrant = reg_months < 12)
  m1 <- glm(irregular ~ exporter_type + reg_months + log(amount_lakh) + nonfiler_pct,
            family = binomial, data = tr)
  m2 <- glm(irregular ~ exporter_type + new_registrant + log(amount_lakh) + nonfiler_pct,
            family = binomial, data = tr)
  auc(predict(m2, te), te$irregular) - auc(predict(m1, te), te$irregular)
})
c(splits = length(auc_gain), new_model_better = sum(auc_gain > 0),
  average_gain = round(mean(auc_gain), 3))

          splits new_model_better     average_gain 
          40.000           38.000            0.028 


The new feature improves the ranking in 38 of 40 random splits, so the gain is real. Features built from audit knowledge, like “registered less than a year ago”, “supplier and claimant share an address” or “claim filed in the last week of the quarter”, often add more than any statistical refinement. Looking at the data first, as we did, is how such features are found.






TipAudit tip



Compare models on the test set, never on the training set. Adding features always improves the fit on the training data, even useless ones. Only the test set tells whether a change really helps on new cases.
