title: 48  Text Analytics
text:
48.1 Where does an auditor meet text?
Text analytics is crucial in data analytics, as text data is becoming increasingly important in almost every field. A large part of the information in any organisation is in the form of text, not numbers. To make full use of it, we need to know how to clean, process, summarise and analyse text. In this chapter, we will learn the basic tools for working with text in R. In the next chapter, we will use them for sentiment analysis, and in the one after that, for visualising text.
Text brings its own challenges. Unlike a table of numbers, text has no fixed structure. The same thing can be written in many ways, with different spellings, abbreviations, cases and punctuation. People mix languages, as in “camp ke baad hospital le gaye”. Words can mean different things in different contexts. So, before analysing text, we must first clean it and bring it into a form that a computer can count.
Auditors deal with text far more often than they may realise.
In each case, reading every document is impossible when there are thousands of them. Text analytics helps the auditor see what is being said, how often, and where.

title: 48  Text Analytics
text:
Public grievances. Complaints received through portals like CPGRAMS, or through scheme helplines. They often describe problems long before these show up in accounts.

Narrations in accounts. Every voucher and journal entry has a description, like “being payment for…” or “adjustment as per instructions”. Unusual narrations are a standard red flag in fraud risk assessment.

Audit reports and inspection reports. Past observations, which can be searched for recurring issues.

Contract and tender documents. Specifications, terms and conditions, and correspondence.

Feedback and survey responses. Comments from beneficiaries, patients or citizens.

Free-text fields in databases. Remarks columns, reasons for rejection, descriptions of goods.

title: 48  Text Analytics
text:
48.2 Prerequisites
We will mainly use the package tidytext, which brings text analysis into the familiar tidyverse way of working. We will also use SnowballC for stemming.

library(tidyverse)
library(tidytext)
library(SnowballC)

title: 48  Text Analytics
section: 48.3 Our data, grievances under a health scheme
text:
48.3 Our data, grievances under a health scheme
We continue with the imaginary Sarvajan Swasthya Yojana (SSY) health insurance scheme of the previous chapters (Chapter 43, Chapter 44 and Chapter 45). This time we look at grievances filed by the public against empanelled hospitals during 2024-25. The data is made up, and is created by tools/make_ssy_text_data.R in the book’s repository.

grievances <- read_csv("Data/ssy_grievances.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
glimpse(grievances)

Rows: 800
Columns: 6
$ grievance_id <chr> "GR0001", "GR0002", "GR0003", "GR0004", "GR0005", "GR0006…
$ received_on  <date> 2024-04-01, 2024-04-02, 2024-04-02, 2024-04-04, 2024-04-…
$ district     <chr> "Devgarh", "Belapur", "Kishanpur", "Kishanpur", "Haripur"…
$ hospital_id  <chr> "H070", "H071", "H063", "H063", "H098", "H063", "H098", "…
$ category     <chr> "Demand of money", "Other", "Quality of care", "Demand of…
$ text         <chr> "Sir ji, At discharge the counter asked 2000/- extra, the…


Each row is a grievance. The category is chosen by the person filing the complaint, from a fixed list. The text is what they wrote in their own words. Let us look at a few.

grievances |>
  slice(c(3, 17, 42, 88, 120)) |>
  pull(text)

[1] "To the officer, Agent of the hospitl told villagers that free operation is available, took us in their van on Sunday. Please look into the matter urgently."
[2] "Agent of the hospital told villagers that free opration is available, took us in their van on Sunday."                                                      
[3] "Doctor did opration of appendix without any test, now my son has pain and they are not attending. We are poor people, please help."                         
[4] "They took money (1000) for blood test and x-ray. Is this not covered under SSY card?"                                                                       
[5] "My uterus was removed at age 35, I had only small stomach pain . Now I feel weak all the time ."                                                            


This is what real complaint text looks like. Some is in capitals, some in lower case. There are spelling mistakes, extra spaces and full stops in odd places. There are amounts and phone numbers. Some words are in Hindi. All of this must be dealt with before analysis.
Let us also see how the complaints are spread across categories.

grievances |>
  count(category, sort = TRUE)

# A tibble: 6 × 2
  category                n
  <chr>               <int>
1 Other                 274
2 Quality of care       158
3 Denial of treatment   121
4 Delay                  95
5 Demand of money        95
6 Card/eligibility       57


The biggest category is Other. This is common in real grievance data. People often cannot find a category that fits, or do not bother to choose. So the categories alone do not tell us what the complaints are about. We have to read the text. Let us see how R can help us do that.

title: 48  Text Analytics
48  Text Analytics
text:
48.5 Tokenisation
Computers cannot understand sentences, but they can count. So we break the text into small units, usually single words, called tokens. This step is called tokenisation.
unnest_tokens() from tidytext does this. It takes a column of text, and produces a new data frame with one row per token. All other columns, like the grievance ID and category, are repeated for each word. This is called the tidy text format.

tokens <- grievances |>
  select(grievance_id, hospital_id, category, clean_text) |>
  unnest_tokens(output = word, input = clean_text)

tokens |> head(12)

# A tibble: 12 × 4
   grievance_id hospital_id category        word     
   <chr>        <chr>       <chr>           <chr>    
 1 GR0001       H070        Demand of money sir      
 2 GR0001       H070        Demand of money ji       
 3 GR0001       H070        Demand of money at       
 4 GR0001       H070        Demand of money discharge
 5 GR0001       H070        Demand of money the      
 6 GR0001       H070        Demand of money counter  
 7 GR0001       H070        Demand of money asked    
 8 GR0001       H070        Demand of money extra    
 9 GR0001       H070        Demand of money they     
10 GR0001       H070        Demand of money said     
11 GR0001       H070        Demand of money card     
12 GR0001       H070        Demand of money amount   


output = word names the new column, and input = clean_text tells which column to split. By default, unnest_tokens() also converts to lower case and removes punctuation. So even if we had not cleaned the text ourselves, much of the cleaning would have been done here.

nrow(tokens)

[1] 15461


The 800 grievances have been broken into 15,461 words. Let us count the most common ones.

tokens |>
  count(word, sort = TRUE) |>
  head(15)

# A tibble: 15 × 2
   word         n
   <chr>    <int>
 1 the        599
 2 is         573
 3 not        456
 4 sir        452
 5 was        367
 6 and        358
 7 to         354
 8 please     306
 9 for        291
10 they       273
11 in         252
12 us         249
13 hospital   232
14 we         217
15 card       202


Not very informative. The top words are the, to, and, was and the like. These are needed for grammar, but tell us nothing about the complaints.

title: 48  Text Analytics
text:
48.6 Stop words
Words like the, is, and and was are called stop words. They appear in almost every text, and we usually remove them before analysis. tidytext comes with a ready list in the data frame stop_words.

stop_words |> head()

# A tibble: 6 × 2
  word      lexicon
  <chr>     <chr>  
1 a         SMART  
2 a's       SMART  
3 able      SMART  
4 about     SMART  
5 above     SMART  
6 according SMART  

nrow(stop_words)

[1] 1149


To remove them, we use anti_join(). It keeps only those rows of the first table that have no match in the second. We have used it before to remove accounted gaps in Chapter 35.

tokens_clean <- tokens |>
  anti_join(stop_words, by = "word")

tokens_clean |>
  count(word, sort = TRUE) |>
  head(15)

# A tibble: 15 × 2
   word          n
   <chr>     <int>
 1 sir         452
 2 hospital    232
 3 card        202
 4 days        192
 5 operation   167
 6 people      154
 7 treatment   132
 8 scheme      122
 9 staff       118
10 poor        115
11 father      114
12 ji          112
13 respected   111
14 mobile      109
15 dear        108


Much better. But some words are still not useful for our purpose. Sir, ji, respected and dear are just polite forms of address. Mobile, contact, matter, urgently, action, poor and people come from the closing lines that many people add, like “please look into the matter urgently” or “we are poor people”. Hospital and scheme appear everywhere in this data, because of what the data is about. Such words are called domain stop words. We make our own list and remove them too.

my_stop_words <- tibble(word = c("sir", "ji", "madam", "respected", "dear", "officer",
                                 "kindly", "please", "help", "action", "matter", "urgently",
                                 "look", "contact", "mobile", "poor", "people",
                                 "hospital", "hospitl", "scheme", "ssy", "patient",
                                 "rs", "rupees", "ke", "le", "kar"))

tokens_clean <- tokens_clean |>
  anti_join(my_stop_words, by = "word")

tokens_clean |>
  count(word, sort = TRUE) |>
  head(15)

# A tibble: 15 × 2
   word           n
   <chr>      <int>
 1 card         202
 2 days         192
 3 operation    167
 4 treatment    132
 5 staff        118
 6 father       114
 7 pending      106
 8 doctor        87
 9 ward          82
10 refused       81
11 discharged    71
12 free          70
13 package       64
14 approval      61
15 insurance     61


Now the top words tell us what the complaints are about. Cards, operations, treatment, staff, pending approvals, refusals and discharge.






TipBuilding a list of domain stop words



There is no ready list of domain stop words. Look at the top words, remove the ones that carry no meaning for your question, and look again. Two or three rounds are usually enough. But be careful not to remove a word only because it is common. In our data, operation is common, and it is very important.

title: 48  Text Analytics
text:
48.7 Stemming
The same word appears in different forms. Operation, operations and operated. Demand, demanded and demanding. For counting, we may want to treat these as one. Stemming cuts words down to their root, called the stem. wordStem() from the package SnowballC does this.

wordStem(c("operation", "operations", "operated", "demand", "demanded",
           "removed", "removal", "discharged", "discharge"))

[1] "oper"     "oper"     "oper"     "demand"   "demand"   "remov"    "remov"   
[8] "discharg" "discharg"


The stems are not always proper words. Operation becomes oper. But all forms of a word now look the same, and will be counted together.

tokens_clean |>
  mutate(stem = wordStem(word)) |>
  count(stem, sort = TRUE) |>
  head(10)

# A tibble: 10 × 2
   stem          n
   <chr>     <int>
 1 dai         229
 2 card        202
 3 oper        179
 4 treatment   132
 5 staff       118
 6 father      114
 7 pend        106
 8 discharg    102
 9 doctor       87
10 ward         82








NoteStemming or not?



Stemming helps when the exact form of a word does not matter, for example when counting themes. It is not helpful when we want to read and present the words, because stems like oper look odd in a report. A more refined method, called lemmatisation, reduces words to proper dictionary forms. For most audit work, simple stemming or no stemming at all is enough.

title: 48  Text Analytics
text:
48.8 Pairs of words, n-grams
Single words lose their context. Removed alone tells little, but uterus removed tells a lot. A sequence of n words is called an n-gram. Two words together are a bigram. unnest_tokens() can produce these too, with token = "ngrams" and n = 2.

bigrams <- grievances |>
  select(grievance_id, hospital_id, category, clean_text) |>
  unnest_tokens(bigram, clean_text, token = "ngrams", n = 2)

bigrams |> head(8)

# A tibble: 8 × 4
  grievance_id hospital_id category        bigram       
  <chr>        <chr>       <chr>           <chr>        
1 GR0001       H070        Demand of money sir ji       
2 GR0001       H070        Demand of money ji at        
3 GR0001       H070        Demand of money at discharge 
4 GR0001       H070        Demand of money discharge the
5 GR0001       H070        Demand of money the counter  
6 GR0001       H070        Demand of money counter asked
7 GR0001       H070        Demand of money asked extra  
8 GR0001       H070        Demand of money extra they   


Each bigram overlaps with the next one. To remove stop words from bigrams, we separate the two words into two columns, and keep only bigrams in which neither word is a stop word.

all_stops <- c(stop_words$word, my_stop_words$word)

bigrams_clean <- bigrams |>
  separate_wider_delim(bigram, delim = " ", names = c("word1", "word2")) |>
  filter(!word1 %in% all_stops, !word2 %in% all_stops) |>
  unite(bigram, word1, word2, sep = " ")

bigrams_clean |>
  count(bigram, sort = TRUE) |>
  head(15)

# A tibble: 15 × 2
   bigram                n
   <chr>             <int>
 1 pre authorisation    46
 2 accepted staff       45
 3 days junior          40
 4 doctor visited       40
 5 junior staff         40
 6 package list         38
 7 refused treatment    38
 8 drinking water       37
 9 staff demanded       33
10 card amount          31
11 blood test           28
12 health camp          27
13 told villagers       23
14 feel weak            20
15 free operation       20


Bigrams tell a much clearer story than single words. Pre authorisation and package list point to delays and denials. Staff demanded and card amount point to money being asked for. And health camp, told villagers, free operation and feel weak point to something quite different, patients being brought in from villages for operations. Such problems do not fit neatly into any category.

title: 48  Text Analytics
section: 48.9 Finding themes with a keyword dictionary
text:
48.9 Finding themes with a keyword dictionary
So far we have looked at what words are common. For audit, we usually have a sharper question. How many complaints are about money being demanded? About camps? About unnecessary surgery? A simple and very effective way to answer this is a keyword dictionary. We list a few words or patterns for each theme, and tag every grievance that matches.

themes <- tribble(
  ~theme,              ~pattern,
  "Money demanded",    "demand|paid|pay |took money|took rs|cash|extra|receipt",
  "Camp or agent",     "camp|vehicle|van |agent|village",
  "Surgery concerns",  "uterus|without any test|second operation|wound|in a hurry|operation kar",
  "Denial or card",    "refused|not valid|not accepted|sent us away|server",
  "Delay",             "pending|delayed|not discharged|wait",
  "Poor facilities",   "dirty|rude|toilet|food|drinking water|visited only"
)

themes

# A tibble: 6 × 2
  theme            pattern                                                      
  <chr>            <chr>                                                        
1 Money demanded   demand|paid|pay |took money|took rs|cash|extra|receipt       
2 Camp or agent    camp|vehicle|van |agent|village                              
3 Surgery concerns uterus|without any test|second operation|wound|in a hurry|op…
4 Denial or card   refused|not valid|not accepted|sent us away|server           
5 Delay            pending|delayed|not discharged|wait                          
6 Poor facilities  dirty|rude|toilet|food|drinking water|visited only           


The patterns are regular expressions, so | means “or”. Now we check each grievance against each pattern. str_detect() returns TRUE where the pattern is found. A grievance can belong to more than one theme.

tagged <- grievances |>
  select(grievance_id, hospital_id, category, clean_text) |>
  cross_join(themes) |>
  filter(str_detect(clean_text, pattern)) |>
  select(-pattern)

tagged |>
  count(theme, sort = TRUE)

# A tibble: 6 × 2
  theme                n
  <chr>            <int>
1 Denial or card     178
2 Poor facilities    159
3 Delay              152
4 Money demanded     149
5 Surgery concerns    99
6 Camp or agent       80


cross_join() pairs every grievance with every theme. filter() then keeps only the pairs where the grievance text matches the theme’s pattern.

48.9.1 What is hiding in “Other”?
Now let us compare the themes we found with the categories that people chose.

tagged |>
  count(category, theme) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = theme, values_from = n, values_fill = 0) |>
  knitr::kable()

The Other category hides every kind of complaint, including many about money being demanded and about delays. More importantly, it holds most of the complaints about camps and agents (56 of 80) and about surgery concerns (63 of 99). The rest of these are filed under Quality of care. None of the fixed categories describes them properly. These are serious matters, and someone looking only at the category-wise count would never notice them.

48.9.2 Which hospitals?
Let us see which hospitals these serious complaints are about.

tagged |>
  filter(theme %in% c("Camp or agent", "Surgery concerns")) |>
  distinct(grievance_id, hospital_id) |>
  count(hospital_id, sort = TRUE, name = "serious_grievances") |>
  head(8)

# A tibble: 8 × 2
  hospital_id serious_grievances
  <chr>                    <int>
1 H071                        25
2 H116                        24
3 H063                        23
4 H070                        21
5 H098                        18
6 H066                        16
7 H036                         2
8 H064                         2


A handful of hospitals account for most of these complaints. These are the same hospitals that showed unusual claims behaviour in the chapters on PCA, clustering and association rules. Patterns in the claims data and patterns in the complaints point to the same places. When two very different sources of evidence agree, the case for a detailed audit becomes strong.






TipAudit tip



A keyword dictionary is simple, transparent and easy to explain in an audit report. Build it by reading a sample of the text, test it on another sample, and refine it. Keep the patterns specific. A pattern like pay alone would also match “payment pending” and “salary paid”. That is why we used pay with a space, and took money.

title: 48  Text Analytics
section: 48.10 Words that set a group apart, tf-idf
text:
48.10 Words that set a group apart, tf-idf
Counting words shows what is common. But often we want to know what is distinctive about one group compared with others. For this, text analysts use a measure called tf-idf, short for term frequency, inverse document frequency.


Term frequency (tf) is how often a word appears in a group, as a share of all words in that group.

Inverse document frequency (idf) is high for words that appear in only a few groups, and zero for words that appear in all groups.

tf-idf multiplies the two. So it is high for words that are frequent in one group and rare in others.

bind_tf_idf() from tidytext calculates it. We need the word counts by group. Here, a “group” is a grievance category.

category_tfidf <- tokens_clean |>
  count(category, word) |>
  bind_tf_idf(word, category, n)

category_tfidf |>
  slice_max(tf_idf, n = 5, by = category, with_ties = FALSE) |>
  select(category, word, tf_idf) |>
  print(n = 30)

   category            word      tf_idf

15 Demand of money     discharge 0.0464

title: 48  Text Analytics
section: 48.11 Audit use case, narrations of journal entries
text:
48.11 Audit use case, narrations of journal entries
The same tools can be used on the narrations of accounting entries. Standards on auditing ask auditors to test journal entries for signs of fraud, especially entries made by senior staff, at the end of the year, for round amounts, or with vague descriptions. Let us create the journal entries of an imaginary organisation for 2024-25. Most of them are routine. We have planted 20 suspicious entries, with vague narrations, round amounts and mostly posted by the finance manager, many in the last days of March.

Code to create the journal entriesset.seed(2402)
n <- 3000
templates <- c("Being payment of electricity bill for MONTH", "Being salary for the month of MONTH",
               "Being purchase of stationery vide bill no NUM", "Being payment to contractor, RA bill NUM",
               "Being advance to staff for tour, adjusted against TA bill NUM", "Being depreciation for MONTH",
               "Being interest accrued on deposits for MONTH", "Being transfer of grant received to project account",
               "Being rent for office building for MONTH", "Being provision for audit fee",
               "Being reversal of duplicate entry no NUM, approved vide note no NUM")

journal <- tibble(
  entry_no  = sprintf("JE%05d", 1:n),
  date      = as.Date("2024-04-01") + sample(0:364, n, TRUE),
  posted_by = sample(c("acct01", "acct02", "acct03", "acct04", "fin_mgr"), n, TRUE,
                     prob = c(.3, .3, .2, .15, .05)),
  amount    = round(rlnorm(n, log(45000), 1.1), 2),
  narration = sample(templates, n, TRUE, prob = c(rep(1, 10), 0.3))
) |>
  mutate(narration = str_replace(narration, "MONTH", month.name[month(date)]),
         narration = str_replace_all(narration, "NUM", as.character(sample(100:999, n, TRUE))))

# Planted. 20 suspicious entries
sus <- sample(1:n, 20)
journal$narration[sus] <- sample(c("Adjustment as per instructions of the director",
                                   "Misc. expenses, details to follow",
                                   "Transfer to suspense account pending clarification",
                                   "Adjusted as discussed", "To be regularised later",
                                   "As per verbal orders", "Write off of old balance",
                                   "Rectification entry"), 20, TRUE)
journal$posted_by[sus] <- sample(c("fin_mgr", "acct04"), 20, TRUE, prob = c(.7, .3))
journal$amount[sus]    <- sample(c(250000, 500000, 750000, 1000000, 1500000), 20, TRUE)
journal$date[sus[1:12]] <- as.Date("2025-03-29") + sample(0:2, 12, TRUE)



head(journal)

# A tibble: 6 × 5
  entry_no date       posted_by  amount narration                               
  <chr>    <date>     <chr>       <dbl> <chr>                                   
1 JE00001  2024-06-07 acct03     36150. Being provision for audit fee           
2 JE00002  2024-07-20 acct02    209375. Being transfer of grant received to pro…
3 JE00003  2024-04-30 acct03    180317. Being purchase of stationery vide bill …
4 JE00004  2025-01-04 acct03     79277. Being rent for office building for Janu…
5 JE00005  2024-12-21 acct01    174080. Being purchase of stationery vide bill …
6 JE00006  2024-09-22 acct03     33598. Being purchase of stationery vide bill …


Step 1, red-flag words. We list words and phrases which often appear in irregular entries. \\b makes sure that, for example, misc is matched only at the beginning of a word.

red_flags <- paste(c("\\badjust", "as per (the )?(instruction|direction|verbal)", "\\bverbal",
                     "\\bmisc", "details? to follow", "\\breversal", "regularis", "suspense",
                     "pending clarification", "\\bwrite.?off", "rectif", "as discussed"),
                   collapse = "|")

journal |>
  filter(str_detect(str_to_lower(narration), red_flags)) |>
  count(narration_start = str_trunc(narration, 45), sort = TRUE)

# A tibble: 91 × 2
   narration_start                                   n
   <chr>                                         <int>
 1 Being advance to staff for tour, adjusted ...   287
 2 Write off of old balance                          4
 3 Adjustment as per instructions of the dire...     3
 4 As per verbal orders                              3
 5 Misc. expenses, details to follow                 3
 6 Transfer to suspense account pending clari...     3
 7 Adjusted as discussed                             2
 8 Being reversal of duplicate entry no 264, ...     2
 9 Being reversal of duplicate entry no 405, ...     2
10 Being reversal of duplicate entry no 452, ...     2
# ℹ 81 more rows


393 entries are flagged. But most of them are routine. Tour advances adjusted against TA bills, and reversals of duplicate entries approved by a note, are normal book-keeping. A good red-flag list also needs a list of known routine phrases, to be excluded.

routine <- "adjusted against ta bill|reversal of duplicate entry no \\d+, approved vide"

journal <- journal |>
  mutate(f_narration = str_detect(str_to_lower(narration), red_flags) &
                       !str_detect(str_to_lower(narration), routine))

sum(journal$f_narration)

[1] 20


Now only 20 entries have a red-flag narration.
Step 2, combine with other signals. A vague narration alone is weak evidence. Together with other risk factors, it becomes much stronger. Let us add four more flags, and add them up into a simple score.

journal_scored <- journal |>
  mutate(f_weekend = wday(date, week_start = 1) >= 6,
         f_round   = amount >= 100000 & amount %% 50000 == 0,
         f_yearend = date >= as.Date("2025-03-25"),
         f_senior  = posted_by == "fin_mgr",
         score     = f_narration + f_weekend + f_round + f_yearend + f_senior)

journal_scored |> count(score)

# A tibble: 6 × 2
  score     n
  <int> <int>
1     0  1951
2     1   974
3     2    57
4     3     4
5     4     5
6     5     9


Only 18 of the 3,000 entries score 3 or more. 17 of them are among the 20 we planted. Let us see the top of the list.

journal_scored |>
  filter(score >= 3) |>
  arrange(desc(score), desc(amount)) |>
  select(entry_no, date, posted_by, amount, narration, score) |>
  head(8)

# A tibble: 8 × 6
  entry_no date       posted_by  amount narration                          score
  <chr>    <date>     <chr>       <dbl> <chr>                              <int>
1 JE01703  2025-03-30 fin_mgr   1500000 Adjustment as per instructions of…     5
2 JE00874  2025-03-30 fin_mgr   1000000 Write off of old balance               5
3 JE02279  2025-03-30 fin_mgr    500000 Adjusted as discussed                  5
4 JE00123  2025-03-29 fin_mgr    250000 Misc. expenses, details to follow      5
5 JE00876  2025-03-29 fin_mgr    250000 Rectification entry                    5
6 JE01611  2025-03-29 fin_mgr    250000 Adjustment as per instructions of…     5
7 JE01658  2025-03-29 fin_mgr    250000 Adjusted as discussed                  5
8 JE02420  2025-03-30 fin_mgr    250000 As per verbal orders                   5








TipAudit tip



Each flag on its own catches many innocent entries. The combination of flags is what separates the few entries worth examining. Keep the scoring simple and explainable, as here, so that the selection of entries for detailed checking can be justified in the working papers.

title: 48  Text Analytics
section: 48.12 Audit use case, brand names in tender specifications
text:
48.12 Audit use case, brand names in tender specifications
Specifications in a tender should describe what is needed, not whose product. The General Financial Rules require specifications to be generic, and where a brand has to be mentioned as a reference, it should be followed by the words “or equivalent”. Specifications written around one brand, or with phrases like “only” and “exclusively”, keep competitors out and may favour a particular supplier.
Let us create 240 item specifications from the tenders of four sections of an imaginary department. The brand names are made up. In the Electrical section, we have planted specifications which name the brand Voltix without “or equivalent”.

Code to create the specificationsset.seed(77)
brands <- c("Zentrix", "Corvalon", "Medisure", "Aquaflo", "Voltix")
generic <- c("LED lamp, 20 W, BIS certified, warranty 2 years",
             "Water purifier, RO and UV, 10 litre storage",
             "Desktop computer, 16 GB RAM, 512 GB SSD, 24 inch monitor",
             "Copper cable, 4 sq mm, ISI marked, 90 m coil",
             "Office chair, high back, adjustable height",
             "MCB, 32 A, double pole, ISI marked",
             "Pulse oximeter, fingertip, with display")

specs <- tibble(
  spec_id = sprintf("S%03d", 1:240),
  section = sample(c("Electrical", "IT", "Health", "General"), 240, TRUE),
  text    = sample(generic, 240, TRUE)
)
# About 15% mention a brand correctly, as a reference with "or equivalent"
ref <- sample(1:240, 36)
specs$text[ref] <- paste0(specs$text[ref], ", make ", sample(brands, 36, TRUE), " or equivalent")

# Planted. Brand-specific specifications in the Electrical section
elec <- setdiff(which(specs$section == "Electrical"), ref)
planted <- sample(elec, 14)
specs$text[planted] <- paste0(specs$text[planted],
                              sample(c(", make Voltix only", ", Voltix make",
                                       ", exclusively of Voltix brand"), 14, TRUE))



specs |> slice(c(1, ref[1], planted[1]))

# A tibble: 3 × 3
  spec_id section    text                                                       
  <chr>   <chr>      <chr>                                                      
1 S001    IT         Office chair, high back, adjustable height                 
2 S084    Health     Pulse oximeter, fingertip, with display, make Aquaflo or e…
3 S052    Electrical Copper cable, 4 sq mm, ISI marked, 90 m coil, Voltix make  


To find a brand name not followed by “or equivalent”, we use a negative look-ahead, which we learnt in Chapter 19. The pattern (?![^.]*or equivalent) means “not followed, anywhere later in the sentence, by or equivalent”.

brand_pattern   <- paste0("\\b(", paste(brands, collapse = "|"), ")\\b")
no_equivalent   <- paste0(brand_pattern, "(?![^.]*or equivalent)")
restrictive     <- "\\bonly\\b|\\bexclusively\\b|\\bsole\\b"

specs_flagged <- specs |>
  mutate(brand           = str_extract(text, regex(brand_pattern, ignore_case = TRUE)),
         brand_specific  = str_detect(text, regex(no_equivalent, ignore_case = TRUE)),
         restrictive_use = str_detect(text, regex(restrictive, ignore_case = TRUE)))

specs_flagged |>
  count(section, brand_specific) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = brand_specific, values_from = n, values_fill = 0)

# A tibble: 4 × 3
  section    `FALSE` `TRUE`
  <chr>        <int>  <int>
1 Electrical      50     14
2 General         53      0
3 Health          70      0
4 IT              53      0


All the brand-specific specifications are in the Electrical section, and they all name the same brand.

specs_flagged |>
  filter(brand_specific) |>
  count(section, brand, restrictive_use)

# A tibble: 2 × 4
  section    brand  restrictive_use     n
  <chr>      <chr>  <lgl>           <int>
1 Electrical Voltix FALSE               8
2 Electrical Voltix TRUE                6








TipAudit tip



A pattern like this across many tenders of one section is a lead. Find out who drafted the specifications, whether the named brand’s dealer won the tenders, and how the prices compared with the market. Brand names in the specifications of goods available from many makers are especially worth questioning.

title: 48  Text Analytics
text:
48.13 A suggested workflow


Understand the text and the question. Read a sample of the documents before writing any code.

Protect personal data. Mask phone numbers, IDs and names.

Clean the text. Lower case, remove numbers or punctuation if not needed, squeeze spaces. Keep the original column.

Tokenise, into words and, where useful, into bigrams.

Remove stop words, both the standard list and your own domain list.

Count and compare. Look at top words and bigrams, and use tf-idf to see what sets groups apart.

Build a keyword dictionary for the themes that matter to the audit, and tag every document.

Link back to structured data. Count themes by unit, period or category, and compare with other evidence.

Read the actual documents behind every finding before reporting.







ImportantRemember



Text analytics counts words. It does not understand them. A complaint saying “they did not demand any money” contains the word demand. Always read a sample of the documents behind every count, before treating the count as evidence.

title: 49  Sentiment Analysis
text:
49.1 Where can sentiment analysis help an auditor?
When we read a comment like “Doctors were very good and caring”, we know at once that the writer is happy. “Staff was rude and the ward was dirty” tells us the opposite. Sentiment analysis tries to make a computer do the same. It measures whether a piece of text expresses a positive or a negative feeling, and how strongly.
For an auditor, sentiment is a quick way to sense where things may be going wrong. Thousands of feedback comments, survey responses or grievances cannot all be read. But if the comments about one hospital, one office or one scheme are much more negative than about others, that is where to look first.

title: 49  Sentiment Analysis
text:
Beneficiary feedback on schemes, hospitals, schools or ration shops. Units with unusually negative feedback deserve attention.

Grievances, to find which ones express the strongest distress, so that serious cases are not lost in the volume.

Survey responses collected during performance audits, where hundreds of beneficiaries answer open questions.

Trends over time. A sudden fall in sentiment about a service may show the effect of a policy change or a breakdown.

Testing what people say against what records show. A hospital whose records look perfect, but whose patients are unhappy, raises questions.

title: 49  Sentiment Analysis
text:
49.2 How does it work?
The simplest and most transparent method uses a sentiment dictionary, also called a lexicon. It is a list of words, each marked as positive or negative. To score a comment, we break it into words, look up each word in the dictionary, and count the positive and negative words. The difference gives a sentiment score.
This is called the dictionary-based or lexicon-based approach. It is easy to understand and explain, which matters in audit. Its weaknesses, which we will see shortly, are also easy to understand and partly fix.

title: 49  Sentiment Analysis
text:
49.3 Prerequisites
We will use tidytext, introduced in Chapter 48.

library(tidyverse)
library(tidytext)

title: 49  Sentiment Analysis
text:
49.4 Our data, patient feedback
We again use the imaginary Sarvajan Swasthya Yojana (SSY). After discharge, patients can leave a short comment and a star rating from 1 to 5. The data is made up, and is created by tools/make_ssy_text_data.R in the book’s repository.

feedback <- read_csv("Data/ssy_feedback.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)

feedback |>
  slice(c(1, 5, 9, 14, 22, 31)) |>
  select(hospital_id, comment, rating)

# A tibble: 6 × 3
  hospital_id comment                                                     rating
  <chr>       <chr>                                                        <dbl>
1 H021        Food was not good.  Thank you, the operation was successfu…      5
2 H104        Very clean ward and good food.                                   5
3 H117        Staff was polite and the doctor was experienced.  Discharg…      4
4 H044        Food was not good.  Treatment was done.                          3
5 H040        Discharged after treatment.                                      3
6 H071        Discharged after treatment.  Doctor was not available, ver…      1


There are 1,500 comments about 120 hospitals. The star rating gives us a useful check. If our sentiment score is any good, it should broadly agree with the stars that patients gave.

title: 49  Sentiment Analysis
text:
49.5 The Bing dictionary
tidytext comes with a ready dictionary called Bing, compiled by Bing Liu and colleagues. get_sentiments("bing") returns it as a data frame.

bing <- get_sentiments("bing")
bing

# A tibble: 6,786 × 2
   word        sentiment
   <chr>       <chr>    
 1 2-faces     negative 
 2 abnormal    negative 
 3 abolish     negative 
 4 abominable  negative 
 5 abominably  negative 
 6 abominate   negative 
 7 abomination negative 
 8 abort       negative 
 9 aborted     negative 
10 aborts      negative 
# ℹ 6,776 more rows

bing |> count(sentiment)

# A tibble: 2 × 2
  sentiment     n
  <chr>     <int>
1 negative   4781
2 positive   2005


It has about 6,786 words, each marked positive or negative.






NoteOther dictionaries



tidytext can also fetch other dictionaries, like AFINN, which gives each word a score from -5 to +5, and NRC, which tags words with emotions like anger, fear and trust. These are downloaded through the textdata package the first time they are used, and have their own licence terms. The Bing dictionary needs no download, so we use it here.

title: 49  Sentiment Analysis
text:
49.6 Scoring each comment
We follow the steps of the last chapter. Break the comments into words, and then keep only the words found in the dictionary. inner_join() does this. It keeps only rows that have a match in both tables.

feedback_words <- feedback |>
  unnest_tokens(word, comment) |>
  inner_join(bing, by = "word")

feedback_words |>
  count(word, sentiment, sort = TRUE) |>
  head(12)

# A tibble: 12 × 3
   word       sentiment     n
   <chr>      <chr>     <int>
 1 good       positive    462
 2 free       positive    199
 3 helpful    positive    189
 4 clean      positive    184
 5 polite     positive    146
 6 successful positive    141
 7 thank      positive    141
 8 excellent  positive    140
 9 properly   positive    130
10 attentive  positive    126
11 available  positive     66
12 poor       negative     66


Now we count the positive and negative words in each comment. The score of a comment is the number of positive words minus the number of negative words.

scores <- feedback_words |>
  count(feedback_id, sentiment) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = sentiment, values_from = n, values_fill = 0)

feedback_scored <- feedback |>
  left_join(scores, by = "feedback_id") |>
  mutate(across(c(positive, negative), \(x) replace_na(x, 0)),
         score = positive - negative)

feedback_scored |>
  select(comment, positive, negative, score, rating) |>
  head(8)

# A tibble: 8 × 5
  comment                                         positive negative score rating
  <chr>                                              <int>    <int> <int>  <dbl>
1 Food was not good.  Thank you, the operation w…        3        0     3      5
2 Discharged after treatment.  Stayed for some d…        0        0     0      3
3 Doctors were very good and caring.                     1        0     1      5
4 Staff was rude and careless.                           0        2    -2      1
5 Very clean ward and good food.                         2        0     2      5
6 Discharged after treatment.  They forced us to…        0        0     0      2
7 Staff was polite and the doctor was experience…        1        0     1      4
8 Not happy with the treatment.  Good hospital, …        3        0     3      2


We used left_join() here, not inner_join(), so that comments without any dictionary word are kept, with a score of zero.

49.6.1 Does the score agree with the stars?
Let us check how well the score agrees with the rating given by the patient. The correlation, which we met in the PCA chapter, is a single number for this.

cor(feedback_scored$score, feedback_scored$rating)

[1] 0.6424695


A correlation of about 0.64 means the two agree fairly well, but far from perfectly. Let us see where the method goes wrong.

title: 49  Sentiment Analysis
49  Sentiment Analysis
section: 49.8 Problem 2, words the dictionary does not know
text:
49.8 Problem 2, words the dictionary does not know
A general dictionary is built from product reviews, news and the like. It does not know the language of every field. Let us see which common words in our comments are not in the dictionary.

feedback |>
  unnest_tokens(word, comment) |>
  anti_join(stop_words, by = "word") |>
  anti_join(bing, by = "word") |>
  count(word, sort = TRUE) |>
  head(25)

# A tibble: 25 × 2
   word            n
   <chr>       <int>
 1 treatment     394
 2 staff         357
 3 operation     309
 4 doctor        247
 5 ward          191
 6 food          185
 7 hospital      182
 8 caring        147
 9 doctors       147
10 experienced   146
# ℹ 15 more rows


Most of these are neutral, like treatment, staff and ward. But some clearly carry feeling in this context. Caring, recovered and experienced are positive. Forced, pay and wait are negative. In a free health scheme, pay is a strongly negative word, because patients should not have to pay at all.
So we add our own words to the dictionary. bind_rows() adds them below the Bing words.

my_words <- tribble(
  ~word,         ~sentiment,
  "caring",      "positive",
  "recovered",   "positive",
  "experienced", "positive",
  "explained",   "positive",
  "forced",      "negative",
  "pay",         "negative",
  "wait",        "negative",
  "nobody",      "negative"
)

my_dictionary <- bind_rows(bing, my_words)

Let us score the comments again, with negation handling and the extended dictionary.

feedback_final <- feedback |>
  unnest_tokens(word, comment) |>
  mutate(previous = lag(word), .by = feedback_id) |>
  inner_join(my_dictionary, by = "word") |>
  mutate(value = if_else(sentiment == "positive", 1, -1),
         value = if_else(previous %in% negations, -value, value)) |>
  score_comments()

cor(feedback_final$score, feedback_final$rating)

[1] 0.8184673


The agreement with the star rating has improved again, to 0.82. Each improvement came from understanding why the method went wrong, and fixing that specific problem.






TipAudit tip



Always check a sentiment method against something you trust, before relying on it. Here we had star ratings. Elsewhere, you can read and score 50 to 100 comments yourself, and compare with the method. If the method disagrees often, find out why, as we did, rather than accepting its numbers.

title: 49  Sentiment Analysis
text:
49.9 Comparing hospitals
Now let us use the scores. The simplest summary is the average score of each hospital, and the share of its comments that are negative.

hospital_sentiment <- feedback_final |>
  summarise(comments     = n(),
            avg_score    = mean(score),
            pct_negative = 100 * mean(score < 0),
            .by = hospital_id) |>
  arrange(avg_score)

hospital_sentiment |>
  head(10) |>
  mutate(across(where(is.double), \(x) round(x, 2)))

# A tibble: 10 × 4
   hospital_id comments avg_score pct_negative
   <chr>          <int>     <dbl>        <dbl>
 1 H071              16     -1.81         93.8
 2 H070              11     -1.36         81.8
 3 H066              12     -0.92         66.7
 4 H063              16     -0.88         62.5
 5 H116              10     -0.5          50  
 6 H102              10     -0.5          50  
 7 H082               9     -0.44         55.6
 8 H107               9     -0.33         55.6
 9 H112              10      0            40  
10 H109              10      0            30  


The five hospitals with the most negative feedback are all among the six “camp” hospitals that stood out in Chapter 44 and Chapter 48. But look at the comments column. Each hospital has only 2 to 23 comments. With so few comments, an average can swing a lot because of one or two unhappy patients.






WarningCaution, small numbers



An average built on ten comments is not reliable. Two hospitals with very different true quality can easily swap places by chance. Before ranking units by sentiment, either set a minimum number of comments, or compare groups of units, which gives larger numbers, as we do next.



49.9.1 Comparing groups
The earlier chapters gave us a group of six hospitals with unusual claims. Let us compare their feedback with that of all other hospitals together.

camp_hospitals <- c("H063", "H066", "H070", "H071", "H098", "H116")  # from the k-means chapter

feedback_final |>
  mutate(group = if_else(hospital_id %in% camp_hospitals,
                         "Six flagged hospitals", "All other hospitals")) |>
  summarise(comments     = n(),
            avg_score    = mean(score),
            pct_negative = 100 * mean(score < 0),
            avg_rating   = mean(rating),
            .by = group) |>
  mutate(across(where(is.double), \(x) round(x, 2)))

# A tibble: 2 × 5
  group                 comments avg_score pct_negative avg_rating
  <chr>                    <int>     <dbl>        <dbl>      <dbl>
1 All other hospitals       1424      1.01         23.0       3.62
2 Six flagged hospitals       76     -0.96         67.1       2.47


With the comments pooled, the difference is clear. Patients of the six flagged hospitals are far more often negative, and give lower star ratings. This is a third, independent source of evidence, after the claims data and the grievances, pointing to the same hospitals.

title: 49  Sentiment Analysis
section: 49.10 Beyond positive and negative, a red-flag dictionary
text:
49.10 Beyond positive and negative, a red-flag dictionary
Sentiment tells us how people feel. For audit, it is often more useful to know what specific problems they mention. We can use the same dictionary method with our own list of red-flag words, which point to possible wrongdoing rather than just unhappiness.

red_flags <- c("forced", "pay", "paid", "money", "cash")

feedback |>
  unnest_tokens(word, comment) |>
  filter(word %in% red_flags) |>
  mutate(group = if_else(hospital_id %in% camp_hospitals,
                         "Six flagged hospitals", "All other hospitals")) |>
  count(group, word) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = word, values_from = n, values_fill = 0)

# A tibble: 2 × 3
  group                 forced   pay
  <chr>                  <int> <int>
1 All other hospitals       46    36
2 Six flagged hospitals      8     9


At first sight, the other hospitals seem to have more such comments. But this is a trap. There are many more comments about the other hospitals, so they will have more of almost everything. A fair comparison needs a rate, for example red-flag comments per 100 comments.

feedback |>
  mutate(group = if_else(hospital_id %in% camp_hospitals,
                         "Six flagged hospitals", "All other hospitals"),
         has_red_flag = str_detect(str_to_lower(comment),
                                   paste0("\\b(", paste(red_flags, collapse = "|"), ")\\b"))) |>
  summarise(comments = n(),
            red_flag_comments = sum(has_red_flag),
            per_100_comments = round(100 * mean(has_red_flag), 1),
            .by = group)

# A tibble: 2 × 4
  group                 comments red_flag_comments per_100_comments
  <chr>                    <int>             <int>            <dbl>
1 All other hospitals       1424                81              5.7
2 Six flagged hospitals       76                17             22.4


Now the picture is the right way round. Comments about the six flagged hospitals mention being forced or having to pay at about four times the rate of comments about other hospitals. Words like forced are much more important for an auditor than a general negative word like bad.






WarningCompare rates, not counts



Whenever groups differ in size, compare rates or percentages, not raw counts. A large district will have more complaints than a small one, simply because it is large. This simple point is behind many wrong conclusions.








TipAudit tip



Build a red-flag dictionary for each audit, with the help of people who know the sector. In a health scheme, it may include words about forced or unnecessary surgery, payments, and agents. In a PDS audit, it may include words about short weighing, refusal of ration, or poor quality grain. Such a dictionary is easy to explain in an audit report, and easy for the auditee to verify.

title: 49  Sentiment Analysis
section: 49.11 Audit use case, feedback that is too good to be true
text:
49.11 Audit use case, feedback that is too good to be true
So far we looked for units with bad feedback. But very good feedback can also be a warning sign. When feedback is collected by the staff of the unit being assessed, some of it may be written by the staff themselves. Such feedback tends to be glowing, uniform, and copied from a few sentences.
Let us take feedback collected through a mobile app from beneficiaries of 25 Fair Price Shops under the Public Distribution System. Each beneficiary writes a short comment and gives a rating. Genuine comments vary. Some praise the shop, many complain about short weighing, poor quality grain, or the shop being closed. In two shops, FPS-07 and FPS-19, we have planted feedback filled in by the shop staff, mostly copies of three sentences with 5 stars.

Code to create the ration shop feedbackset.seed(909)
positive_bits <- c("Ration received on time.", "Dealer behaviour is good.", "Grain quality was fine.",
                   "Full quantity given.", "Shop opens regularly.")
negative_bits <- c("Less quantity given than entitled.", "Shop was closed on the notified day.",
                   "Grain was of poor quality with stones.", "Dealer asked extra money.",
                   "Told to come again next week.", "Weighing machine is not working.")
neutral_bits  <- c("Took ration for the family.", "Came with my ration card.", "Collected wheat and rice.")

genuine_comment <- function() {
  k <- sample(1:2, 1)
  mood <- sample(c("pos", "neg", "mix"), 1, prob = c(0.4, 0.35, 0.25))
  bits <- switch(mood,
                 pos = sample(positive_bits, k),
                 neg = sample(negative_bits, k),
                 mix = c(sample(positive_bits, 1), sample(negative_bits, 1)))
  rating <- switch(mood, pos = sample(4:5, 1), neg = sample(1:2, 1), mix = sample(2:4, 1))
  # Each beneficiary also mentions what they collected, in their own way
  detail <- sprintf(sample(c("Got %d kg wheat and %d kg rice.", "Collected %d kg wheat, %d kg rice.",
                             "Family of %d, got rice %d kg."), 1),
                    sample(3:35, 1), sample(3:35, 1))
  tibble(comment = paste(c(sample(neutral_bits, 1), detail, bits), collapse = " "), rating = rating)
}

shops <- sprintf("FPS-%02d", 1:25)
fps_feedback <- map_dfr(shops, function(s) {
  map_dfr(1:sample(35:60, 1), \(i) genuine_comment()) |> mutate(shop = s, .before = 1)
})

# Planted. Staff-written feedback in two shops
templates <- c("Very good service, ration received on time, thank you.",
               "Excellent dealer, full quantity given, very happy.",
               "Good quality grain and very good behaviour, thank you.")
staff_written <- which(fps_feedback$shop %in% c("FPS-07", "FPS-19"))
staff_written <- sample(staff_written, round(0.65 * length(staff_written)))
fps_feedback$comment[staff_written] <- sample(templates, length(staff_written), TRUE)
fps_feedback$rating[staff_written]  <- 5

fps_feedback <- fps_feedback |> mutate(feedback_id = row_number(), .before = 1)



fps_feedback |> slice_sample(n = 5)

# A tibble: 5 × 4
  feedback_id shop   comment                                              rating
        <int> <chr>  <chr>                                                 <dbl>
1         342 FPS-07 Very good service, ration received on time, thank y…      5
2         770 FPS-15 Came with my ration card. Got 29 kg wheat and 7 kg …      1
3         613 FPS-13 Came with my ration card. Collected 33 kg wheat, 35…      4
4         160 FPS-04 Collected wheat and rice. Family of 14, got rice 15…      1
5         252 FPS-06 Took ration for the family. Family of 8, got rice 2…      2


First, let us score the comments with the Bing dictionary, handling negation as before, and rank the shops by their average score.

fps_scores <- fps_feedback |>
  unnest_tokens(word, comment, drop = FALSE) |>
  mutate(previous = lag(word), .by = feedback_id) |>
  inner_join(bing, by = "word") |>
  mutate(value = if_else(sentiment == "positive", 1, -1),
         value = if_else(previous %in% negations, -value, value)) |>
  summarise(score = sum(value), .by = feedback_id)

fps_scored <- fps_feedback |>
  left_join(fps_scores, by = "feedback_id") |>
  mutate(score = replace_na(score, 0))

fps_scored |>
  summarise(comments = n(), avg_score = round(mean(score), 2), avg_rating = round(mean(rating), 2),
            .by = shop) |>
  arrange(desc(avg_score)) |>
  head(5)

# A tibble: 5 × 4
  shop   comments avg_score avg_rating
  <chr>     <int>     <dbl>      <dbl>
1 FPS-07       59      1.58       4.25
2 FPS-19       46      1.39       4.2 
3 FPS-25       41      0.34       3.51
4 FPS-04       41      0.32       3.61
5 FPS-09       52      0.29       3.02


The two shops come out as the best in the district. If we stopped here, we would praise them. Now let us look at how many of each shop’s comments are word-for-word copies of another comment of the same shop. We first standardise the text, so that differences of case and spacing do not hide a copy.

fps_dupes <- fps_scored |>
  mutate(std_comment = str_squish(str_to_lower(comment))) |>
  add_count(shop, std_comment, name = "copies") |>
  summarise(comments       = n(),
            pct_duplicated = round(100 * mean(copies > 1), 1),
            pct_five_star  = round(100 * mean(rating == 5), 1),
            avg_score      = round(mean(score), 2),
            .by = shop) |>
  arrange(desc(pct_duplicated))

head(fps_dupes, 5)

# A tibble: 5 × 5
  shop   comments pct_duplicated pct_five_star avg_score
  <chr>     <int>          <dbl>         <dbl>     <dbl>
1 FPS-07       59           67.8          72.9      1.58
2 FPS-19       46           60.9          63        1.39
3 FPS-01       46            0            17.4      0.28
4 FPS-02       60            0            18.3      0.28
5 FPS-03       46            0            26.1      0.13


In the two shops, most of the comments are copies of each other, and most ratings are 5 stars. In the other shops, not a single comment is a copy of another. Genuine beneficiaries write in their own words, mention their own quantities, and complain about different things. In real data, very short comments like “good” or “ok” will repeat by chance, so compare a unit with its peers rather than expecting zero duplicates.






TipAudit tip



Look at how people write, not only what they write. Many identical comments, uniform top ratings, and unusually high sentiment in one unit together suggest that the feedback was not written by the beneficiaries. Verify by contacting a sample of the beneficiaries whose names appear against those comments. The same check works for inspection reports, monitoring notes, and site visit remarks copied from one report to the next.

title: 49  Sentiment Analysis
text:
49.12 Limitations






WarningWhat dictionary methods cannot do





Sarcasm and irony. “Great service, waited only six hours!” will be scored as positive.

Context. Free is positive in “treatment was free”, but has nothing to do with sentiment in “free health camp”.

Mixed comments. A comment praising the doctor and complaining about the food gets a score near zero, which hides both points.

Other languages. Words in Hindi or other languages, and mixed-language text, are not in English dictionaries.

Longer negations. Our fix handles “not good”, but not “not at all good” or “I would not say it was good”.

More advanced methods, based on machine learning and large language models, handle some of these better. But they are harder to explain, and their errors are harder to spot. For audit work, a simple, transparent method that you have checked carefully is often the better choice.

title: 49  Sentiment Analysis
text:
49.13 A suggested workflow


Read a sample of the text to understand how people write about the subject.

Choose a dictionary. Start with Bing, which needs no download.

Tokenise, join with the dictionary, and score each document.

Check the scores against something you trust, such as ratings or your own reading of a sample.

Fix the main problems, especially negation and missing domain words.

Summarise by unit or group, with enough documents behind each number.

Add a red-flag dictionary for the specific risks of the audit.

Read the actual comments behind every unit you flag.







ImportantRemember



A sentiment score is a summary of many opinions, not a fact. Use it to decide where to look. The actual comments, read in full, are the evidence.

title: 50  Visualising Text
text:
50.1 Prerequisites
Suppose an auditor of a State health insurance scheme has hundreds of grievances from patients. The audit report must tell its readers, in a page or two, what all this text is about. A table of word counts is accurate, but few readers will study it. A good picture of text can show, at a glance, what a long document or a large set of documents is about. It can also show how the complaints about one group of hospitals differ from those about all the others. Such a picture often makes the case for a closer look better than a page of words.
In the last two chapters, we learnt to clean text, count words and measure sentiment. The results were tables of words and numbers. In this chapter, we will turn such results into pictures. We will practise first on the Union Budget speech. Then we will turn to the grievances of the imaginary health scheme of Chapter 48, where six hospitals have already drawn our attention.
We will learn four kinds of charts.
library(tidyverse)
library(tidytext)
library(wordcloud)   # install.packages("wordcloud")

title: 50  Visualising Text
section: 50.2 A first picture, the Union Budget speech
text:
50.2 A first picture, the Union Budget speech
As our first example, we will look at the Budget speech of the Finance Minister for 2022-231. The full text of the speech is available in the file budget.txt in the Data folder.

50.2.1 Step 1. Read the text
The file is a plain text file, with one paragraph on each line. readLines() reads such a file, giving one element for each line. We then put the lines into a data frame, one row per paragraph.

speech <- readLines("Data/budget.txt", encoding = "UTF-8", warn = FALSE)

speech_df <- tibble(paragraph = seq_along(speech), text = speech)

speech_df |>
  slice(1:4)

# A tibble: 4 × 2
  paragraph text                                                                
      <int> <chr>                                                               
1         1 "Hon’ble Speaker, "                                                 
2         2 "I present theBudget for the year 2022-23."                         
3         3 "Introduction"                                                      
4         4 "1.\tAt the outset, I want to take a moment to express my empathy f…


The speech has 284 lines, from the opening “Hon’ble Speaker” to the last paragraph.

50.2.2 Step 2. Tokenise and count words
As in Chapter 48, we break the text into words with unnest_tokens(), and count them.

speech_words <- speech_df |>
  unnest_tokens(word, text) |>
  count(word, sort = TRUE)

speech_words |>
  head(10)

# A tibble: 10 × 2
   word      n
   <chr> <int>
 1 the     428
 2 of      359
 3 and     333
 4 to      273
 5 in      204
 6 for     189
 7 will    180
 8 be      137
 9 a       106
10 this     82



50.2.3 Step 3. Remove stop words
The top words are stop words, as expected. We remove them with the standard list. We also remove numbers, which the speech has in plenty, like paragraph numbers, years and amounts.

speech_clean <- speech_words |>
  anti_join(stop_words, by = "word") |>
  filter(!str_detect(word, "^[0-9]"))

We may also remove some words specific to this document. To know which ones, we can first skip this step and make the chart directly. After a first look, we identify the words that carry no meaning here, and remove them. Cent comes from “per cent”, crore and lakh from amounts, and sir from addressing the Speaker.

speech_stop_words <- tibble(word = c("cent", "pm", "crore", "lakh",
                                     "set", "level", "sir"))

speech_clean <- speech_clean |>
  anti_join(speech_stop_words, by = "word")

speech_clean |>
  head(10)

# A tibble: 10 × 2
   word               n
   <chr>          <int>
 1 digital           34
 2 capital           33
 3 government        30
 4 development       29
 5 tax               28
 6 infrastructure    26
 7 investment        26
 8 provide           26
 9 income            22
10 customs           20








TipAudit tip



The words we remove change the picture. So keep the list of custom stop words in the working papers, along with the reason for removing each word. A reviewer can then see that no meaningful word was dropped to make the chart look a certain way.

title: 50  Visualising Text
text:
50.3 Frequency plots
The simplest and most accurate picture of word counts is a bar chart. We take the top words, and draw one bar for each (Figure 50.1).

speech_clean |>
  slice_max(n, n = 20) |>
  ggplot(aes(n, fct_reorder(word, n))) +
  geom_col(fill = "steelblue") +
  labs(x = "Number of times used", y = NULL) +
  theme_bw()






Figure 50.1: Most frequent words in the Budget speech 2022-23




fct_reorder(word, n) orders the words by their count, so that the longest bar is at the top. Without it, the words would appear in alphabetical order. We learnt about ordering factors in Chapter 24.
The chart tells us at once what the speech emphasised. Digital, capital, government, development, tax, infrastructure, investment, and so on. Each bar can be read and compared exactly.

title: 50  Visualising Text
text:
50.4 Word clouds
A word cloud draws the words themselves, with more frequent words in larger letters. It is less precise than a bar chart, but it is striking, and it can show many more words in the same space. This makes it popular in presentations.
The function wordcloud() from the package wordcloud draws it. Its main arguments are these.


words and freq are the words and their counts.

max.words is the maximum number of words to draw.

random.order = FALSE puts the most frequent words in the centre.

colors gives the colours to use. We take a palette from RColorBrewer, which we discussed in Appendix D.

scale gives the range of letter sizes, from the largest to the smallest.

The output of the following code can be seen in Figure 50.2.

pal <- RColorBrewer::brewer.pal(8, "Dark2")

set.seed(123)
speech_clean |>
  with(wordcloud(words = word,
                 freq = n,
                 random.order = FALSE,
                 max.words = 40,
                 colors = pal,
                 scale = c(2.5, 0.5)))






Figure 50.2: Word Cloud of FM’s Budget Speech 2022




The positions of words in a cloud are partly random. We used set.seed() so that the cloud looks the same every time the code is run.






WarningCaution



Word clouds look good, but they read poorly. The human eye is not good at comparing the sizes of words. A long word looks more important than a short one of the same count. And the colours usually carry no meaning. So use word clouds to give a quick impression, especially in presentations. For analysis, and for any comparison that matters, use a bar chart.

title: 50  Visualising Text
text:
50.5 Comparing groups of documents
In audit, we usually want to compare. What do complaints about one set of hospitals say, compared with complaints about others? Let us return to the grievances of the imaginary Sarvajan Swasthya Yojana from Chapter 48.

grievances <- read_csv("Data/ssy_grievances.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)

griev_stop_words <- tibble(word = c("sir", "ji", "madam", "respected", "dear", "officer",
                                    "kindly", "please", "help", "action", "matter",
                                    "urgently", "look", "contact", "mobile", "poor",
                                    "people", "hospital", "hospitl", "scheme", "ssy",
                                    "patient", "rs", "rupees", "ke", "le", "kar"))

griev_words <- grievances |>
  unnest_tokens(word, text) |>
  anti_join(stop_words, by = "word") |>
  anti_join(griev_stop_words, by = "word") |>
  filter(!str_detect(word, "[0-9]"))

These are the same cleaning steps as in Chapter 48.

50.5.1 Top words in each category, side by side
To compare the top words of several groups, we draw one small bar chart for each group, side by side, with facet_wrap(). There is one problem. Each group has its own order of words. fct_reorder() can only give one order for the whole chart. tidytext solves this with two helper functions. reorder_within() orders the words separately within each group, and scale_y_reordered() cleans up the labels (Figure 50.3).

griev_words |>
  count(category, word) |>
  slice_max(n, n = 6, by = category, with_ties = FALSE) |>
  ggplot(aes(n, reorder_within(word, n, category))) +
  geom_col(fill = "steelblue") +
  scale_y_reordered() +
  facet_wrap(~category, scales = "free_y", ncol = 2) +
  labs(x = "Number of times used", y = NULL) +
  theme_bw()






Figure 50.3: Most frequent words in each category of grievance




Each panel shows the top words of one category. The panel for Other stands out. Its top word is operation, by a wide margin, followed by words like free and camp. These do not belong to any of the fixed categories. This is the same finding as in Chapter 48, now visible in one picture.

title: 50  Visualising Text
section: 50.6 Audit use case, grievances about six flagged hospitals
text:
50.6 Audit use case, grievances about six flagged hospitals
In Chapter 44, six hospitals stood out for their unusual claims. In Chapter 48 and Chapter 49, their grievances also looked different. Let us now make a picture that shows, to a reader of the audit report, how the grievances about these six hospitals differ from those about all other hospitals.

50.6.1 A comparison cloud
A comparison cloud shows two or more groups in one cloud. Each word is placed in the part of the cloud belonging to the group in which it is relatively more frequent. Let us compare grievances about the six flagged hospitals with grievances about all other hospitals.
The function comparison.cloud() needs the counts in a matrix, with words as rows and groups as columns. We prepare it with pivot_wider(), and convert it with column_to_rownames() and as.matrix().

camp_hospitals <- c("H063", "H066", "H070", "H071", "H098", "H116")  # flagged in the k-means chapter

compare_matrix <- griev_words |>
  mutate(group = if_else(hospital_id %in% camp_hospitals,
                         "Six flagged hospitals", "Other hospitals")) |>
  count(word, group) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = group, values_from = n, values_fill = 0) |>
  column_to_rownames("word") |>
  as.matrix()

head(compare_matrix)

         Other hospitals Six flagged hospitals
accepted              41                     4
active                41                     2
admit                 41                     2
admitted               2                    10
age                    3                    17
agent                  5                    18


Now we draw it (Figure 50.4).

set.seed(123)
comparison.cloud(compare_matrix,
                 max.words = 60,
                 colors = c("grey40", "firebrick"),
                 title.size = 1.2,
                 scale = c(2.5, 0.5))






Figure 50.4: Words relatively more frequent in grievances about each group of hospitals




The two halves tell two different stories. Grievances about other hospitals are mostly about cards, refusals, pending approvals and the ward. Grievances about the six flagged hospitals are about operations, camps, agents, villages, pain and the uterus being removed. For an audit presentation, this one picture can make the case for a closer look at those six hospitals.

50.6.2 A more precise comparison, the log ratio
A comparison cloud gives an impression, but it does not tell us how much more common a word is in one group. For an audit report, a bar chart of the log ratio is better. For each word, we take its share among all the words of each group, and compare the two shares.
\[
\text{log ratio} = \log_2 \left( \frac{\text{share of the word in flagged hospitals}}{\text{share of the word in other hospitals}} \right)
\tag{50.1}\]
A log ratio of 1 means the word is twice as common, relatively, in grievances about the flagged hospitals. A log ratio of -1 means it is twice as common about the other hospitals. Zero means no difference. We add 1 to every count before dividing, so that a word missing from one group does not give a division by zero. We also keep only words used at least 10 times, since ratios of very small counts are unreliable.

log_ratios <- as_tibble(compare_matrix, rownames = "word") |>
  rename(flagged = `Six flagged hospitals`, other = `Other hospitals`) |>
  filter(flagged + other >= 10) |>
  mutate(log_ratio = log2(((flagged + 1) / sum(flagged + 1)) /
                          ((other + 1) / sum(other + 1))))

# Top 10 words on each side
bind_rows(slice_max(log_ratios, log_ratio, n = 10, with_ties = FALSE),
          slice_min(log_ratios, log_ratio, n = 10, with_ties = FALSE)) |>
  mutate(group = if_else(log_ratio > 0, "More common, flagged hospitals",
                         "More common, other hospitals")) |>
  ggplot(aes(log_ratio, fct_reorder(word, log_ratio), fill = group)) +
  geom_col() +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("firebrick", "grey50")) +
  labs(x = "Log ratio (base 2)", y = NULL, fill = NULL) +
  theme_bw() +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")






Figure 50.5: Words that set the two groups of hospitals apart




Each bar can be read exactly. For example, camp has a log ratio of 3.6, so it is about 12 times as common, relatively, in grievances about the flagged hospitals. The other words at the top, like vehicle, panchayat, bhawan, village and healed, describe the same story of camps held in villages and wounds that have not healed. At the other end, pre, authorisation, delayed, pending and approval are typical of the routine complaints about other hospitals.

50.6.3 Back to the grievances
A picture points to a theme. The auditor still needs the grievances behind it. Let us pick out the grievances about the six hospitals that mention a camp, a vehicle or a village, and count them by hospital.

camp_grievances <- grievances |>
  filter(hospital_id %in% camp_hospitals,
         str_detect(str_to_lower(text), "camp|vehicle|village"))

camp_grievances |>
  count(hospital_id, sort = TRUE)

# A tibble: 6 × 2
  hospital_id     n
  <chr>       <int>
1 H070           15
2 H063           11
3 H066           11
4 H071           11
5 H098           10
6 H116            9


There are 67 such grievances. They come from all six hospitals, so the pattern is not the work of one hospital alone. Let us read a few of them.

camp_grievances |>
  slice_head(n = 3) |>
  pull(text)

[1] "To the officer, Agent of the hospitl told villagers that free operation is available, took us in their van on Sunday. Please look into the matter urgently."
[2] "Camp ke baad hospital le gaye, operation kar diya. Nobody explained anything to us."                                                                        
[3] "sir ji, agent of the hospital told villagers that free operation is available, took us in their van on sunday. we are poor people, please help."            


The words in the pictures are now backed by the patients’ own accounts.






TipAudit tip



Put the chart in the report, but keep the list of grievances behind it in the working papers. A reader may question a picture. A list of dated grievances, each with an ID, is evidence.


The next steps for the auditor follow from here.

Match these grievances with the claims of the same hospitals, by patient and by date of admission.
Check whether the patients came from the same villages, on the same days, as a camp would suggest.
Ask the scheme authority what action it took on each grievance.
Where needed, plan a survey of beneficiaries in those villages.

title: 50  Visualising Text
text:
50.7 Word networks
Bar charts and clouds show single words. To see how words are connected, we can draw a network of bigrams. Each word is a point (a node), and an arrow (an edge) joins two words that appear one after the other. We will study networks in detail in Chapter 51, with the package igraph. Here we use igraph only to build the network. We draw it with ggraph, which draws networks in the style of ggplot2.

library(igraph)
library(ggraph)

First, we count bigrams, after removing stop words from both words, as in Chapter 48. We keep only the more frequent ones, so that the picture is readable.

all_stops <- c(stop_words$word, griev_stop_words$word)

bigram_counts <- grievances |>
  unnest_tokens(bigram, text, token = "ngrams", n = 2) |>
  separate_wider_delim(bigram, delim = " ", names = c("word1", "word2")) |>
  filter(!word1 %in% all_stops, !word2 %in% all_stops,
         !str_detect(word1, "[0-9]"), !str_detect(word2, "[0-9]")) |>
  count(word1, word2, sort = TRUE) |>
  filter(n >= 15)

bigram_counts

# A tibble: 17 × 3
   word1    word2             n
   <chr>    <chr>         <int>
 1 pre      authorisation    46
 2 accepted staff            45
 3 days     junior           40
 4 doctor   visited          40
 5 junior   staff            40
 6 package  list             38
 7 refused  treatment        38
 8 drinking water            37
 9 staff    demanded         33
10 card     amount           31
11 blood    test             28
12 health   camp             27
13 told     villagers        23
14 feel     weak             20
15 free     operation        20
16 stomach  pain             20
17 gaye     operation        17


graph_from_data_frame() from igraph turns this table into a network. The first two columns become the two ends of each edge, and n becomes an edge attribute.

bigram_graph <- graph_from_data_frame(bigram_counts)

set.seed(2024)
ggraph(bigram_graph, layout = "fr") +
  geom_edge_link(aes(edge_alpha = n),
                 arrow = grid::arrow(length = unit(2, "mm")),
                 end_cap = circle(2, "mm"), show.legend = FALSE) +
  geom_node_point(colour = "steelblue", size = 3) +
  geom_node_text(aes(label = name), vjust = 1.5, size = 3.5) +
  theme_void()






Figure 50.6: Network of frequent word pairs in grievances




In Figure 50.6, the arrows follow the order of words, and darker arrows mean more frequent pairs. layout = "fr" places strongly connected words near each other. We can now read short phrases straight from the picture, like health camp, told villagers, free operation and staff demanded.

50.7.1 An interactive word network
For exploring, an interactive network is often more useful than a static one. We can drag the words apart, zoom in, and click a word to highlight the words joined to it. The package visNetwork, which we will use again in Chapter 51 and Chapter 52, draws one directly from the igraph object (Figure 50.7).

library(visNetwork)

bigram_vis <- toVisNetworkData(bigram_graph)
bigram_vis$edges <- bigram_vis$edges |>
  mutate(value = n, title = paste0(from, " ", to, ", ", n, " times"))

visNetwork(bigram_vis$nodes, bigram_vis$edges, width = "100%", height = "450px") |>
  visEdges(arrows = "to", color = list(color = "grey")) |>
  visNodes(color = "steelblue", font = list(size = 18)) |>
  visIgraphLayout(layout = "layout_with_fr", randomSeed = 2024) |>
  visOptions(highlightNearest = TRUE)






Figure 50.7: Interactive network of frequent word pairs. Click a word to highlight its neighbours.









NotePairs across punctuation



Look at the pair accepted → staff. It comes from sentences like “card is not accepted, staff says server is down”. unnest_tokens() removes the comma before forming pairs, so the last word of one phrase gets joined to the first word of the next. Such pairs are artefacts, not real phrases. If they matter, split the text into sentences or phrases first, for example with unnest_tokens(token = "sentences"), and then form bigrams within each.

title: 50  Visualising Text
text:
50.9 A suggested workflow


Clean and count the text, as in Chapter 48.

Start with a bar chart of the top words. It is the most honest picture.

Refine the stop words after the first look, and redraw.

Compare groups with faceted bar charts or comparison clouds.

Use bigram networks when phrases matter more than single words.

Use word clouds for presentation, and set a seed so they can be reproduced.

Check every striking picture against the documents behind it. Pull out the records behind each theme, and keep them in the working papers.







ImportantRemember



A picture of text is a summary, and every summary leaves things out. The most frequent words are not always the most important ones. A single grievance about a death in a hospital matters more than a hundred about dirty toilets. Use the pictures to see the broad picture, and the documents to see what really happened.
