Persons with IDs 6 and 10 share none of the three IDs, Mobile, Email and PAN. But look closely. ID-6 shares the mobile number with ID-1, who in turn shares the PAN with ID-2. ID-2 further shares both the email and the mobile number with ID-10. So ID-6 and ID-10 are linked, through a chain. Such chains are impossible to see in a table of thousands of rows. But they are obvious in a network, as in Figure 52.1. Note that we are not using names to find duplicates. Names are easily changed and often spelt differently.

id_long <- dummy_data |>
  pivot_longer(-ID, names_to = "id_type", values_to = "value") |>
  mutate(person = paste0("ID-", ID),
         id_node = paste(id_type, value, sep = ":"))

id_nodes <- bind_rows(
  tibble(id = unique(id_long$person), group = "Person"),
  distinct(id_long, id = id_node, group = id_type)
) |>
  mutate(label = if_else(group == "Person", id, ""), title = id)

visNetwork(id_nodes, select(id_long, from = person, to = id_node),
           width = "100%", height = "450px") |>
  visGroups(groupname = "Person", color = "steelblue", shape = "dot") |>
  visGroups(groupname = "Mobile", color = "orange", shape = "square") |>
  visGroups(groupname = "Email", color = "seagreen", shape = "triangle") |>
  visGroups(groupname = "PAN", color = "tomato", shape = "diamond") |>
  visOptions(highlightNearest = TRUE) |>
  visLegend()






Figure 52.1: Network of persons (blue) and their IDs. Hover or click to explore.



Notice the structure of this graph. It is bipartite. Persons are connected only to IDs, and IDs only to persons. Two persons are related if there is any path between them. In graph theory terms, all related persons fall in the same connected component. So all we have to do is find the components of this graph.

52.2.1 The algorithm
Here is the complete algorithm.

id_cols <- c("Mobile", "Email", "PAN")

dummy_data |>
  mutate(across(all_of(id_cols), as.character)) |>
  pivot_longer(cols = all_of(id_cols), names_to = "id_type",
               values_to = "value", values_drop_na = TRUE) |>
  mutate(id_node = paste(id_type, value, sep = ":")) |>
  select(ID, id_node) |>
  graph_from_data_frame(directed = FALSE) |>
  components() |>
  _$membership |>
  stack() |>
  set_names(c("UNIQUE_ID", "ID")) |>
  filter(!str_detect(ID, ":")) |>
  mutate(ID = as.integer(as.character(ID))) |>
  right_join(dummy_data, by = "ID")

   UNIQUE_ID ID     Mobile          Email        PAN
1          1  1 9111111111 aaaa@gmail.com PANNO0000A
2          1  2 9222222222 bbbb@gmail.com PANNO0000A
3          2  3 9333333333 cccc@gmail.com PANNO1111B
4          3  4 9444444444 dddd@gmail.com PANNO2222C
5          1  5 9111111111 eeee@gmail.com PANNO3333D
6          1  6 9111111111 ffff@gmail.com PANNO4444E
7          4  7 9555555555 gggg@gmail.com PANNO5555F
8          4  8 9666666666 hhhh@gmail.com PANNO5555F
9          2  9 9333333333 iiii@gmail.com PANNO6666G
10         1 10 9222222222 bbbb@gmail.com PANNO7777H


We now have a UNIQUE_ID for each person, based on all three IDs together. Persons 1, 2, 5, 6 and 10 share one UNIQUE_ID, so they may be the same person, or a group acting together. Let us understand the algorithm step by step.
Step 1. All the ID columns must be of the same type. Real data often has a mix of character and numeric IDs, like a numeric mobile number and an alphanumeric PAN. Using across() inside mutate(), we convert all of them to character. Readers may refer to Section 1.4.1 for changing types, and Section 13.15 for changing many columns at once with across().
id_cols <- c("Mobile", "Email", "PAN")
dummy_data |>
  mutate(across(all_of(id_cols), as.character))
Step 2. Pivot all the ID columns into a longer format, so that each row links one person with one ID. Two things should be kept in mind. First, the data must have a column which identifies each record, here ID. If there is none, create one with row_number() before pivoting. Second, missing IDs must be removed while pivoting, using values_drop_na = TRUE. Otherwise, all persons with a missing PAN would be linked through the common value NA.
Step 3. Prefix each ID value with its type, like Mobile:9111111111. This is important. Without it, a value appearing in two different columns would become one vertex. For example, a record number "12" and a ward number "12" would wrongly link two records. Then we keep only the two columns we need, the record ID and the prefixed id_node. Up to this step, our data looks like this.






NoteNormalise the IDs first



In real data, the same ID is written in many ways, and each way would become a separate vertex. Before Step 2, standardise every ID column. Mobile numbers lose their +91 or 0 prefix with clean_mobile(), and email IDs are normalised with normalise_email(), both from Section 19.10. The second is especially important. Gmail ignores dots and +tags in the user name, so r.kumar@gmail.com and rkumar+scheme@gmail.com reach the same mailbox. Someone registering several times may use exactly this trick, and without normalising, the network would never connect those registrations.




# A tibble: 6 × 2
     ID id_node             
  <int> <chr>               
1     1 Mobile:9111111111   
2     1 Email:aaaa@gmail.com
3     1 PAN:PANNO0000A      
4     2 Mobile:9222222222   
5     2 Email:bbbb@gmail.com
6     2 PAN:PANNO0000A      


Step 4. We create an undirected graph from this data, using graph_from_data_frame(). Each row becomes an edge between a person and an ID. Readers may plot it, but for large data the plot will be a cluttered hairball. The tips at the end of this chapter explain how to deal with that.
Step 5. components() finds the connected components of the graph. Its element $membership is a named vector, giving the component number of each vertex.

id_graph <- graph_from_data_frame(id_edges, directed = FALSE)
components(id_graph)$membership

                   1                    2                    3 
                   1                    1                    2 
                   4                    5                    6 
                   3                    1                    1 
                   7                    8                    9 
                   4                    4                    2 
                  10    Mobile:9111111111 Email:aaaa@gmail.com 
                   1                    1                    1 
      PAN:PANNO0000A    Mobile:9222222222 Email:bbbb@gmail.com 
                   1                    1                    1 
   Mobile:9333333333 Email:cccc@gmail.com       PAN:PANNO1111B 
                   2                    2                    2 
   Mobile:9444444444 Email:dddd@gmail.com       PAN:PANNO2222C 
                   3                    3                    3 
Email:eeee@gmail.com       PAN:PANNO3333D Email:ffff@gmail.com 
                   1                    1                    1 
      PAN:PANNO4444E    Mobile:9555555555 Email:gggg@gmail.com 
                   1                    4                    4 
      PAN:PANNO5555F    Mobile:9666666666 Email:hhhh@gmail.com 
                   4                    4                    4 
Email:iiii@gmail.com       PAN:PANNO6666G       PAN:PANNO7777H 
                   2                    2                    1 


The native pipe placeholder _$membership extracts this element inside a pipe. We then convert the named vector into a data frame with stack(), and name its two columns with set_names().
Step 6. The membership includes the ID vertices too, like Mobile:9111111111. We keep only the person vertices, which have no : in their name. Their names are characters, so we convert them back to integers. Finally, we join the result back to the original data with right_join().

52.2.2 A bigger example, beneficiaries of a scheme
The small register showed the idea. Let us now try it on a more realistic register of 3,000 beneficiaries of an imaginary State scheme. The scheme pays ₹6,000 a year to each beneficiary, by direct benefit transfer into the bank account. Each beneficiary has a mobile number and a bank account. About 60% of them have also given a PAN. We have planted a few cases.

60 pairs of beneficiaries share a mobile number. These are families, and genuine.
A ring of 7 registrations, each sharing one ID with the previous one, as if one person kept registering again, changing one ID at a time.
An agent’s mobile number, entered against 30 beneficiaries.
A placeholder mobile number, 9999999999, entered by data entry operators against 45 beneficiaries who did not give a number.

As usual, the code to create the data is folded.

Code to create the beneficiary registerset.seed(1234)
n <- 3000
rand_mobile <- function(k) paste0(sample(6:9, k, TRUE), sprintf("%09d", sample(0:999999999, k)))
rand_acct   <- function(k) sprintf("%011.0f", runif(k, 1e10, 9e10))
rand_pan    <- function(k) paste0(replicate(k, paste(sample(LETTERS, 5, TRUE), collapse = "")),
                                  sprintf("%04d", sample(0:9999, k, TRUE)), sample(LETTERS, k, TRUE))

ben <- tibble(ben_id  = sprintf("B%05d", 1:n),
              mobile  = rand_mobile(n),
              bank_ac = rand_acct(n),
              pan     = rand_pan(n))

# Genuine. 60 families share a mobile number
fam <- sample(1:n, 120)
ben$mobile[fam[61:120]] <- ben$mobile[fam[1:60]]

# Planted. A ring of 7 registrations, each sharing one ID with the previous one
ring <- c(101, 502, 903, 1304, 1705, 2106, 2507)

# PAN not given by about 40% of beneficiaries
ben$pan[sample(setdiff(1:n, ring), 0.4 * n)] <- NA

for (i in 2:length(ring)) {
  col <- c("mobile", "bank_ac", "pan")[(i %% 3) + 1]
  ben[[col]][ring[i]] <- ben[[col]][ring[i - 1]]
}

# Planted. An agent's mobile number on 30 beneficiaries
agent <- sample(setdiff(1:n, c(ring, fam)), 30)
ben$mobile[agent] <- "9876543210"

# Placeholder number entered when the mobile was not given
junk <- sample(setdiff(1:n, c(ring, fam, agent)), 45)
ben$mobile[junk] <- "9999999999"



head(ben)

# A tibble: 6 × 4
  ben_id mobile     bank_ac     pan       
  <chr>  <chr>      <chr>       <chr>     
1 B00001 9917386478 18050509803 XOXWL9138R
2 B00002 9370227021 56371950097 <NA>      
3 B00003 7167562714 21329966281 LYMCW8437B
4 B00004 7550824366 76115990430 <NA>      
5 B00005 6444067445 43472028691 <NA>      
6 B00006 9758995374 32394157834 DGJHX1642S


Let us convert it into the long format, with prefixed IDs, as before.

ben_long <- ben |>
  pivot_longer(-ben_id, names_to = "id_type", values_to = "value",
               values_drop_na = TRUE) |>
  mutate(id_node = paste(id_type, value, sep = ":"))

First, look at the most shared IDs. Before building any graph, let us count how many beneficiaries each ID is linked with.

ben_long |>
  count(id_node, sort = TRUE) |>
  head(5)

# A tibble: 5 × 2
  id_node                 n
  <chr>               <int>
1 mobile:9999999999      45
2 mobile:9876543210      30
3 bank_ac:14356289729     2
4 bank_ac:55509169120     2
5 mobile:6018888444       2


Two values stand out at once. 9999999999 is obviously a placeholder, not a real number. If we keep it, it will link 45 unrelated beneficiaries into one false group. The other value, 9876543210, is linked with 30 beneficiaries. It looks genuine, and is exactly the kind of hub an auditor wants to find. It may be the number of an agent or a middleman, who registered and perhaps controls these beneficiaries. We drop the placeholder and keep the rest. In larger data, such junk values can be found systematically, before building any graph. A number made of one repeated digit is matched by the regex ^(\\d)\\1{9}$. IDs which fail their format or check digit can also be listed. Both are explained in Section 19.10 and Section 19.11.

ben_long <- ben_long |>
  filter(value != "9999999999")

Next, drop the leaf nodes. Most IDs belong to exactly one beneficiary. In the graph, such an ID is a leaf, a vertex with only one edge. A leaf can never link two beneficiaries, so it adds nothing to our analysis. It only makes the graph bigger. Let us compare the graph with and without them.

g_full <- graph_from_data_frame(select(ben_long, ben_id, id_node), directed = FALSE)

# Keep only IDs shared by at least two beneficiaries
ben_shared <- ben_long |>
  add_count(id_node) |>
  filter(n > 1)

g_ben <- graph_from_data_frame(select(ben_shared, ben_id, id_node), directed = FALSE)

tibble(graph    = c("All IDs", "Shared IDs only"),
       vertices = c(vcount(g_full), vcount(g_ben)),
       edges    = c(ecount(g_full), ecount(g_ben)))

# A tibble: 2 × 3
  graph           vertices edges
  <chr>              <dbl> <dbl>
1 All IDs            10660  7755
2 Shared IDs only      224   162


The graph has shrunk from 10,660 vertices to just 224, and the answer is not affected at all. Beneficiaries who share nothing with anyone have dropped out too, which is what we want. With real data of lakhs of records, this one step often makes the difference between a graph R can handle easily and one it cannot.
Now find the groups. Let us find the components, and count how many beneficiaries each one has.

ben_groups <- components(g_ben)$membership |>
  stack() |>
  set_names(c("group", "node")) |>
  filter(str_starts(node, "B")) |>
  count(group, name = "beneficiaries", sort = TRUE)

ben_groups |> count(beneficiaries, name = "number_of_groups")

  beneficiaries number_of_groups
1             2               60
2             7                1
3            30                1


There are 60 groups of two. These are mostly the families who share a mobile, which is normal. There is one group of 30, around the agent’s number. And there is one group of 7, the ring we planted. At ₹6,000 a year each, the ring draws ₹42,000 a year. The beneficiaries around the agent’s number draw ₹1.8 lakh a year. These amounts are at risk until the beneficiaries are verified. Let us draw the second largest group, in Figure 52.2.

# ben_groups is sorted by size. Take the second largest group.
ring_id <- ben_groups$group[2]
ring_nodes <- names(which(components(g_ben)$membership == ring_id))

ring_graph <- induced_subgraph(g_ben, ring_nodes)

ring_vis <- toVisNetworkData(ring_graph)
ring_vis$nodes <- ring_vis$nodes |>
  mutate(group = if_else(str_starts(id, "B"), "Beneficiary", str_extract(id, "^[a-z_]+")),
         title = id)

visNetwork(ring_vis$nodes, ring_vis$edges, width = "100%", height = "400px") |>
  visGroups(groupname = "Beneficiary", color = "steelblue", shape = "dot") |>
  visGroups(groupname = "mobile", color = "orange", shape = "square") |>
  visGroups(groupname = "bank_ac", color = "purple", shape = "triangle") |>
  visGroups(groupname = "pan", color = "tomato", shape = "diamond") |>
  visOptions(highlightNearest = TRUE) |>
  visLegend()






Figure 52.2: A ring of 7 registrations linked through changing IDs



Each beneficiary in the chain shares only one ID with the next. No check on a single ID column would find more than a pair. Only the network shows the whole ring.
What next? The auditor would list the seven registrations with their names, addresses and dates of registration, and ask the scheme office to verify them. If they turn out to be one person, the payments to the extra registrations are recoverable. The agent’s number needs a field visit, to find out who the agent is and whether the 30 beneficiaries exist and receive their money.






TipAudit tip



The degree of an ID vertex, that is, the number of beneficiaries linked to it, is a quick way to find hubs. A mobile number or bank account linked with many beneficiaries deserves verification in the field. Who is the person behind it, and are the beneficiaries real?

title: 52  Network Analysis in Audit
section: 52.3 Audit use case 2, bidders who bid together
text:
52.3 Audit use case 2, bidders who bid together
Community detection, which we learnt in Chapter 51, classifies the vertices of a network into groups of closely linked vertices. In Section 51.10, we used it on links between firms from their registration papers. Often the auditor has no such papers, only the bids. Let us use the bids alone to find bid rigging. A cartel of firms agree among themselves who will win a tender. The others put in higher cover bids, to make the tender look competitive. Firms of a cartel therefore keep appearing in the same tenders. We looked for such firms with association rules in Chapter 45. Let us now look at the same problem as a network.
We create bids for 200 tenders of an imaginary Public Works Division over a few years. There are 40 firms, and 3 to 6 firms bid in each tender. We have planted a cartel of 5 firms, which bid together in every fourth tender.

Code to create the bidsset.seed(77)
firms  <- sprintf("F%02d", 1:40)
cartel <- c("F05", "F11", "F23", "F31", "F38")

bids <- map_dfr(1:200, function(t) {
  b <- sample(firms, sample(3:6, 1))
  if (t %% 4 == 0) {
    # Cartel tender. 3 to 5 cartel firms, with 0 to 2 outsiders
    b <- union(sample(cartel, sample(3:5, 1)),
               sample(setdiff(firms, cartel), sample(0:2, 1)))
  }
  tibble(tender = sprintf("T%03d", t), firm = b)
})



head(bids)

# A tibble: 6 × 2
  tender firm 
  <chr>  <chr>
1 T001   F05  
2 T001   F37  
3 T001   F29  
4 T001   F22  
5 T002   F20  
6 T002   F31  


Tenders and firms form a bipartite graph. But we are interested in the relation between firms. So we project the bipartite graph onto the firms. In the projected graph, two firms are connected if they bid in at least one common tender. The edge weight is the number of tenders in which they bid together. The function bipartite_projection() does this. It needs a logical vertex attribute type, which tells which set each vertex belongs to.

bid_graph <- graph_from_data_frame(bids, directed = FALSE)
V(bid_graph)$type <- V(bid_graph)$name %in% bids$firm

firm_graph <- bipartite_projection(bid_graph, which = "true")
firm_graph

IGRAPH 9cb6cc2 UNW- 40 666 -- 
+ attr: name (v/c), weight (e/n)
+ edges from 9cb6cc2 (vertex names):
 [1] F05--F37 F05--F29 F05--F22 F05--F11 F05--F23 F05--F38 F05--F31 F05--F24
 [9] F05--F08 F05--F27 F05--F20 F05--F06 F05--F14 F05--F17 F05--F30 F05--F35
[17] F05--F36 F05--F34 F05--F33 F05--F15 F05--F19 F05--F18 F05--F32 F05--F03
[25] F05--F04 F05--F21 F05--F39 F05--F28 F05--F16 F05--F10 F05--F40 F05--F07
[33] F05--F02 F05--F25 F37--F29 F37--F22 F37--F25 F37--F36 F37--F23 F37--F31
[41] F37--F10 F37--F27 F37--F28 F37--F26 F37--F21 F37--F14 F37--F18 F37--F15
[49] F37--F20 F37--F33 F37--F19 F37--F13 F37--F34 F37--F30 F37--F04 F37--F08
[57] F37--F40 F37--F11 F37--F03 F37--F32 F37--F38 F37--F07 F29--F22 F29--F11
+ ... omitted several edges


Let us see how many times pairs of firms have bid together.

table(E(firm_graph)$weight)


  1   2   3   4   5   6   7   8  25  29  31  32  33  36 
217 199 145  59  27   5   3   1   2   2   2   2   1   1 


Most pairs of firms have met in only one or two tenders, and no ordinary pair has met in more than 8. But a few pairs have met 25 to 36 times. That is a clear break. Let us keep only the edges with 10 or more joint bids, and see which firms remain.

frequent <- delete_edges(firm_graph, E(firm_graph)[weight < 10])
frequent <- delete_vertices(frequent, V(frequent)[degree(frequent) == 0])
V(frequent)$name

[1] "F05" "F31" "F11" "F23" "F38"


These are exactly the five firms of our planted cartel. Without choosing any threshold, community detection with the Louvain method reaches the same answer.

set.seed(1)
firm_comm <- cluster_louvain(firm_graph)
sizes(firm_comm)

Community sizes
 1  2  3 
 5 15 20 

firm_comm[[which.min(sizes(firm_comm))]]

[1] "F05" "F31" "F11" "F23" "F38"


The smallest community found is again the cartel. Figure 52.3 shows the network of firms, coloured by community, with thicker edges for more joint bids. With 40 firms there are 666 edges, and drawing all of them gives an unreadable hairball. So we draw only the pairs which bid together 4 or more times.

cartel_vis <- toVisNetworkData(firm_graph)
cartel_vis$nodes$group <- paste("Community", membership(firm_comm))
cartel_vis$edges <- cartel_vis$edges |>
  filter(weight >= 4) |>
  mutate(value = weight, title = paste("Joint bids:", weight))

visNetwork(cartel_vis$nodes, cartel_vis$edges, width = "100%", height = "500px") |>
  visIgraphLayout(layout = "layout_with_fr", randomSeed = 7) |>
  visOptions(highlightNearest = TRUE, nodesIdSelection = TRUE) |>
  visLegend()






Figure 52.3: Firms coloured by community. Only pairs with 4 or more joint bids are drawn, and edge width is the number of joint bids.









WarningCaution



Firms may bid together often for genuine reasons. There may be only a few qualified firms for specialised work in a district. Joint bidding is a lead. Look for further signs. Do the firms win in turn (bid rotation)? Are the losing bids always slightly higher than the winning bid? Were the bids uploaded from the same computer or IP address? Do the firms share an address, a partner or a bank account? Are there the same mistakes in their bid documents?

title: 52  Network Analysis in Audit
text:
52.4 Audit use case 3, circular trading
In circular trading, a group of firms issue invoices to each other in a circle. A sells to B, B to C, C to D, and D back to A, often for nearly the same amount, within a few days. No real goods move. The purpose may be to show a false turnover to get bank loans, or to pass on input tax credit under GST fraudulently. In a network of invoices, where each firm is a vertex and each invoice a directed edge from seller to buyer, such trading shows up as a cycle.
Let us create the invoices of the financial year 2023-24 among the firms of a district. There are 15 manufacturers, 40 wholesalers and 150 retailers. Genuine goods flow one way, from manufacturers to wholesalers to retailers, so genuine trade has no cycles. We have planted two rings of circular trading. One ring of 4 firms went round twice, in September and November. Another ring of 3 retailers went round once, in January.

Code to create the invoicesset.seed(99)
mk <- sprintf("M%02d", 1:15)    # manufacturers
ws <- sprintf("W%02d", 1:40)    # wholesalers
rt <- sprintf("R%03d", 1:150)   # retailers

invoices <- bind_rows(
  tibble(seller = sample(mk, 400, TRUE), buyer = sample(ws, 400, TRUE)),
  tibble(seller = sample(ws, 900, TRUE), buyer = sample(rt, 900, TRUE))
) |>
  mutate(date   = as.Date("2023-04-01") + sample(0:364, n(), TRUE),
         amount = round(rlnorm(n(), log(2e5), 0.8)))

# Planted circular trading. Each invoice a little higher than the last, two days apart
circle <- function(firms, start, amount) {
  k <- length(firms) - 1
  tibble(seller = head(firms, -1), buyer = firms[-1],
         date   = start + (0:(k - 1)) * 2,
         amount = round(amount * (1 + cumsum(runif(k, 0, 0.01)))))
}
ring1 <- c("W07", "R015", "R088", "W23", "W07")
ring2 <- c("R040", "R121", "R063", "R040")

invoices <- bind_rows(invoices,
                      circle(ring1, as.Date("2023-09-11"), 4850000),
                      circle(ring1, as.Date("2023-11-20"), 5200000),
                      circle(ring2, as.Date("2024-01-08"), 2975000)) |>
  mutate(invoice_no = sprintf("INV%05d", row_number())) |>
  relocate(invoice_no)



head(invoices)

# A tibble: 6 × 5
  invoice_no seller buyer date       amount
  <chr>      <chr>  <chr> <date>      <dbl>
1 INV00001   M01    W10   2023-06-23  94037
2 INV00002   M12    W29   2023-10-03 163762
3 INV00003   M06    W36   2024-03-23 141778
4 INV00004   M06    W31   2023-04-04 314428

Let us create a directed graph. The invoice number, date and amount become edge attributes.

inv_graph <- graph_from_data_frame(select(invoices, seller, buyer, everything()),
                                   directed = TRUE)
inv_graph

IGRAPH 9cd2533 DN-- 202 1311 -- 
+ attr: name (v/c), invoice_no (e/c), date (e/n), amount (e/n)
+ edges from 9cd2533 (vertex names):
 [1] M01->W10 M12->W29 M06->W36 M06->W31 M05->W20 M03->W24 M10->W38 M14->W38
 [9] M02->W06 M06->W01 M13->W17 M04->W22 M04->W36 M15->W39 M04->W39 M09->W19
[17] M02->W09 M08->W14 M14->W17 M06->W26 M04->W12 M13->W15 M14->W28 M04->W26
[25] M14->W28 M01->W36 M07->W35 M02->W21 M07->W04 M06->W37 M14->W32 M05->W33
[33] M08->W26 M07->W08 M10->W19 M06->W24 M05->W12 M14->W06 M12->W38 M10->W19
[41] M15->W24 M01->W06 M14->W05 M12->W14 M15->W36 M06->W39 M15->W36 M06->W36
[49] M07->W26 M15->W23 M04->W25 M05->W25 M15->W19 M07->W03 M01->W30 M11->W06
[57] M06->W31 M13->W26 M13->W18 M12->W37 M09->W06 M09->W31 M03->W32 M13->W21
+ ... omitted several edges


Strongly connected components. In a directed graph, a strongly connected component is a group of vertices in which each vertex can reach every other following the arrows. A vertex which is not part of any cycle forms a component on its own. So components of more than one vertex contain cycles.

scc <- components(inv_graph, mode = "strong")
table(scc$csize)


  1   3   4 
195   1   1 


All firms are on their own, except one group of 4 and one group of 3. These are our two rings.
Pruning sources and sinks. There is another way to reach the same answer, which also makes big graphs much smaller. A firm which only sells and never buys (a source, with in-degree 0) cannot be part of a cycle. Neither can a firm which only buys and never sells (a sink, with out-degree 0). So we can delete them. But deleting them may turn other firms into sources or sinks, so we repeat until nothing more can be deleted. This is the directed version of dropping leaf nodes.

pruned <- inv_graph
repeat {
  drop <- V(pruned)[degree(pruned, mode = "in") == 0 | degree(pruned, mode = "out") == 0]
  if (length(drop) == 0) break
  pruned <- delete_vertices(pruned, drop)
}
pruned

IGRAPH 9cd8ca0 DN-- 7 12 -- 
+ attr: name (v/c), invoice_no (e/c), date (e/n), amount (e/n)
+ edges from 9cd8ca0 (vertex names):
 [1] W23 ->R063 W07 ->R015 R015->R088 R088->W23  W23 ->W07  W07 ->R015
 [7] R015->R088 R088->W23  W23 ->W07  R040->R121 R121->R063 R063->R040


Out of the 202 firms which traded during the year, only 7 remain. Every one of them is part of a cycle.
Listing the cycles. Now simple_cycles() lists each cycle. Since the first ring went round twice, there are two invoices for each of its links. So we first combine repeated edges into one with simplify(), to list each ring only once.

rings <- simple_cycles(simplify(pruned))
lapply(rings$vertices, names)

[[1]]
[1] "W23"  "W07"  "R015" "R088"

[[2]]
[1] "R063" "R040" "R121"


Let us pull out the invoices of these rings, and look at their dates and amounts. Note that we keep only the invoices where the seller and the buyer belong to the same ring. The two rings may also have genuine dealings with each other, which are not part of any cycle.

ring_firms <- names(scc$membership)[scc$membership %in% which(scc$csize > 1)]

# Invoices where the seller and buyer are in the same ring
ring_invoices <- invoices |>
  filter(seller %in% ring_firms, buyer %in% ring_firms) |>
  filter(scc$membership[seller] == scc$membership[buyer]) |>
  arrange(date)
ring_invoices

# A tibble: 11 × 5
   invoice_no seller buyer date        amount
   <chr>      <chr>  <chr> <date>       <dbl>
 1 INV01301   W07    R015  2023-09-11 4855941
 2 INV01302   R015   R088  2023-09-13 4887598
 3 INV01303   R088   W23   2023-09-15 4891067
 4 INV01304   W23    W07   2023-09-17 4898134
 5 INV01305   W07    R015  2023-11-20 5241151
 6 INV01306   R015   R088  2023-11-22 5277501
 7 INV01307   R088   W23   2023-11-24 5303338
 8 INV01308   W23    W07   2023-11-26 5324791
 9 INV01309   R040   R121  2024-01-08 2975970
10 INV01310   R121   R063  2024-01-10 3004580
11 INV01311   R063   R040  2024-01-12 3020018


The pattern is unmistakable. The same amount, a little higher each time, goes round the ring within a week. Together these 11 invoices are worth ₹5.0 crore, without any goods moving. Figure 52.4 shows the rings.

# One edge per seller and buyer, with all its invoices in the tooltip
circ_edges <- ring_invoices |>
  group_by(from = seller, to = buyer) |>
  summarise(label = paste0("₹", round(sum(amount) / 1e5), " lakh (", n(), ")"),
            title = paste0(invoice_no, " (", date, "), ₹",
                           round(amount / 1e5, 2), " lakh", collapse = "<br>"),
            .groups = "drop")
circ_nodes <- tibble(id = ring_firms, label = ring_firms)

visNetwork(circ_nodes, circ_edges, width = "100%", height = "450px") |>
  visIgraphLayout(layout = "layout_with_kk", randomSeed = 3) |>
  visEdges(arrows = "to", smooth = list(enabled = TRUE, type = "curvedCW", roundness = 0.15),
           font = list(size = 11, align = "middle")) |>
  visNodes(color = "orange") |>
  visOptions(highlightNearest = TRUE)






Figure 52.4: Circular trading. Each arrow shows the total invoiced from a seller to a buyer, with the number of invoices in brackets. Hover for details.



What next? The auditor would ask the GST office for the e-way bills and transport records of these invoices, and check the input tax credit claimed on them. The bank statements of the firms, where available, would show whether money really changed hands.






WarningCaution



Not every cycle is a fraud. Goods may be returned, or two firms may genuinely buy different goods from each other. Look at the amounts, the dates, the goods described, and whether there is any proof of movement of goods, like e-way bills or transport receipts. Circular trading usually shows nearly equal amounts going round quickly, often between firms with few other transactions.

title: 52  Network Analysis in Audit
section: 52.5 Audit use case 4, vendors linked with employees
text:
52.5 Audit use case 4, vendors linked with employees
A vendor which is secretly owned or controlled by an employee of the organisation is a classic conflict of interest. The employee may push its bills, approve inflated rates, or pass on inside information. Such a link usually leaves traces in the data. The employee and the vendor may share a bank account, a mobile number or an address. Sometimes the link is indirect, through a relative or a third firm.
This is the same problem as use case 1, but across two masters. Let us create an employee master of 150 employees and a vendor master of 80 vendors, each with a bank account, a mobile number and an address. We have planted three links.

Vendor V023 has the same bank account as employee E107.
Vendor V051 has the same address as employee E033.
Vendor V064 shares a mobile number with vendor V012, whose address is the same as that of employee E088. This is an indirect link, two steps away.


Code to create the employee and vendor mastersset.seed(31)
emp <- tibble(
  emp_id  = sprintf("E%03d", 1:150),
  bank_ac = rand_acct(150),
  mobile  = rand_mobile(150),
  address = paste("H.No.", sample(1:999, 150),
                  sample(c("Sector 4", "Civil Lines", "Model Town", "Gandhi Nagar",
                           "Shastri Nagar"), 150, TRUE))
)
ven <- tibble(
  vendor_id = sprintf("V%03d", 1:80),
  bank_ac   = rand_acct(80),
  mobile    = rand_mobile(80),
  address   = paste("Shop", sample(1:300, 80),
                    sample(c("Main Bazar", "Industrial Area", "Station Road"), 80, TRUE))
)

# Planted links
ven$bank_ac[23] <- emp$bank_ac[107]
ven$address[51] <- emp$address[33]
ven$mobile[64]  <- ven$mobile[12]
ven$address[12] <- emp$address[88]


We stack both masters together and pivot them longer. Then we prefix the IDs and keep only the shared IDs, exactly as in use case 1. In real data, addresses must first be cleaned and standardised, as discussed in Chapter 32 and Section 18.17. Two more links are worth adding where the data has them. The first is the email ID, after normalising Gmail dot and plus aliases. The second is the PAN embedded in each vendor’s GSTIN (characters 3 to 12). It may match the PAN of an employee or a relative. Both are explained in Section 19.10, where three “different” vendors turned out to share one Gmail box.

ev_long <- bind_rows(
  emp |> rename(entity = emp_id),
  ven |> rename(entity = vendor_id)
) |>
  pivot_longer(-entity, names_to = "id_type", values_to = "value") |>
  mutate(id_node = paste(id_type, value, sep = ":")) |>
  add_count(id_node) |>
  filter(n > 1)

ev_graph <- graph_from_data_frame(select(ev_long, entity, id_node), directed = FALSE)

Now we find the components which contain both an employee and a vendor.

components(ev_graph)$membership |>
  stack() |>
  set_names(c("group", "node")) |>
  filter(str_detect(node, "^[EV]\\d")) |>
  group_by(group) |>
  filter(any(str_starts(node, "E")), any(str_starts(node, "V"))) |>
  summarise(entities = paste(sort(as.character(node)), collapse = ", "))

# A tibble: 3 × 2
  group entities        
  <dbl> <chr>           
1     1 E033, V051      
2     2 E088, V012, V064
3     3 E107, V023      


All three planted links are found, including the indirect one. To explain how a vendor is linked to an employee, we use shortest_paths().

shortest_paths(ev_graph, from = "V064", to = "E088")$vpath[[1]]

+ 5/11 vertices, named, from 9ced086:
[1] V064                           mobile:7220817946             
[3] V012                           address:H.No. 912 Gandhi Nagar
[5] E088                          


The path reads like the finding itself. Vendor V064 has the same mobile number as vendor V012, which has the same address as employee E088. Figure 52.5 shows the links. For each link, the auditor would next list the bills of the vendor that the employee dealt with, and their total in rupees. The office would then be asked to explain the link, and whether the employee had declared it.

ev_vis <- toVisNetworkData(ev_graph)
ev_vis$nodes <- ev_vis$nodes |>
  mutate(group = case_when(str_starts(id, "E") ~ "Employee",
                           str_starts(id, "V") ~ "Vendor",
                           TRUE ~ "Shared detail"),
         label = if_else(group == "Shared detail", "", id),
         title = id)

visNetwork(ev_vis$nodes, ev_vis$edges, width = "100%", height = "400px") |>
  visGroups(groupname = "Employee", color = "tomato", shape = "dot") |>
  visGroups(groupname = "Vendor", color = "steelblue", shape = "dot") |>
  visGroups(groupname = "Shared detail", color = "grey", shape = "square", size = 10) |>
  visOptions(highlightNearest = TRUE) |>
  visLegend()






Figure 52.5: Employees (red) linked with vendors (blue) through shared details









TipAudit tip



Extend the employee master with the details of close relatives, where these are available from declarations, nominations or pension papers. Many conflicts of interest run through a spouse, a son or a brother-in-law, not through the employee directly.

title: 52  Network Analysis in Audit
section: 52.6 Tips for working with big networks
text:
52.6 Tips for working with big networks
Real audit data has lakhs of records. A network built carelessly from such data can be too big to analyse, or full of false links. Here are some tips which help.
1. Drop the leaf nodes. Most IDs belong to only one record. In the graph, these are leaves, vertices with only one edge, and they can never link two records. Dropping them shrinks the graph enormously without changing the answer. We can drop them either before building the graph, or after.

# Before building the graph, with dplyr
edges_shared <- edges_long |>
  add_count(id_node) |>
  filter(n > 1)

# After building the graph, with igraph.
# Delete ID vertices with one edge, then records left with no edge
g <- delete_vertices(g, V(g)[degree(g) == 1 & str_detect(name, ":")])
g <- delete_vertices(g, V(g)[degree(g) == 0])

In a directed graph where we look for cycles, we drop sources and sinks repeatedly, as we did in use case 3. For an undirected graph where we look for tightly knit groups, the same idea is the k-core. The 2-core is what remains after repeatedly removing all vertices with fewer than 2 edges. coreness() gives the core number of each vertex, so induced_subgraph(g, V(g)[coreness(g) >= 2]) keeps the 2-core.
2. Prefix every ID with its type. Write mobile:9876543210, not 9876543210. Otherwise two different kinds of ID which happen to have the same value become one vertex, and create false links.
3. Look at the most connected IDs first, and remove junk values. Some values are only placeholders, like 9999999999, 0000000000, NA, test@gmail.com, XXXXX0000X, or the address of the office itself. Such a value links hundreds of unrelated records into one giant group. Always run count(id_node, sort = TRUE) before building the graph. Remove the junk values, and keep the genuine hubs aside for separate examination.
4. Clean before you connect. 9876543210, +91 98765 43210 and 09876543210 are the same mobile number. r.kumar@gmail.com and rkumar+bids@gmail.com are the same Gmail box. Standardise IDs before building the graph, with the functions of Chapter 18 and Section 19.10, like clean_mobile() and normalise_email(). Otherwise real links are missed.
5. Validate before you connect. An ID in the wrong format, or with a wrong check digit, cannot be a genuine shared ID. A mistyped Aadhaar or GSTIN may by chance equal someone else’s, and create a false link. Run the format and check digit tests of Section 19.10 and Section 19.11 first. Keep the invalid IDs out of the graph, and report them separately as data quality findings.
6. Work with components, not with the whole graph. Use components() to split the graph, and then study the components of interest one at a time with induced_subgraph(). Sort them by size. Groups of 2 are usually families or genuine. Very large groups usually mean a junk value is still present.
7. Beware of bipartite projection with hubs. When we project a bipartite graph, an ID shared by \(d\) records creates \(d(d-1)/2\) edges. One junk value shared by 10,000 records would create about five crore edges. Remove junk values and big hubs before projecting.
8. Draw only what matters, and draw it fast. Plot a component or an ego network, not the whole graph. For visNetwork, use visIgraphLayout(), so that the layout is calculated once in R and the browser does not have to run its slow physics simulation. Keep labels short, and put details in the title (tooltip).
9. Keep the record keys and amounts. Keep the original record IDs, invoice numbers, amounts and dates as attributes of vertices and edges. Every finding has to be traced back to the documents, and quantified in rupees.






TipShare the network



visSave(network, file = "ring.html") saves an interactive network as a single HTML file. It can be emailed to the audit team or attached to the working papers, and opened in any browser without R.

title: 52  Network Analysis in Audit
text:
52.7 A suggested workflow


Decide the vertices and edges. What are the entities (persons, firms, accounts), and what links them (shared IDs, bids, invoices)? Is the graph directed?

Prepare the data. Clean, standardise and validate the IDs (Section 19.10), prefix them with their type, and pivot to one row per link.

Look at the most connected IDs. Remove junk values. Note the genuine hubs.

Reduce the graph. Drop leaves, sources and sinks, or take the k-core, depending on the question.

Find the structure. Components for related entities, communities for groups, cycles for circular flows, shortest paths to explain a link, centrality for key players.

Visualise the parts of interest with visNetwork, and share them.

Go back to the records. Verify every lead with documents, and quantify it.







ImportantRemember



A link in a network shows that two records share something. It does not show why. Family members share mobiles, neighbours share addresses, and specialised firms meet in the same tenders. A network gives leads, not findings. Every lead must be verified with documents, and where needed, in the field.

title: 53  Maps
text:
53.1 Where can maps help an auditor?
Almost everything that government does happens somewhere. A hospital, a school, a road, a ration shop, a beneficiary’s house. Records usually carry this location, as a district name, a pin code, or increasingly as exact coordinates captured by a mobile phone. When we put such data on a map, patterns appear that no table can show. Which areas are well covered, which are left out, and which records do not fit where they claim to be.
R can work with maps as easily as with tables. In this chapter, we will learn to read map data, draw maps, join data to locations, and measure distances. As always, we will apply each skill to an audit question.

title: 53  Maps
text:
Coverage and equity. Are benefits reaching every district, or are some areas left out? A map of beneficiaries per lakh population shows this at a glance.

Verifying geotagged evidence. Many schemes now require geotagged photos, of houses built, assets created, or inspections done. A photo whose location does not match the claimed site is a red flag.

Distance checks. Patients travelling unusually far to a hospital, students enrolled in a school far from their homes, or travel claims for distances that do not match the map.

Location mismatches. A beneficiary recorded in one district but living in another, or a vendor whose address is far from where supplies were delivered.

Spatial clusters. Many claims, complaints or failures concentrated in one area.

title: 53  Maps
text:
53.2 Basic ideas

53.2.1 Types of map data
Map data comes in two main kinds. Vector data describes features by their shape.


Points, such as the location of a hospital, a school or a photo.

Lines, such as roads, rivers or canals.

Polygons, which are closed shapes, such as the boundary of a district or a plot of land.

Raster data describes the earth as a grid of cells, like a photograph. Satellite images and land-use maps are raster data. In this chapter we will work only with vector data, which is what most audit work needs.

53.2.2 File formats
Vector map data is commonly stored in these formats.


Shapefile. The oldest and most common format. A single “shapefile” is really a set of files with the same name and different extensions, such as .shp (the shapes), .shx (an index), .dbf (the attribute table) and .prj (the coordinate system). All of them must be kept together. If the .shp file is missing, the shapes are lost.

GeoPackage (.gpkg). A modern, single-file format, which can hold several layers.

GeoJSON (.geojson). A text format, popular on the web.

53.2.3 Coordinate reference systems
Every location is described by a pair of numbers. But numbers mean nothing unless we know the system they belong to. This system is called the coordinate reference system or CRS.


Geographic systems use latitude and longitude, in degrees. The most common one is called WGS 84, used by GPS and mobile phones. Its code is EPSG:4326.

Projected systems flatten the round earth onto a plane, and use metres or kilometres. Distances and areas are easier to measure in them.

We will learn more about CRS, with real latitudes and longitudes, in the chapter on geocoding. In this chapter, our map uses a simple flat grid in kilometres.






WarningMaps of India in publications



When publishing a map that shows the boundaries of India or its states, use boundaries from an authoritative source, such as those published by the Survey of India, and follow the applicable guidelines. Many freely available world maps show India’s boundaries incorrectly. That is one reason why the examples in this chapter use an imaginary state.

title: 53  Maps
text:
53.3 Prerequisites
The package sf, short for simple features, is the standard tool for vector map data in R. An sf object is simply a data frame with a special column, usually called geometry, that holds the shape of each row. So everything we know about dplyr works on it, and ggplot2 can draw it directly.

library(tidyverse)
library(sf)

title: 53  Maps
section: 53.4 Our data, a map of the imaginary state
text:
53.4 Our data, a map of the imaginary state
We continue with the imaginary Sarvajan Swasthya Yojana (SSY) of the earlier chapters. The scheme runs in an imaginary state, Sarvajan Pradesh, with eight districts. All shapes and locations are made up, and are created by tools/make_ssy_geo_data.R in the book’s repository.
The map is stored in a GeoPackage file. st_layers() lists the layers in it.

st_layers("Data/ssy_map.gpkg")

Driver: GPKG 
Available layers:
  layer_name geometry_type features fields crs_name
1      state       Polygon        1      1  unknown
2  districts       Polygon        8      2  unknown


There are two layers, the outline of the state and its districts. st_read() reads a layer.

state     <- st_read("Data/ssy_map.gpkg", layer = "state", quiet = TRUE)
districts <- st_read("Data/ssy_map.gpkg", layer = "districts", quiet = TRUE)

The printout shows that this is an sf object with 8 features (rows), each a polygon. Besides the geom column, it has the district name and its population in lakh. Note the line Projected CRS. Let us check the units of our coordinate system.

st_crs(districts)$units

[1] "km"


So all coordinates and distances are in kilometres.

title: 53  Maps
text:
53.5 Drawing maps
The quickest way to see an sf object is the base R plot() function. It draws one small map for each attribute column. Here we draw just the geometry, with st_geometry().

plot(st_geometry(districts))






Figure 53.1: Districts of the imaginary state, drawn with plot()




For better maps, we use ggplot2. The geom geom_sf() draws sf objects. It needs no x or y aesthetic, because the geometry column already holds the shapes. geom_sf_text() places a label at the centre of each shape (Figure 53.2).

ggplot(districts) +
  geom_sf(aes(fill = district), colour = "white", show.legend = FALSE) +
  geom_sf_text(aes(label = district), size = 3.5) +
  theme_void()






Figure 53.2: The eight districts of Sarvajan Pradesh




theme_void() removes the axes and gridlines, which are rarely needed on a map.

title: 53  Maps
text:
53.6 Adding points from a table
Locations often come as plain columns of numbers in a table. Our hospital locations are in a CSV file, with two columns, x_km and y_km.

hospitals <- read_csv("Data/ssy_hospitals.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)

hosp_locations <- read_csv("Data/ssy_hospital_locations.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
head(hosp_locations, 3)

# A tibble: 3 × 3
  hospital_id  x_km  y_km
  <chr>       <dbl> <dbl>
1 H001         82.5  144.
2 H002        134.   178.
3 H003        201.   234.


To make them map points, we use st_as_sf(). We tell it which columns hold the coordinates, and which CRS they are in. Since these coordinates are on the same grid as our districts, we use the district map’s CRS.

hosp_sf <- hosp_locations |>
  left_join(hospitals, by = "hospital_id") |>
  st_as_sf(coords = c("x_km", "y_km"), crs = st_crs(districts))

title: 53  Maps
53  Maps
section: 53.8 A map of claims per lakh population
text:
53.8 A map of claims per lakh population
A choropleth is a map where each area is coloured according to a value. Let us colour each district by the number of claims raised by its hospitals, per lakh population.
First we count claims by the district of the hospital, and join the counts to the district map with an ordinary left_join(). The result is still an sf object, so it can be drawn.

claims <- read_csv("Data/ssy_claims.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)

claims_by_district <- claims |>
  left_join(hospitals |> select(hospital_id, district), by = "hospital_id") |>
  count(district, name = "claims")

district_map <- districts |>
  left_join(claims_by_district, by = "district") |>
  mutate(claims_per_lakh = claims / population_lakh)

district_map |>
  st_drop_geometry() |>
  arrange(desc(claims_per_lakh))

1   Amarpur            17.7   5765        325.7062
2   Devgarh            26.9   6536        242.9740
3   Haripur            16.6   3383        203.7952

ggplot(district_map) +
  geom_sf(aes(fill = claims_per_lakh), colour = "white") +
  geom_sf_text(aes(label = district), size = 3) +
  scale_fill_distiller(palette = "YlOrRd", direction = 1) +
  labs(fill = "Claims per\nlakh population") +
  theme_void()






Figure 53.4: Claims per lakh population, by district of the hospital




The darker districts in Figure 53.4 have many more claims for their population. This alone is not a finding. A district may have more claims because it has more hospitals, or because patients come to it from other districts. But it shows the auditor where to start asking questions.






TipAudit tip



Always map rates, like claims per lakh population or beneficiaries per thousand households, rather than raw counts. A map of raw counts mostly shows where more people live. We met the same point while comparing groups in Chapter 49.

title: 53  Maps
section: 53.9 Audit use case 1, how far do patients travel?
text:
53.9 Audit use case 1, how far do patients travel?
Most patients go to a hospital near their home. A hospital whose patients come mostly from far away deserves a closer look. Patients may be brought in by agents, or the claims may be for patients who never visited at all.
For a sample of claims, we have the location of the patient’s home. Let us turn these into points.

homes <- read_csv("Data/ssy_patient_homes.csv", show_col_types = FALSE) |>
  st_as_sf(coords = c("home_x_km", "home_y_km"), crs = st_crs(districts))

nrow(homes)

[1] 4000


st_distance() measures the distance between features. With by_element = TRUE, it measures between the first home and the first hospital, the second home and the second hospital, and so on, instead of between every pair. So we first line up, for each home, the location of its hospital.

hospital_of_home <- hosp_sf[match(homes$hospital_id, hosp_sf$hospital_id), ]

homes <- homes |>
  mutate(distance_km = as.numeric(st_distance(homes, hospital_of_home, by_element = TRUE)))

summary(homes$distance_km)

   Min. 1st Qu.  Median    Mean 3rd Qu.    Max. 
  0.000   3.809   9.164  17.158  18.573 199.863 


st_distance() returns the distances with their units attached. as.numeric() removes the units, so that we can use them like ordinary numbers. Half of the patients live within about 9 km of their hospital. Now let us see, for each hospital, what share of its patients come from more than 50 km away.

travel <- homes |>
  st_drop_geometry() |>
  summarise(patients = n(),
            median_km = median(distance_km),
            pct_over_50km = 100 * mean(distance_km > 50),
            .by = hospital_id) |>
  filter(patients >= 15) |>
  arrange(desc(pct_over_50km))

travel |>
  head(8) |>
  mutate(across(where(is.double), \(x) round(x, 1)))

# A tibble: 8 × 4
  hospital_id patients median_km pct_over_50km
  <chr>          <int>     <dbl>         <dbl>
1 H116              21      88.1          71.4
2 H071              19      97            63.2
3 H066              59      81.8          59.3
4 H070              99      77            58.6
5 H063              69      92.6          58  
6 H098              26      71.2          57.7
7 H095              15       5.8           6.7
8 H039              60      10.3           6.7


We kept only hospitals with at least 15 patients in the sample, to avoid judging a hospital on very few cases. The result is striking. For most hospitals, very few patients come from beyond 50 km. But for a group of six hospitals, more than half do. These are the same six “camp” hospitals that stood out in the chapters on PCA, clustering, association rules and text analytics.
A picture makes the point even more clearly. Let us draw lines from each patient’s home to the hospital, for one of these hospitals and for an ordinary hospital (Figure 53.5).

two_hospitals <- c(travel$hospital_id[1],
                   travel$hospital_id[travel$pct_over_50km == 0][1])

lines_df <- homes |>
  filter(hospital_id %in% two_hospitals) |>
  mutate(home_x = st_coordinates(geometry)[, 1],
         home_y = st_coordinates(geometry)[, 2]) |>
  st_drop_geometry() |>
  left_join(hosp_locations, by = "hospital_id") |>
  mutate(hospital_id = factor(hospital_id, levels = two_hospitals))

ggplot() +
  geom_sf(data = districts, fill = "grey95", colour = "grey70") +
  geom_segment(data = lines_df,
               aes(x = x_km, y = y_km, xend = home_x, yend = home_y),
               colour = "steelblue", alpha = 0.4) +
  geom_point(data = lines_df |> distinct(hospital_id, x_km, y_km),
             aes(x_km, y_km), colour = "firebrick", size = 3) +
  facet_wrap(~hospital_id) +
  theme_void()






Figure 53.5: Where patients come from, for a flagged hospital and an ordinary one




st_coordinates() extracts the x and y values of points, so that we can use them with ordinary ggplot2 geoms like geom_segment(). The hospital on the left draws its patients from across the state. The one on the right serves its own neighbourhood, as one would expect.

title: 53  Maps
section: 53.10 Audit use case 2, were the inspections really done?
text:
53.10 Audit use case 2, were the inspections really done?
Each empanelled hospital must be inspected twice a year. The inspector uploads a photo from the hospital, and the phone records the location where the photo was taken. This location is called the geotag. If the photo was really taken at the hospital, its geotag should be within a few hundred metres of the hospital.

inspections <- read_csv("Data/ssy_inspections.csv", show_col_types = FALSE) |>
  st_as_sf(coords = c("photo_x_km", "photo_y_km"), crs = st_crs(districts))

head(inspections, 3)

Simple feature collection with 3 features and 4 fields
Geometry type: POINT
Dimension:     XY
Bounding box:  xmin: 82.442 ymin: 144.385 xmax: 133.703 ymax: 177.922
Projected CRS: +proj=tmerc +lat_0=0 +lon_0=0 +k=1 +x_0=0 +y_0=0 +ellps=WGS84 +units=km +no_defs
# A tibble: 3 × 5
  hospital_id inspection_no inspection_date inspector          geometry
  <chr>               <dbl> <date>          <chr>          <POINT [km]>
1 H001                    1 2024-07-07      INS-01     (82.442 144.426)
2 H001                    2 2024-08-27      INS-03      (82.46 144.385)
3 H002                    1 2025-03-10      INS-03    (133.703 177.922)


As before, we measure the distance from each photo to its hospital.

hospital_of_photo <- hosp_sf[match(inspections$hospital_id, hosp_sf$hospital_id), ]

inspections <- inspections |>
  mutate(distance_km = as.numeric(st_distance(inspections, hospital_of_photo,
                                              by_element = TRUE)))

inspections |>
  st_drop_geometry() |>
  summarise(photos = n(),
            median_metres = 1000 * median(distance_km),
            over_1km = sum(distance_km > 1))

# A tibble: 1 × 3
  photos median_metres over_1km
   <int>         <dbl>    <int>
1    240          104.        7


Most photos were taken within about 104 metres of the hospital. But some were taken more than a kilometre away. Let us list them.

inspections |>
  st_drop_geometry() |>
  filter(distance_km > 1) |>
  arrange(desc(distance_km)) |>
  mutate(distance_km = round(distance_km, 1))

# A tibble: 7 × 5
  hospital_id inspection_no inspection_date inspector distance_km
  <chr>               <dbl> <date>          <chr>           <dbl>
1 H010                    2 2024-06-11      INS-05           88.7
2 H042                    2 2024-04-18      INS-04           87.6
3 H024                    2 2025-03-14      INS-03           63.1
4 H109                    2 2024-09-11      INS-03           51  
5 H084                    2 2024-08-08      INS-03           47.1
6 H115                    2 2024-04-19      INS-02           32.3
7 H066                    2 2024-06-15      INS-05           32.2


These photos were taken tens of kilometres from the hospitals they claim to show. The inspections were, most likely, reported without anyone visiting the hospital. The table also shows the inspector and the date of each, which is what an audit observation needs. Two things stand out. One inspector, INS-03, accounts for three of the seven cases, which suggests a pattern in that inspector’s work rather than an odd mistake. And one of the hospitals, H066, is again among the six flagged hospitals of the earlier chapters.






WarningCaution



GPS locations on phones can be off by a few metres, sometimes by a few hundred metres in crowded areas or indoors. So never flag a photo for being 50 metres away. Use a sensible threshold, like one kilometre in our case, and look at how far beyond it each case lies. Also remember that geotags can be faked with special apps. A correct geotag does not prove a visit, but a wrong one is a strong sign of trouble.

title: 53  Maps
section: 53.11 Audit use case 3, one house, many beneficiaries
text:
53.11 Audit use case 3, one house, many beneficiaries
Under rural housing schemes, the final instalment is released when a geotagged photo of the completed house is uploaded. A known fraud is to photograph one completed house again and again, and upload it for several beneficiaries whose houses were never built. Each photo looks genuine, and each has a valid geotag. The trick shows only when we notice that photos of different beneficiaries were taken at almost the same spot.
Let us create the data of 500 beneficiaries in 25 villages of the district Amarpur. For each beneficiary, we have the location of the house site, recorded at the time of sanction, and the geotag of the completion photo. Genuine photos are taken at the house, with a GPS error of about 10 metres. We have planted a group of 10 beneficiaries, from different villages, whose completion photos were all taken at one house. That house belongs to one of the ten. For the other nine, the photo shows someone else’s house.

Code to create the housing dataset.seed(55)
amarpur <- districts |> filter(district == "Amarpur")

# 25 villages inside the district
villages <- st_sample(amarpur, 25) |>
  st_coordinates() |>
  as_tibble() |>
  mutate(village = sprintf("Village-%02d", 1:25))

n <- 500
houses <- tibble(ben_id  = sprintf("PH%04d", 1:n),
                 village = sample(villages$village, n, TRUE)) |>
  left_join(villages, by = "village") |>
  # houses clustered within about 100 metres of the village centre
  mutate(site_x  = X + rnorm(n, 0, 0.1),
         site_y  = Y + rnorm(n, 0, 0.1),
         # genuine photos, at the house, with about 10 metres of GPS error
         photo_x = site_x + rnorm(n, 0, 0.010),
         photo_y = site_y + rnorm(n, 0, 0.010)) |>
  select(ben_id, village, site_x, site_y, photo_x, photo_y)

# Planted. Ten beneficiaries of different villages, all photographed at one house
fake <- houses |> distinct(village, .keep_all = TRUE) |> slice(2:11) |> pull(ben_id)
spot <- houses |> filter(ben_id == fake[1])
houses <- houses |>
  mutate(photo_x = if_else(ben_id %in% fake, spot$site_x + rnorm(n, 0, 0.004), photo_x),
         photo_y = if_else(ben_id %in% fake, spot$site_y + rnorm(n, 0, 0.004), photo_y))



head(houses, 3)

# A tibble: 3 × 6
  ben_id village    site_x site_y photo_x photo_y
  <chr>  <chr>       <dbl>  <dbl>   <dbl>   <dbl>
1 PH0001 Village-01   49.5   124.    49.5    124.
2 PH0002 Village-25   26.0   202.    26.0    202.
3 PH0003 Village-15   58.5   182.    26.0    202.


Let us turn the photo geotags into points.

photos <- houses |>
  st_as_sf(coords = c("photo_x", "photo_y"), crs = st_crs(districts), remove = FALSE)

st_is_within_distance() finds, for each photo, all photos taken within a given distance of it. Our distances are in kilometres, so 15 metres is 0.015. The result is a list, with one element for each photo, holding the row numbers of the photos near it.

near <- st_is_within_distance(photos, dist = 0.015)
near[1:3]

[[1]]
[1]   1 123

[[2]]
[1]  2  3  4  5  9 11 12 14

[[3]]
 [1]  2  3  4  5  7  8  9 11 12 14


Every photo is near itself, so most elements hold just their own row number. To form groups of photos taken at the same spot, we treat each pair of nearby photos as an edge of a network, and find the connected components, as we did in Chapter 52. If photo A is near B, and B is near C, all three fall in one group.

library(igraph)

near_pairs <- tibble(from = rep(seq_along(near), lengths(near)),
                     to   = unlist(near)) |>
  filter(from < to)

photo_graph <- graph_from_data_frame(near_pairs, directed = FALSE,
                                     vertices = tibble(id = seq_len(nrow(photos))))

photos$group <- components(photo_graph)$membership

photo_groups <- photos |>
  st_drop_geometry() |>
  summarise(beneficiaries = n(),
            villages      = n_distinct(village),
            .by = group) |>
  filter(beneficiaries > 1) |>
  arrange(desc(beneficiaries))

photo_groups

# A tibble: 18 × 3
   group beneficiaries villages
   <dbl>         <int>    <int>
 1     2            10       10
 2   189             6        1
 3    30             3        1
 4     1             2        1
 5     5             2        1
 6    20             2        1
 7    63             2        1
 8    78             2        1
 9    86             2        1
10    90             2        1
11   117             2        1
12   172             2        1
13   199             2        1
14   206             2        1
15   207             2        1
16   219             2        1
17   253             2        1
18   422             2        1


There are 18 groups of photos taken within 15 metres of each other. 17 of them lie entirely within one village, with up to 6 beneficiaries each. These are most likely neighbours, whose houses stand next to each other, which is common in villages. In a crowded lane, house A may be within 15 metres of B, and B of C, so that a whole row of houses forms one group. So the size of a group alone is not the signal. The signal is a group that spans several villages, since houses in different villages cannot be next to each other. One group stands apart. 10 beneficiaries, from 10 different villages, have completion photos taken at the same spot. Figure 53.6 shows where their houses were supposed to be, and where the photos were taken.

same_spot <- photos |>
  st_drop_geometry() |>
  filter(group == big$group)

ggplot() +
  geom_sf(data = amarpur, fill = "grey95", colour = "grey60") +
  geom_point(data = houses, aes(site_x, site_y), colour = "grey75", size = 0.6) +
  geom_segment(data = same_spot, aes(x = site_x, y = site_y, xend = photo_x, yend = photo_y),
               colour = "firebrick", alpha = 0.6) +
  geom_point(data = same_spot, aes(site_x, site_y), colour = "steelblue", size = 2.5) +
  geom_point(data = same_spot, aes(photo_x, photo_y), colour = "firebrick", size = 3) +
  theme_void()






Figure 53.6: Sanctioned house sites (blue) of ten beneficiaries, and the single spot where all their completion photos were taken (red)




We can also measure, for each beneficiary, how far the photo was taken from the sanctioned site, as we did for the inspections.

photos |>
  st_drop_geometry() |>
  mutate(site_to_photo_km = sqrt((photo_x - site_x)^2 + (photo_y - site_y)^2),
         same_spot_group  = group == big$group) |>
  summarise(beneficiaries = n(),
            median_metres = round(1000 * median(site_to_photo_km)),
            .by = same_spot_group)

# A tibble: 2 × 3
  same_spot_group beneficiaries median_metres
  <lgl>                   <int>         <dbl>
1 FALSE                     490            12
2 TRUE                       10         39397


Here, on our flat grid in kilometres, the distance is simply the length of the straight line between the two points. Genuine photos were taken a few metres from the house site. The photos of the suspicious group were taken kilometres away from the sites. Both checks point to the same ten beneficiaries.






TipAudit tip



Use both checks together. The distance from the sanctioned site catches a photo taken at the wrong place. The grouping of photos catches the same house shown for many beneficiaries, even when the sanctioned sites were recorded carelessly. In the field, visit the sites of a sample of the group, and check whether a house exists there at all.

title: 53  Maps
text:
53.12 Buffers
A buffer is the area within a given distance of a feature. st_buffer() draws one. For example, the area within 25 km of every public hospital shows which parts of the state are served by public hospitals (Figure 53.7).

public_cover <- hosp_sf |>
  filter(type == "Public") |>
  st_buffer(dist = 25) |>
  st_union()

ggplot() +
  geom_sf(data = districts, fill = "grey95", colour = "grey60") +
  geom_sf(data = public_cover, fill = "seagreen", alpha = 0.3, colour = NA) +
  geom_sf(data = hosp_sf |> filter(type == "Public"), colour = "seagreen", size = 1) +
  theme_void()






Figure 53.7: Areas within 25 km of a public hospital




st_union() merges the overlapping circles into one shape. Areas outside the green shading are more than 25 km from any public hospital. In a performance audit of health services, such a map can show gaps in coverage.

title: 53  Maps
text:
53.13 A suggested workflow


Get the map layers you need, from an authoritative source, and check that all parts of each file are present.

Check the CRS of every layer. Use a projected CRS in metres or kilometres for distances and areas.

Turn location columns into points with st_as_sf().

Check locations against recorded areas with st_join().

Map rates, not counts, with geom_sf().

Measure distances with st_distance(), and look for records that are unusually far from where they should be.

Set sensible thresholds, allowing for GPS error.

Verify each flagged case with records and, where needed, a field visit.







ImportantRemember



A map is a powerful way to show a finding, but it is easy to mislead with it. Large areas catch the eye even when few people live there. Colours can exaggerate small differences. Make sure the map shows exactly the point you want to make, and that the numbers behind it are right.
