title: 54  Geocoding
text:
54.1 Where can geocoding help an auditor?
Most records give location as an address, not as coordinates. A vendor’s address, a beneficiary’s village, a hospital’s location. To put such records on a map, or to measure distances between them, we must first convert the address into latitude and longitude. This is called geocoding.
The reverse, converting latitude and longitude into an address, is called reverse geocoding. We will learn it in the next chapter.

title: 54  Geocoding
text:
Checking claimed distances. Travel allowance, transport charges and freight claims depend on distance. Geocoding the places lets us compare the claimed distance with the actual one.

Shared locations. Two “different” vendors, or many beneficiaries, at the same address can point to fake entities or duplicate registration. This complements the duplicate tests of Chapter 32.

Distance between supplier and site. A supplier located far away from the delivery site may be a front for someone else, or may be charging for transport that never happened.

Mapping records which only have addresses, so that the techniques of Chapter 53 can be applied.

title: 54  Geocoding
text:
54.2 How geocoding works
A geocoding service keeps a large database of places and addresses with their coordinates. We send it an address as text. It searches for the best match, and returns the coordinates, along with details like the full address it matched.
Several services are available.


OpenStreetMap Nominatim. Free and open, based on the OpenStreetMap community map. It is the default in R’s tidygeocoder package. Its usage policy allows only light use, about one request per second, and asks users to credit OpenStreetMap.

Commercial services, such as those offered by Google, ArcGIS and several Indian map providers. They often give better results for Indian addresses, but need an account and an API key, and usually charge beyond a free limit.







WarningNever send personal data to a public service



Geocoding sends your addresses to someone else’s server. Do not send addresses of beneficiaries, patients, employees or taxpayers to public services. Use only services approved by your organisation for such data. In this chapter, we geocode only public places, such as monuments and well-known markets.

title: 54  Geocoding
text:
54.3 Prerequisites
We will use tidygeocoder for geocoding, and sf for distances.

library(tidyverse)
library(tidygeocoder)
library(sf)

title: 54  Geocoding
text:
54.4 Geocoding a few places
The function geocode() from tidygeocoder works on a data frame. We tell it which column holds the address, and which service (method) to use. Let us geocode a few well-known places.

places <- tibble(place = c("Taj Mahal, Agra",
                           "Hawa Mahal, Jaipur",
                           "Charminar, Hyderabad",
                           "Victoria Memorial, Kolkata",
                           "Gateway of India, Mumbai",
                           "Xyzabc Nagar, Nowhere"))

places_geo <- places |>
  geocode(address = place, method = "osm")

places_geo

# A tibble: 6 × 3
  place                        lat  long
  <chr>                      <dbl> <dbl>
1 Taj Mahal, Agra             27.2  78.0
2 Hawa Mahal, Jaipur          26.9  75.8
3 Charminar, Hyderabad        17.4  78.5
4 Victoria Memorial, Kolkata  22.5  88.3
5 Gateway of India, Mumbai    18.9  72.8
6 Xyzabc Nagar, Nowhere       NA    NA  


geocode() has added two columns, lat and long. The last “place” is made up, and the service could not find it. So its coordinates are NA. Always check for such failures before going ahead.

places_geo |>
  filter(is.na(lat))

# A tibble: 1 × 3
  place                   lat  long
  <chr>                 <dbl> <dbl>
1 Xyzabc Nagar, Nowhere    NA    NA








TipGeocode once, save the result



Geocoding is slow, and free services limit how much you can use them. Do not geocode the same addresses again and again. Geocode once, save the result with write_csv(), and read the saved file in later work.



54.4.1 More details about each match
With full_results = TRUE, the service returns everything it knows about the match. This is useful to judge the quality of each match.

places_geo_full <- places |>
  slice(1:3) |>
  geocode(address = place, method = "osm", full_results = TRUE)

places_geo_full |>
  select(place, lat, long, display_name, class, type)

# A tibble: 3 × 6
  place                  lat  long display_name                      class type 
  <chr>                <dbl> <dbl> <chr>                             <chr> <chr>
1 Taj Mahal, Agra       27.2  78.0 Taj Mahal, Taj East Gate Road, T… hist… tomb 
2 Hawa Mahal, Jaipur    26.9  75.8 Hawa Mahal, Amer Road, Ramganj, … tour… attr…
3 Charminar, Hyderabad  17.4  78.5 Charminar, Charminar Circle, Laa… tour… attr…


The display_name column shows the full address that the service actually matched. The class and type columns tell what kind of place it is. Reading these is the best way to catch wrong matches.






WarningBeware of approximate matches



When a service cannot find the exact address, it often returns the centre of the town, district or pin code instead, without any warning. In Indian addresses, which are often written in very different ways, this is common. So two vendors may appear to be at “the same location” only because both were matched to the centre of the same town. Always look at what was matched, before drawing conclusions.

title: 54  Geocoding
text:
54.5 From coordinates to map points
Latitude and longitude are in the WGS 84 coordinate system, whose code is EPSG:4326. We met coordinate systems in Chapter 53. To turn the geocoded table into map points, we use st_as_sf(). Note that the longitude comes first, because it is the x-coordinate.

places_sf <- places_geo |>
  filter(!is.na(lat)) |>
  st_as_sf(coords = c("long", "lat"), crs = 4326)

places_sf

Simple feature collection with 5 features and 1 field
Geometry type: POINT
Dimension:     XY
Bounding box:  xmin: 72.83457 ymin: 17.3616 xmax: 88.34255 ymax: 27.17501
Geodetic CRS:  WGS 84
# A tibble: 5 × 2
  place                                 geometry
* <chr>                              <POINT [°]>
1 Taj Mahal, Agra             (78.0421 27.17501)
2 Hawa Mahal, Jaipur         (75.82687 26.92393)
3 Charminar, Hyderabad        (78.47464 17.3616)
4 Victoria Memorial, Kolkata (88.34255 22.54496)
5 Gateway of India, Mumbai   (72.83457 18.92197)



54.5.1 Measuring distances
st_distance() measures distances between points. For latitude and longitude, sf correctly measures along the curved surface of the earth, and returns the result in metres. Let us find the distances between our places, in kilometres.

dist_matrix <- st_distance(places_sf)

dist_km <- round(units::drop_units(dist_matrix) / 1000)
dimnames(dist_km) <- list(places_sf$place, places_sf$place)

dist_km

                           Taj Mahal, Agra Hawa Mahal, Jaipur
Taj Mahal, Agra                          0                221
Hawa Mahal, Jaipur                     221                  0
Charminar, Hyderabad                  1092               1098
Victoria Memorial, Kolkata            1159               1354
Gateway of India, Mumbai              1061                941
                           Charminar, Hyderabad Victoria Memorial, Kolkata
Taj Mahal, Agra                            1092                       1159
Hawa Mahal, Jaipur                         1098                       1354
Charminar, Hyderabad                          0                       1181
Victoria Memorial, Kolkata                 1181                          0
Gateway of India, Mumbai                    621                       1661
                           Gateway of India, Mumbai
Taj Mahal, Agra                                1061
Hawa Mahal, Jaipur                              941
Charminar, Hyderabad                            621
Victoria Memorial, Kolkata                     1661
Gateway of India, Mumbai                          0


st_distance() with a single set of points returns a matrix of the distance between every pair. units::drop_units() removes the unit “m”, so that we can divide by 1,000 to get kilometres.
These are straight-line distances, as a bird would fly. Roads and railway lines are always longer. This simple fact is the basis of our first audit check.

title: 54  Geocoding
section: 54.6 Audit use case 1, checking claimed travel distances
text:
54.6 Audit use case 1, checking claimed travel distances
Suppose a department pays travel allowance partly on the basis of the distance claimed by the employee. Let us check a few claims. The table below is made up. The places are well-known towns.

ta_claims <- tribble(
  ~claim_no, ~from,               ~to,                   ~claimed_km,
  "TA-01",   "Lucknow",           "Varanasi",            320,
  "TA-02",   "Bhopal",            "Indore",              195,
  "TA-03",   "Patna",             "Gaya",                115,
  "TA-04",   "Jaipur",            "Ajmer",               60,
  "TA-05",   "Dehradun",          "Haridwar",            160,
  "TA-06",   "Bhubaneswar",       "Puri",                65
)

We need the coordinates of each town. Since a town appears in more than one claim, we geocode each town only once.

towns <- tibble(town = unique(c(ta_claims$from, ta_claims$to))) |>
  mutate(address = paste0(town, ", India")) |>
  geocode(address = address, method = "osm")

towns

# A tibble: 12 × 4
   town        address              lat  long
   <chr>       <chr>              <dbl> <dbl>
 1 Lucknow     Lucknow, India      26.8  80.9
 2 Bhopal      Bhopal, India       23.3  77.4
 3 Patna       Patna, India        25.6  85.1
 4 Jaipur      Jaipur, India       26.9  75.8
 5 Dehradun    Dehradun, India     30.3  78.0
 6 Bhubaneswar Bhubaneswar, India  20.3  85.8
 7 Varanasi    Varanasi, India     25.3  83.0
 8 Indore      Indore, India       22.7  75.9
 9 Gaya        Gaya, India         24.8  85.0
10 Ajmer       Ajmer, India        26.5  74.6
11 Haridwar    Haridwar, India     29.9  78.1
12 Puri        Puri, India         19.8  85.8


We added “, India” to each name, so that the service does not pick a town of the same name in another country. Now we join the coordinates to both ends of each claim, and measure the straight-line distance.

from_pts <- ta_claims |>
  left_join(towns, by = c("from" = "town")) |>
  st_as_sf(coords = c("long", "lat"), crs = 4326)

to_pts <- ta_claims |>
  left_join(towns, by = c("to" = "town")) |>
  st_as_sf(coords = c("long", "lat"), crs = 4326)

ta_checked <- ta_claims |>
  mutate(straight_km = round(as.numeric(st_distance(from_pts, to_pts, by_element = TRUE)) / 1000),
         ratio = round(claimed_km / straight_km, 2))

ta_checked

# A tibble: 6 × 6
  claim_no from        to       claimed_km straight_km ratio
  <chr>    <chr>       <chr>         <dbl>       <dbl> <dbl>
1 TA-01    Lucknow     Varanasi        320         266  1.2 
2 TA-02    Bhopal      Indore          195         168  1.16
3 TA-03    Patna       Gaya            115          91  1.26
4 TA-04    Jaipur      Ajmer            60         127  0.47
5 TA-05    Dehradun    Haridwar        160          44  3.64
6 TA-06    Bhubaneswar Puri             65          50  1.3 


How do we read the ratio? Road distance in India is usually around 1.2 to 1.5 times the straight-line distance. So a ratio in that range is normal.

A ratio below 1 is impossible. No road is shorter than a straight line. Such a claim is certainly wrong. Here, that means the claim from Jaipur to Ajmer.
A ratio far above 1.5 suggests an inflated claim. Here, the claim from Dehradun to Haridwar is more than three times the straight-line distance.


ta_checked |>
  filter(ratio < 1 | ratio > 1.8)

# A tibble: 2 × 6
  claim_no from     to       claimed_km straight_km ratio
  <chr>    <chr>    <chr>         <dbl>       <dbl> <dbl>
1 TA-04    Jaipur   Ajmer            60         127  0.47
2 TA-05    Dehradun Haridwar        160          44  3.64








NoteStraight-line or road distance?



The straight-line distance is a quick filter, not the final answer. For the flagged claims, check the actual road or rail distance from official tables, or from a routing service. Some routes are genuinely long because of hills, rivers or the lack of a direct road.

title: 54  Geocoding
section: 54.7 Audit use case 2, different vendors, same place
text:
54.7 Audit use case 2, different vendors, same place
In Chapter 32, we found look-alike vendor names. Another sign of fake or related vendors is that their addresses point to the same place, even though they are written differently. Let us look at a few vendors of a department. The addresses are of well-known commercial areas, and the vendors are made up.

vendors <- tribble(
  ~vendor,                   ~address,
  "Shubh Laxmi Traders",     "Nehru Place, New Delhi",
  "Gupta Office Supplies",   "Chandni Chowk, Delhi",
  "Shree Balaji Enterprises","Nehru Place, Delhi",
  "Raj Computers",           "Lajpat Nagar, New Delhi",
  "Om Sai Suppliers",        "Karol Bagh, New Delhi",
  "Modern Stationers",       "Nehru Place Market, New Delhi"
)


vendors_geo <- vendors |>
  geocode(address = address, method = "osm")

vendors_geo

# A tibble: 6 × 4
  vendor                   address                         lat  long
  <chr>                    <chr>                         <dbl> <dbl>
1 Shubh Laxmi Traders      Nehru Place, New Delhi         28.6  77.2
2 Gupta Office Supplies    Chandni Chowk, Delhi           28.7  77.2
3 Shree Balaji Enterprises Nehru Place, Delhi             28.5  77.3
4 Raj Computers            Lajpat Nagar, New Delhi        28.6  77.2
5 Om Sai Suppliers         Karol Bagh, New Delhi          28.6  77.2
6 Modern Stationers        Nehru Place Market, New Delhi  28.5  77.3


Three vendors give addresses in Nehru Place, written in three different ways. To find vendors at the same place, we round the coordinates to three decimal places, which is about 100 metres, and look for vendors that share a rounded location.

vendors_geo |>
  mutate(spot = paste(round(lat, 3), round(long, 3))) |>
  filter(n() > 1, .by = spot) |>
  arrange(spot)

# A tibble: 2 × 5
  vendor                   address                         lat  long spot       
  <chr>                    <chr>                         <dbl> <dbl> <chr>      
1 Shree Balaji Enterprises Nehru Place, Delhi             28.5  77.3 28.549 77.…
2 Modern Stationers        Nehru Place Market, New Delhi  28.5  77.3 28.549 77.…


Two vendors share a location. But what happened to the third Nehru Place vendor? Let us see what the service actually matched for each of the three addresses.

vendors |>
  filter(str_detect(address, "Nehru Place")) |>
  geocode(address = address, method = "osm", full_results = TRUE) |>
  select(vendor, address, display_name)

# A tibble: 3 × 3
  vendor                   address                       display_name           
  <chr>                    <chr>                         <chr>                  
1 Shubh Laxmi Traders      Nehru Place, New Delhi        Motilal Nehru Place, C…
2 Shree Balaji Enterprises Nehru Place, Delhi            Nehru Place, South, De…
3 Modern Stationers        Nehru Place Market, New Delhi Mahadev communications…


“Nehru Place, New Delhi” has been matched to Motilal Nehru Place, a road in central Delhi, several kilometres away from the Nehru Place market. A small difference in how the address was written led to a completely different place. This is exactly the problem of approximate matches that we warned about earlier. An auditor who relied on the coordinates alone would have missed that all three vendors are in the same market.
So the analysis finds two vendors at one spot, and a careful reading of the matched addresses adds the third. Three “different” vendors are located in the same market. This is not wrong by itself. A market like Nehru Place has hundreds of shops. But if these three vendors also bid in the same tenders, as in Chapter 45, or share a phone number or bank account, the case for a closer look becomes strong.






TipAudit tip



Rounding to three decimal places groups points within about 100 metres. Rounding to four places, about 10 metres, is stricter. Choose according to the quality of your addresses. With precise addresses, use four places. With addresses that only give a locality, three or even two places may be better.

title: 54  Geocoding
section: 54.8 Audit use case 3, excess lead charges in works
text:
54.8 Audit use case 3, excess lead charges in works
In road and building works, contractors are paid for carrying materials like stone aggregate from a quarry to the work site. This carriage charge is called lead, and it is paid per cubic metre per kilometre. So the longer the claimed lead, the bigger the payment. Two common irregularities are,

claiming carriage from a distant quarry, when an approved quarry is much nearer, and
claiming a lead much longer than the actual distance to the quarry named.

Excess payment on lead is a frequent finding in audits of works. Let us check six works in Rajasthan. The work sites are real towns. The quarries, quantities and claims are made up, and the carriage rate is imaginary.

works <- tribble(
  ~work_id, ~site,       ~quantity_cum, ~claimed_quarry,  ~claimed_lead_km,
  "W-01",   "Churu",      12000,        "Bikaner",         175,
  "W-02",   "Sikar",      15000,        "Kotputli",        150,
  "W-03",   "Nagaur",      9000,        "Jodhpur",         135,
  "W-04",   "Jhunjhunu",  18000,        "Jodhpur",         410,
  "W-05",   "Tonk",       10000,        "Sawai Madhopur",   85,
  "W-06",   "Bhilwara",   14000,        "Kishangarh",      290
)

approved_quarries <- c("Kishangarh", "Bikaner", "Jodhpur", "Kotputli", "Sawai Madhopur")
rate_per_cum_km <- 4.5   # rupees, imaginary

We geocode each town once, sites and quarries together.

rj_towns <- tibble(town = unique(c(works$site, approved_quarries))) |>
  mutate(address = paste0(town, ", Rajasthan, India")) |>
  geocode(address = address, method = "osm")

rj_sf <- rj_towns |> st_as_sf(coords = c("long", "lat"), crs = 4326)
quarry_sf <- rj_sf |> filter(town %in% approved_quarries)

For each work, we need two distances. First, the straight-line distance to the quarry it claims. Second, the straight-line distance to the nearest approved quarry. st_nearest_feature() gives, for each point, the row number of the nearest feature in another layer.

site_sf <- works |>
  left_join(rj_towns, by = c("site" = "town")) |>
  st_as_sf(coords = c("long", "lat"), crs = 4326)

claimed_sf <- quarry_sf[match(works$claimed_quarry, quarry_sf$town), ]
nearest_sf <- quarry_sf[st_nearest_feature(site_sf, quarry_sf), ]

lead_check <- works |>
  mutate(km_to_claimed  = round(as.numeric(st_distance(site_sf, claimed_sf, by_element = TRUE)) / 1000),
         nearest_quarry = nearest_sf$town,
         km_to_nearest  = round(as.numeric(st_distance(site_sf, nearest_sf, by_element = TRUE)) / 1000),
         lead_ratio     = round(claimed_lead_km / km_to_claimed, 2))

lead_check |>
  select(work_id, site, claimed_quarry, claimed_lead_km, km_to_claimed, lead_ratio,
         nearest_quarry, km_to_nearest) |>
  print(width = Inf)

# A tibble: 6 × 8
  work_id site      claimed_quarry claimed_lead_km km_to_claimed lead_ratio
  <chr>   <chr>     <chr>                    <dbl>         <dbl>      <dbl>
1 W-01    Churu     Bikaner                    175           136       1.29
2 W-02    Sikar     Kotputli                   150           115       1.3 
3 W-03    Nagaur    Jodhpur                    135           104       1.3 
4 W-04    Jhunjhunu Jodhpur                    410           317       1.29
5 W-05    Tonk      Sawai Madhopur              85            65       1.31
6 W-06    Bhilwara  Kishangarh                 290           125       2.32
  nearest_quarry km_to_nearest
  <chr>                  <dbl>
1 Bikaner                  136
2 Kotputli                 115
3 Jodhpur                  104
4 Kotputli                  77
5 Sawai Madhopur            65
6 Kishangarh               125


Two works stand out.


W-04 at Jhunjhunu claims stone from Jodhpur, although the approved quarry at Kotputli is much nearer. Its lead ratio is normal. The distance claimed is genuine, but the quarry choice is not.

W-06 at Bhilwara names the nearest quarry, Kishangarh, but claims a lead of more than twice the straight-line distance.

To estimate the excess payment, we take a reasonable lead as 1.3 times the straight-line distance to the nearest approved quarry, as discussed in use case 1. Any lead claimed beyond this is excess.

lead_excess <- lead_check |>
  mutate(reasonable_lead_km = round(1.3 * km_to_nearest),
         excess_km          = pmax(claimed_lead_km - reasonable_lead_km, 0),
         excess_rupees      = excess_km * quantity_cum * rate_per_cum_km) |>
  filter(excess_km > 0.2 * reasonable_lead_km) |>
  select(work_id, site, claimed_lead_km, reasonable_lead_km, excess_km, quantity_cum, excess_rupees)

lead_excess |> print(width = Inf)

# A tibble: 2 × 7
  work_id site      claimed_lead_km reasonable_lead_km excess_km quantity_cum
  <chr>   <chr>               <dbl>              <dbl>     <dbl>        <dbl>
1 W-04    Jhunjhunu             410                100       310        18000
2 W-06    Bhilwara              290                162       128        14000
  excess_rupees
          <dbl>
1      25110000
2       8064000


We keep only works whose claimed lead exceeds the reasonable lead by more than 20%, to allow for genuinely longer roads. The two works together involve an estimated excess payment of about ₹3.32 crore.

54.8.1 An interactive map
For presenting such findings, and for exploring them, an interactive map helps. The package leaflet draws maps which can be zoomed and clicked, with OpenStreetMap as the background. Unlike our imaginary state in Chapter 53, these are real places with latitude and longitude, so leaflet can place them on a real map (Figure 54.1). Click a line to see the claim.

library(leaflet)

# One straight line from each work site to its claimed quarry
route_lines <- map2(st_geometry(site_sf), st_geometry(claimed_sf),
                    \(a, b) st_linestring(rbind(st_coordinates(a), st_coordinates(b)))) |>
  st_sfc(crs = 4326) |>
  st_sf(geometry = _) |>
  mutate(work_id = works$work_id,
         flagged = work_id %in% lead_excess$work_id,
         popup   = paste0(work_id, ": ", works$site, " to ", works$claimed_quarry,
                          "<br>Claimed lead ", works$claimed_lead_km, " km"))

leaflet(width = "100%", height = 450) |>
  addTiles() |>
  addPolylines(data = route_lines, color = ~if_else(flagged, "red", "grey"),
               weight = 3, popup = ~popup) |>
  addCircleMarkers(data = site_sf, radius = 5, color = "steelblue", label = ~site) |>
  addCircleMarkers(data = quarry_sf, radius = 6, color = "darkgreen", label = ~town)






Figure 54.1: Claimed carriage routes. Red lines are works with excess lead.









TipAudit tip



When a work claims material from a distant quarry, ask why the nearer approved quarry was not used. Sometimes there is a good reason, like the quality of stone or the nearer quarry being closed. That reason must be on record, with the approval of the competent authority, before the work was done. Also compare the claimed lead with the lead chart approved for the district, if one exists.

title: 54  Geocoding
text:
54.9 A suggested workflow


Use an approved service. Never send personal addresses to a public geocoder.

Clean the addresses first. Add the state and “India”, remove extra spaces, and expand common short forms.

Geocode each unique address once, and save the results.

Check the failures (NA coordinates) and the quality of matches, using full_results = TRUE.

Turn the results into points with st_as_sf(coords = c("long", "lat"), crs = 4326).

Measure distances with st_distance(), and compare with claims.

Look for shared locations, by rounding coordinates.

Verify each flagged case with records, and with official distance tables or site visits.







ImportantRemember



Geocoding gives the location of the address as written, not necessarily the location of the thing. A wrong or vague address gives a wrong or vague location. Treat geocoded locations as approximate, and always look at the matched address before drawing a conclusion.

title: 55  Reverse Geocoding
text:
55.1 Introduction
Geocoding, which we learnt in Chapter 54, is the process of converting a human-readable address into geographic coordinates, such as latitude and longitude. It lets us place addresses on a map.
Reverse geocoding, on the other hand, is the process of converting geographic coordinates (latitude and longitude) into a human-readable address, such as a street, village or city, district, state and country. In other words, it determines the address of a place from its coordinates.
Both are important in geospatial data analysis. They allow us to link spatial information with non-spatial information, such as demographic data or land records, and to see patterns and relationships based on location.
Reverse geocoding is especially useful in forensic data analysis. Mobile phones and handheld devices now record the coordinates of almost every activity. A photo of a newly built house, an attendance marked by a field worker, a ration distributed through a point-of-sale machine, a payment made at an ATM. Each comes with a latitude and a longitude. Reverse geocoding turns these numbers into places that an auditor can read and check, such as “is this photo really from the village where the work was claimed?”.

title: 55  Reverse Geocoding
text:
55.2 Widely used databases
OpenStreetMap (OSM) is one of the most popular and widely used databases for geocoding and reverse geocoding. OSM is a free and open map of the world, created and maintained by a community of volunteers. It has a rich and detailed set of spatial data, including street names, addresses and other points of interest. Its free service, called Nominatim, allows only light use, about one request per second.
Other popular services include Google Maps, ArcGIS and several Indian map providers. They provide geocoding and reverse geocoding through paid APIs, and are widely used in web and mobile applications.






WarningPrivacy



Coordinates of a beneficiary’s home are personal data, just like the address. Do not send such coordinates to public services. Use only services approved by your organisation. In this chapter, we use the coordinates of well-known monuments only.

title: 55  Reverse Geocoding
text:
55.3 Example in R

55.3.1 Prerequisites

library(tidyverse)
library(tidygeocoder)


55.3.2 Function to be used
We will use the reverse_geo() function from tidygeocoder. Its main arguments are these.
reverse_geo(
  lat,
  long,
  method = "osm",
  address = "address",
  full_results = FALSE,
  ...
)


lat and long are, as the names suggest, the latitude and longitude of the place whose address is to be found.

method is the service to be used. The default is osm. Other services available include arcgis, geocodio and google.

address is the name of the output column holding the address.

full_results is FALSE by default. If set to TRUE, it returns all available details from the service, such as the city, district, state and postcode in separate columns.
For other arguments, please check the help of the function.

55.3.3 A single place
Let us find the address of the Taj Mahal, from its coordinates.

reverse_geo(lat = 27.1751, long = 78.0421, method = "osm")

# A tibble: 1 × 3
    lat  long address                                                           
  <dbl> <dbl> <chr>                                                             
1  27.2  78.0 Taj Mahal, Taj East Gate Road, Taj Ganj, Agra, Uttar Pradesh, 282…








TipCoordinates need care



Each digit of a coordinate matters. One degree of latitude is about 111 km, so the third decimal place is about 100 metres. If the longitude above is mistyped as 78.421 instead of 78.0421, the “Taj Mahal” turns out to be a village in Firozabad district, about 40 km away. When coordinates are typed by hand, always check a few of them on a map.



55.3.4 Several places at once
reverse_geo() is vectorised. We can give it vectors of latitudes and longitudes, and it returns one row for each. Let us build a sample dataset of four places of interest in India.

sample_places <- tibble(
  lat  = c(27.1751, 24.8318, 27.1795, 28.5245),
  long = c(78.0421, 79.9199, 78.0211, 77.1855)
)

knitr::kable(sample_places)

results <- sample_places |>
  reverse_geocode(lat = lat, long = long, method = "osm", full_results = TRUE)

results |>
  select(lat, long, address, any_of(c("state_district", "state", "postcode"))) |>
  knitr::kable()

title: 55  Reverse Geocoding
section: 55.4 Audit use case 1, checking geotagged photos
text:
55.4 Audit use case 1, checking geotagged photos
Many government schemes ask field staff to upload a geotagged photo of each completed work, such as a house, a pond or a road. The work is claimed to be at a particular place. Reverse geocoding the photo’s coordinates tells us where the photo was actually taken.
Let us use our four coordinates as the geotags of four such photos. Each comes with the place where the work was claimed to be. One of the claims is wrong.

photos <- sample_places |>
  mutate(photo_id      = c("PH-101", "PH-102", "PH-103", "PH-104"),
         claimed_place = c("Agra", "Khajuraho", "Mathura", "Delhi"),
         .before = 1)

photos

# A tibble: 4 × 4
  photo_id claimed_place   lat  long
  <chr>    <chr>         <dbl> <dbl>
1 PH-101   Agra           27.2  78.0
2 PH-102   Khajuraho      24.8  79.9
3 PH-103   Mathura        27.2  78.0
4 PH-104   Delhi          28.5  77.2


We reverse geocode the photos, and check whether the address returned contains the claimed place.

photos_checked <- photos |>
  reverse_geocode(lat = lat, long = long, method = "osm") |>
  mutate(matches_claim = str_detect(str_to_lower(address), str_to_lower(claimed_place)))

photos_checked |>
  select(photo_id, claimed_place, address, matches_claim)

# A tibble: 4 × 4
  photo_id claimed_place address                                   matches_claim
  <chr>    <chr>         <chr>                                     <lgl>        
1 PH-101   Agra          Taj Mahal, Taj East Gate Road, Taj Ganj,… TRUE         
2 PH-102   Khajuraho     Khajuraho, Jatkra, Rajnagar Tahsil, Chha… TRUE         
3 PH-103   Mathura       Agra Fort, Metcalfe Road, Agra, Uttar Pr… FALSE        
4 PH-104   Delhi         Qutb Minar, Kalka Das Marg, Mehrauli, So… TRUE         


Photo PH-103 was claimed to show a work in Mathura. But its geotag is in Agra, more than 50 km away. Such a photo needs explanation. It may be a photo of a different work, or of no work at all.






WarningCaution



Comparing text in this way is a rough first check. Place names are spelt in many ways, such as Gurgaon and Gurugram, and the address returned by the service may use a different name, or a larger or smaller unit, than the claim. Treat a mismatch as a question to be checked, not as a finding. For large data, it is better to compare codes, such as district codes, or to use the map-based checks of Chapter 53, where we measured the distance between a geotag and the site directly.

title: 55  Reverse Geocoding
section: 55.5 Audit use case 2, checking geotags without sending them anywhere
text:
55.5 Audit use case 2, checking geotags without sending them anywhere
Reverse geocoding needs an online service, and we cannot send the coordinates of beneficiaries’ homes or works to a public one. But many problems in geotags can be found without any service at all, using only the numbers themselves. Let us take the geotags of 1,000 works completed under a scheme in a district of Rajasthan. We have planted five common problems.

15 geotags with latitude and longitude swapped, a frequent error when data passes between systems.
8 geotags of 0, 0, which is what some devices record when the GPS has failed.
20 geotags with only two decimal places, which suggests they were typed by hand, not captured by the phone.
3 geotags outside India altogether.
40 works in different villages, all geotagged at exactly the same spot. This is the block office, from where the photos were actually uploaded.


Code to create the geotagsset.seed(7)
n <- 1000
geotags <- tibble(work_id = sprintf("WK%04d", 1:n),
                  village = sprintf("Village-%02d", sample(1:60, n, TRUE)),
                  lat  = round(runif(n, 26.60, 27.20), 6),
                  long = round(runif(n, 75.50, 76.10), 6))

problem_rows <- sample(1:n, 86)
swapped <- problem_rows[1:15]
zeros   <- problem_rows[16:23]
typed   <- problem_rows[24:43]
office  <- problem_rows[44:83]
abroad  <- problem_rows[84:86]

geotags <- geotags |>
  mutate(
    tmp  = lat,
    lat  = if_else(row_number() %in% swapped, long, lat),
    long = if_else(row_number() %in% swapped, tmp, long),
    lat  = if_else(row_number() %in% zeros, 0, lat),
    long = if_else(row_number() %in% zeros, 0, long),
    lat  = if_else(row_number() %in% typed, round(lat, 2), lat),
    long = if_else(row_number() %in% typed, round(long, 2), long),
    lat  = if_else(row_number() %in% office, 26.912437, lat),
    long = if_else(row_number() %in% office, 75.787271, long),
    lat  = if_else(row_number() %in% abroad, lat - 30, lat)
  ) |>
  select(-tmp)


Let us add one column for each check. India lies roughly between latitudes 6° and 38° north, and longitudes 68° and 98° east. A swapped point has its latitude in the range of India’s longitudes, and the other way round.

count_decimals <- function(x) {
  str_length(coalesce(str_extract(as.character(x), "(?<=\\.)\\d+"), ""))
}

geotag_checks <- geotags |>
  add_count(lat, long, name = "same_spot") |>
  mutate(
    zero_point    = lat == 0 & long == 0,
    swapped       = between(lat, 68, 98) & between(long, 6, 38),
    outside_india = !zero_point & !swapped &
                    !(between(lat, 6, 38) & between(long, 68, 98)),
    low_precision = !zero_point & (count_decimals(lat) <= 2 | count_decimals(long) <= 2),
    shared_spot   = same_spot >= 5 & !zero_point
  )

geotag_checks |>
  summarise(across(zero_point:shared_spot, sum))

# A tibble: 1 × 5
  zero_point swapped outside_india low_precision shared_spot
       <int>   <int>         <int>         <int>       <int>
1          8      15             3            20          40


count_decimals() uses a look-behind, (?<=\\.), which we learnt in Chapter 19, to take the digits after the decimal point and count them. A phone usually gives five or six decimals. Two decimals mean an accuracy of only about a kilometre.
Every planted problem has been found. The most serious is the shared spot. Let us look at it.

geotag_checks |>
  filter(shared_spot) |>
  summarise(works = n(), villages = n_distinct(village), .by = c(lat, long))

# A tibble: 1 × 4
    lat  long works villages
  <dbl> <dbl> <int>    <int>
1  26.9  75.8    40       29


40 works, in 29 different villages, have exactly the same geotag, to the sixth decimal place. No two houses or ponds can be at the same spot. These photos were taken, or at least uploaded, at one place. This one location, unlike a beneficiary’s home, is an office, so it can be reverse geocoded to confirm what it is.






TipAudit tip



Run these checks first, on the whole data, before any mapping or reverse geocoding. They need no internet, raise no privacy concern, and often find the most important problems. Swapped and zero coordinates are data errors to be corrected. Typed coordinates and shared spots suggest that the photo was not taken at the site, and need verification in the field.

title: 55  Reverse Geocoding
text:
55.6 A suggested workflow


Use an approved service for any coordinates that relate to people.

Check the coordinates offline first, for swapped, zero, typed, outside-India and shared values, as in the second use case.

Reverse geocode each unique location once, using reverse_geocode() on a data frame, and save the results.

Compare the returned place with the claimed place, by name or preferably by code.

Measure the distance between the geotag and the claimed site, where the site’s coordinates are known.

Verify every mismatch with records or a field visit.







ImportantRemember



A geotag tells us where the phone was, not necessarily where the work is. And geotags can be faked. A correct geotag supports a claim, but does not prove it. A wrong one is a strong reason to look closer.

title: Part IX: Reporting
text:
Analysis has to end in a report. This part shows how to produce the reports themselves from code, so that every number in them is computed and none is copied by hand.
You will build a report for every district from one template, and Excel working papers for the field party.

title: 56  Reproducible Audit Reports
text:
56.1 Our audit, a scheme in five districts
Every analysis in this book ends the same way. The results have to reach someone: the audit officer, the head of the audit party, the auditee, or the report. Too often, this last step is done by hand. Figures are copied from the R console into Word, tables are pasted into Excel and formatted, and the whole process is repeated for each district, each month, each audit. Every copy is a chance for a mistake, and when the data changes, everything has to be done again.
In this chapter we learn to produce the reports themselves with code.
This book itself is written in Quarto, so everything you see here is a small version of the same idea.
Prerequisites
For rendering reports from R we also need the package quarto (install.packages("quarto")), and Quarto itself, which comes with RStudio.
A State’s Kisan Sahayata scheme pays each eligible farmer ₹2,000 in each of three instalments a year. We have the payment register and the beneficiary list for 2024-25, for five districts, and four checks to run.
The audit party wants one report for each district, to send to the District Collector, and one Excel workbook of the exceptions for each district, for verification in the field.
Code to create the data filesproject_dir <- file.path(tempdir(), "kisan_audit")
dir.create(project_dir, showWarnings = FALSE)

set.seed(2025)
districts <- c("Amarpur", "Belapur", "Chandpur", "Devgarh", "Fatehpur")
n_ben <- 2500
beneficiaries <- tibble(
  ben_id   = sprintf("KS%06d", 1:n_ben),
  district = sample(districts, n_ben, TRUE),
  status   = sample(c("Active", "Deceased", "Ineligible"), n_ben, TRUE, prob = c(0.96, 0.025, 0.015)),
  account  = sprintf("%011.0f", runif(n_ben, 1e10, 9.99e10))
)
instalments <- tibble(instalment = 1:3,
                      due = as.Date(c("2024-06-15", "2024-10-15", "2025-02-15")))
payments <- beneficiaries |>
  filter(status == "Active" | runif(n()) < 0.5) |>      # some not-active beneficiaries still paid
  cross_join(instalments) |>
  mutate(paid_on = due + sample(0:20, n(), TRUE), amount = 2000) |>
  select(ben_id, district, instalment, paid_on, amount, account)
# Planted. Instalments paid twice, more often in Chandpur
dup <- payments |>
  slice_sample(n = 60, weight_by = if_else(district == "Chandpur", 5, 1)) |>
  mutate(paid_on = paid_on + sample(1:30, n(), TRUE))
payments <- bind_rows(payments, dup)
# Planted. Wrong amounts
wrong <- sample(nrow(payments), 40)
payments$amount[wrong] <- sample(c(4000, 20000, 6000), 40, TRUE)
# Planted. Six beneficiaries in Devgarh sharing one account
share <- beneficiaries |> filter(district == "Devgarh") |> slice_sample(n = 6) |> pull(ben_id)
beneficiaries$account[beneficiaries$ben_id %in% share] <- "50012345678"
payments$account[payments$ben_id %in% share] <- "50012345678"

write_csv(arrange(payments, paid_on), file.path(project_dir, "payments.csv"))
write_csv(beneficiaries, file.path(project_dir, "beneficiaries.csv"))
list.files(project_dir)

[1] "beneficiaries.csv" "payments.csv"

title: 56  Reproducible Audit Reports
text:
Was any instalment paid more than once to the same beneficiary?
Was any payment different from the entitlement of ₹2,000?
Was anything paid to a beneficiary marked deceased or ineligible?
Is any bank account shared by more than one beneficiary?

title: 56  Reproducible Audit Reports
section: 56.2 Step 1. Put the checks in functions
text:
56.2 Step 1. Put the checks in functions
The first step towards any repeatable report is to write each check as a function (Chapter 3), which takes the data of one district and returns its exceptions. The functions are kept in one file, checks.R, which every report and every script then uses with source("checks.R"). A correction made once in this file applies everywhere.

check_duplicates <- function(pay) {
  pay |> filter(n() > 1, .by = c(ben_id, instalment)) |> arrange(ben_id, instalment, paid_on)
}
check_amount <- function(pay, entitlement = 2000) {
  pay |> filter(amount != entitlement)
}
check_status <- function(pay, ben) {
  pay |>
    inner_join(ben |> select(ben_id, status), by = "ben_id") |>
    filter(status != "Active")
}
check_shared_accounts <- function(ben) {
  ben |> filter(n() > 1, .by = account) |> arrange(account)
}

run_checks <- function(pay, ben) {
  list(duplicates      = check_duplicates(pay),
       wrong_amount    = check_amount(pay),
       not_active      = check_status(pay, ben),
       shared_accounts = check_shared_accounts(ben))
}

run_checks() returns a list of four data frames, one for each check. Let us try it on one district, and make the summary that the report will show.

payments_all <- read_csv(file.path(project_dir, "payments.csv"), show_col_types = FALSE)
benef_all    <- read_csv(file.path(project_dir, "beneficiaries.csv"), show_col_types = FALSE,
                         col_types = cols(account = col_character()))

summarise_checks <- function(results, entitlement = 2000) {
  dup <- results$duplicates
  tibble(
    check  = c("Same instalment paid more than once",
               "Amount different from the entitlement",
               "Payment to deceased or ineligible beneficiaries",
               "Bank account shared by more than one beneficiary"),
    cases  = c(nrow(dup) - nrow(distinct(dup, ben_id, instalment)),
               nrow(results$wrong_amount),
               nrow(results$not_active),
               n_distinct(results$shared_accounts$account)),
    amount = c(sum(dup$amount) - sum(distinct(dup, ben_id, instalment, .keep_all = TRUE)$amount),
               sum(results$wrong_amount$amount - entitlement),
               sum(results$not_active$amount),
               NA)
  )
}

chandpur <- run_checks(filter(payments_all, district == "Chandpur"),
                       filter(benef_all, district == "Chandpur"))
summarise_checks(chandpur)

# A tibble: 4 × 3
  check                                            cases amount
  <chr>                                            <int>  <dbl>
1 Same instalment paid more than once                 27  54000
2 Amount different from the entitlement               10  72000
3 Payment to deceased or ineligible beneficiaries     21  42000
4 Bank account shared by more than one beneficiary     0     NA


For duplicates, the cases and the amount count only the extra payments, not the first, legitimate one. The shared accounts are counted as accounts, and are not valued, since the money may have reached the right people.

title: 56  Reproducible Audit Reports
text:
56.3 Step 2. Formatted tables with gt

A tibble printed in the console is fine for the analyst, but a report needs a proper table. The package gt builds one step by step, much as ggplot2 builds a chart: a title, formatted numbers, a note for missing values.

summarise_checks(chandpur) |>
  gt() |>
  cols_label(check = "Check", cases = "Cases", amount = "Amount (₹)") |>
  fmt_number(columns = amount, decimals = 0) |>
  sub_missing(columns = amount, missing_text = "Not valued") |>
  tab_header(title = "Summary of exceptions", subtitle = "Chandpur district, 2024-25") |>
  tab_source_note("Source: payment register and beneficiary list of the scheme.")

title: 56  Reproducible Audit Reports
text:
56.4 Step 3. A parameterised Quarto report
A Quarto document is a plain text file with the extension .qmd. It has three kinds of content.

A header, between two lines of ---, written in a format called YAML. It gives the title, the output formats, and other options.

Text, written in Markdown: ## for headings, *italics*, **bold**, lists with -, and so on.

Code chunks, between ```{r} and ```, whose results (tables, charts, numbers) appear in the report. Numbers can also be placed inside sentences with inline code, written as a backtick, the letter r, the code, and a closing backtick.

The key to producing many reports from one file is a parameter. In the header, under params:, we declare a value with a default, here the district. Inside the document, the value is available as params$district. Change the parameter, and the same document becomes the report for another district.
Here is the complete template, audit_report.qmd.
---
title: "Kisan Sahayata payments: audit findings"
subtitle: "District report"
date: today
format:
  html:
    embed-resources: true
  docx: default
params:
  district: "Amarpur"
  payments_file: "payments.csv"
  beneficiaries_file: "beneficiaries.csv"
execute:
  echo: false
  warning: false
  message: false
---

```{r}
#| label: setup
library(tidyverse)
library(gt)
source("checks.R")

pay_all <- read_csv(params$payments_file, show_col_types = FALSE)
ben_all <- read_csv(params$beneficiaries_file, show_col_types = FALSE,
                    col_types = cols(account = col_character()))
pay <- pay_all |> filter(district == params$district)
ben <- ben_all |> filter(district == params$district)
results <- run_checks(pay, ben)
summary_tbl <- summarise_checks(results)

lakh <- function(x) paste0("₹", format(round(x / 1e5, 2), nsmall = 2), " lakh")
```

## District: `r params$district`

During 2024-25, `r format(nrow(pay), big.mark = ",")` payments totalling
`r lakh(sum(pay$amount))` were made to `r n_distinct(pay$ben_id)` beneficiaries
in `r params$district` district. The results of the checks are summarised below.

```{r}
summary_tbl |>
  gt() |>
  cols_label(check = "Check", cases = "Cases", amount = "Amount (₹)") |>
  fmt_number(columns = amount, decimals = 0) |>
  sub_missing(columns = amount, missing_text = "Not valued")
```

In all, `r lakh(sum(summary_tbl$amount, na.rm = TRUE))` was paid irregularly
in the cases that could be valued.

## Payments by month

```{r}
#| fig-height: 3
pay |>
  count(month = floor_date(paid_on, "month"), wt = amount, name = "amount") |>
  ggplot(aes(month, amount / 1e5)) +
  geom_col(fill = "steelblue") +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "₹ lakh") +
  theme_minimal()
```

## About this report

```{r}
data_hash <- unname(tools::md5sum(c(params$payments_file, params$beneficiaries_file)))
```

Generated on `r format(Sys.time(), "%d %B %Y, %H:%M")` from `r params$payments_file`
(MD5 `r data_hash[1]`) and `r params$beneficiaries_file` (MD5 `r data_hash[2]`),
with `r R.version.string`.
A few points about the template.


execute: echo: false hides the code, so that the report shows only results. A report for the Collector should not contain R code.

embed-resources: true packs the charts and styles into the single HTML file, so that it can be sent by email.
Every number in the text is inline code. None is typed in, so none can go out of date.
The last section records when the report was made, from which data files, identified by their hashes (Section 8.6), and with which version of R. Anyone can later confirm that the report came from those files. This is the working-paper trail.

summarise_checks() is also kept in checks.R, along with the four checks.

To produce the report for one district from RStudio, open the file and click Render. The default district, Amarpur, is used.

title: 56  Reproducible Audit Reports
section: 56.5 Step 4. One report for every district
text:
56.5 Step 4. One report for every district
To render the template for every district, we call quarto_render() from the package quarto in a loop, giving a different parameter each time with execute_params. Since the subtitle is part of the header, not the code, we pass it as metadata with quarto_args. Each report gets its own file name.

library(quarto)

districts <- c("Amarpur", "Belapur", "Chandpur", "Devgarh", "Fatehpur")

walk(districts, \(d) {
  for (fmt in c("html", "docx")) {
    quarto_render(
      input          = "audit_report.qmd",
      output_format  = fmt,
      output_file    = paste0("audit_report_", d, ".", fmt),
      execute_params = list(district = d),
      quarto_args    = c("--metadata", paste0("subtitle:District report, ", d)),
      quiet          = TRUE
    )
  }
})

This produces ten files, an HTML and a Word report for each district, in under a minute, each with its own figures, table and chart. (We have not run the loop while building this book, since it renders separate documents, but it was tested on the files created above.) When the data is corrected, or a new month’s data arrives, running the loop again regenerates every report.






TipAudit tip



Word (docx) output is usually the most convenient for audit, since draft paras and reports go through several rounds of editing by people who do not use R. Generate the Word report from Quarto, so that the numbers are right, and let the editing happen in Word. Quarto can also use your office’s Word template for styles and letterhead, through the reference-doc option of the docx format.

title: 56  Reproducible Audit Reports
text:
56.6 Step 5. Excel working papers
The field party needs the exceptions themselves, one row per case, to verify against the records. An Excel workbook is the most convenient form. With openxlsx we can build it exactly as we want: a summary sheet, a sheet for each check, a bold header, number formats, filters and frozen header rows.
We write a function that builds the workbook for one district.

write_working_paper <- function(district, pay_all, ben_all, folder) {
  pay <- filter(pay_all, district == !!district)
  ben <- filter(ben_all, district == !!district)
  results <- run_checks(pay, ben)

  wb <- createWorkbook()
  header_style <- createStyle(textDecoration = "bold", fgFill = "#DDEBF7", border = "bottom")
  money_style  <- createStyle(numFmt = "#,##0")

  # Summary sheet
  addWorksheet(wb, "Summary")
  writeData(wb, "Summary", paste("Kisan Sahayata audit, 2024-25:", district, "district"),
            startRow = 1)
  addStyle(wb, "Summary", createStyle(textDecoration = "bold", fontSize = 13), rows = 1, cols = 1)
  writeData(wb, "Summary", summarise_checks(results), startRow = 3, headerStyle = header_style)
  addStyle(wb, "Summary", money_style, rows = 4:7, cols = 3)
  setColWidths(wb, "Summary", cols = 1:3, widths = c(50, 10, 14))

  # One sheet per check
  for (check in names(results)) {
    addWorksheet(wb, check)
    writeData(wb, check, results[[check]], headerStyle = header_style, withFilter = TRUE)
    freezePane(wb, check, firstRow = TRUE)
    setColWidths(wb, check, cols = seq_along(results[[check]]), widths = "auto")
  }
  file <- file.path(folder, paste0("working_paper_", district, ".xlsx"))
  saveWorkbook(wb, file, overwrite = TRUE)
  file
}

A few details. withFilter = TRUE adds the filter buttons to the header row, freezePane() keeps the header visible while scrolling, and setColWidths(widths = "auto") fits the columns to their contents. The !!district inside filter() uses the value of the function’s argument, not a column of the same name, as in Section 17.4.
Now one workbook for each district.

wp_folder <- file.path(project_dir, "working_papers")
dir.create(wp_folder, showWarnings = FALSE)

wp_files <- map_chr(districts, \(d) write_working_paper(d, payments_all, benef_all, wp_folder))

title: 56  Reproducible Audit Reports
text:
56.7 Organising an audit project
When reports are produced by code, the files of an audit fall naturally into a simple structure, as suggested in Chapter 8.
kisan_audit/
  data/                 the files received, never edited
  checks.R              the check functions, used by everything else
  audit_report.qmd      the report template
  run_all.R             the loop that renders every report and working paper
  reports/              the generated reports
  working_papers/       the generated workbooks
The rule is that nothing in reports/ or working_papers/ is ever edited by hand. If something is wrong, the fix goes into the data, the checks or the template, and run_all.R is run again. Then the reports, the working papers and the code always agree, and the whole audit can be reproduced from the data files by anyone, at any time.






Caution



Generated reports are only as right as the code behind them. Before sending reports to auditees, check one or two of them thoroughly by hand: recount a few cases from the raw data, and confirm the totals against the source. Once a template is verified, every report from it can be trusted to the same standard, which is far more than can be said for reports typed by hand.

title: 56  Reproducible Audit Reports
text:
56.8 A suggested workflow


Write each check as a function, in one file, and test it on one unit.

Make a summary function that turns the results into a report-ready table.

Write the report template in Quarto, with a parameter for the unit, inline code for every number, and a section recording the data files, their hashes, and the date.

Render it once for the default unit, and check it thoroughly.

Render for every unit in a loop with quarto_render() and execute_params.

Generate the Excel working papers with openxlsx, one workbook per unit.

Never edit outputs by hand. Fix the inputs and re-run.







ImportantRemember




A report generated by code has no copying errors, and updates itself when the data changes.
Parameters, declared under params: and used as params$name, turn one template into many reports.

quarto_render(execute_params = ...) renders a template for each value in a loop.

gt makes formatted tables for HTML and Word; openxlsx makes formatted Excel working papers.
Record the data files, their hashes and the date in every report, so that it can be reproduced and verified.

title: Appendix A — Audit Question Finder

Start here when you have an audit question and want to know where the book answers it. The questions are grouped by audit area. Each row names the technique and the section that shows it at work.
Type a word in the box to narrow the list, for example duplicate, vendor, pension or map.

title: Appendix B — Datasets Used in This Book
text:
B.1 Datasets that come with R
The book uses two kinds of data: datasets that come with R and its packages, which are convenient for showing how a function works, and data simulated for this book, which carry the audit examples.
The following datasets are available in every installation of R. Their descriptions below are taken from R’s own help pages.
The appendix on colours also uses mpg, a dataset of car models that comes with the package ggplot2, for a quick demonstration of palettes.

iris: This famous (Fisher’s or Anderson’s) iris data set gives the measurements in centimeters of the variables sepal length and width and petal length and width, respectively, for 50 flowers from each of 3

B.2 Data simulated for this book
Most audit examples use data simulated in R, because real audit data cannot be published. The data is made to look like what auditors receive, and irregularities are planted in it for the analysis to find. All names of persons, firms, offices and places are made up, and do not relate to any real entity.
In most chapters, the code that creates the data is shown, folded, at the start of the example, so that readers can see exactly what was planted, change it, and run it again. The table lists these datasets, chapter by chapter, in the order of the book. Chapters which use only a few values typed in by hand are left out.

The Sarvajan Swasthya Yojana data
Several chapters share one larger dataset, for an imaginary State health insurance scheme, Sarvajan Swasthya Yojana (SSY). They are the chapters on principal components (Chapter 43), clustering (Chapter 44), association rules (Chapter 45), text (Chapter 48, Chapter 49 and Chapter 50) and maps (Chapter 53). Its files are in the Data folder of the book’s repository. The code that creates them is in tools/make_health_scheme_data.R, tools/make_ssy_text_data.R and tools/make_ssy_geo_data.R.

Planted in it are six hospitals behaving like “camps” (high claims per bed, short stays, weekend admissions, repeated admissions, unbundled packages) and two hospitals upcoding to intensive care, which the chapters find in different ways. The text and map files carry the same story. Grievances and feedback complain about the camp hospitals, their patients come from far away, and some inspection photos were taken far from the hospital.

title: Appendix C — R Packages Used in This Book
text:
C.1 Packages by part
R comes with a large set of functions, called base R. Most of the work in this book also uses packages, collections of functions written by others and shared freely, mostly through CRAN, the Comprehensive R Archive Network. Section 5 explains how packages are installed and loaded. This appendix lists all the packages used in the book, with a single command to install them.
MASS, lattice and nnet, also used in the book, come with every installation of R and need no separate installation.

text:
C.2 Installing all the packages
The following command installs every CRAN package used in the book. It needs an internet connection, and may take a while the first time. If your office network blocks downloads, see the note on installing packages on an office network in Section 5.

install.packages(c(
  "tidyverse", "conflicted", "readxl", "writexl", "openxlsx", "janitor",
  "pdftools", "tidyxl", "unpivotr", "data.table", "duckdb", "dbplyr",
  "scales", "ggrepel", "patchwork", "psych", "skimr", "GGally", "PerformanceAnalytics", "broom",
  "rebus", "stringdist", "phonics", "PGRdup",
  "validate", "pointblank", "benford.analysis", "bupaR", "processmapR", "edeaR", "processcheckR",
  "performance", "car", "moderndive", "rpart", "rpart.plot", "ranger", "cluster", "factoextra",
  "arules", "forecast", "timetk", "zoo", "outliers", "FNN", "dbscan", "isotree", "changepoint", "deaR",
  "tidytext", "SnowballC", "wordcloud",
  "igraph", "igraphdata", "ggraph", "visNetwork",
  "sf", "leaflet", "tidygeocoder",
  "gt", "quarto", "RColorBrewer", "colorspace", "palmerpenguins", "remotes"
))

Two packages are not on CRAN, and are installed from GitHub with the package remotes.

# fullmetaphone, Double Metaphone with full-length codes, by Atharv Tyagi and the author
remotes::install_github("anilyayavar/dblmetaphone")
# Seasonal Hybrid ESD anomaly detection, by Twitter
remotes::install_github("twitter/AnomalyDetection")

The first of these, fullmetaphone, is a full implementation of the Double Metaphone algorithm keeping phonetic codes of up to 32 characters. It was developed by Atharv Tyagi and the author, and has been submitted to CRAN. It is used in Chapter 33, Chapter 32 and Chapter 34.






TipKeeping an analysis reproducible



Packages are updated from time to time, and occasionally a function changes its behaviour. For an audit that must be reproducible, record the versions used, as shown in Section 7 with sessionInfo(). For larger projects, the package renv keeps a separate, fixed set of package versions for each project, so that an analysis written today runs the same way next year.

title: Appendix D — Colours in R
text:
D.1 Choosing colours by name
An audit report is read by busy people. A Secretary, a member of the Public Accounts Committee or a journalist may look at a chart for a few seconds only. In that time the colours do much of the talking. Red is read as a warning, a loss or a shortfall, and green as safe or good. A chart that colours the districts with savings in red, and those with excess expenditure in green, sends the wrong message before anyone reads a number.
Well-chosen colours make the important points stand out, separate categories clearly, and show gradients that text alone cannot. Badly chosen colours mislead, or simply cannot be told apart by some readers. This appendix shows how colours are chosen in R, and which palettes suit audit charts.
The default colours of ggplot2 are chosen only to be distinct, not to carry meaning, so they often need changing. The example in Figure D.1 uses the built-in mpg dataset, which is handy for a quick demonstration. It shows the mean highway mileage of each class of cars. Colour marks the classes with mileage above the average.
The default colours are not effective here. ggplot2 has given red, a colour usually read as bad, to the classes with better than average mileage, simply because “Above” comes first in alphabetical order.
It is also important to use colours that readers with colour blindness can tell apart. About 8% of men and 0.5% of women have some form of colour blindness. The most common form is difficulty in telling red from green, the very pair most often used for “bad” and “good”. Palettes designed with this in mind, such as those of ColorBrewer described below, make a chart readable for everyone. In audit reports, which may also be printed in black and white, it helps to choose colours that differ in lightness as well as in hue.
Readers who wish to learn more about the use of colour in charts may refer to this blog post. Let us now see how to choose colours in R.
In base R plots, colours are given with the argument col, while in ggplot2 they are set with the fill or colour aesthetics. R has more than 600 named colours, listed by the function colors().
# See names of random 20 colors
set.seed(123)
sample(colors(), 20)

 [1] "lightgoldenrodyellow" "mediumorchid1"        "gray26"              
 [4] "palevioletred2"       "gray42"               "deeppink2"           
 [7] "grey38"               "gray76"               "gray91"              
[10] "azure1"               "indianred2"           "slategray3"          
[13] "slategray4"           "darkorange1"          "grey87"              
[16] "grey94"               "blue"                 "paleturquoise"       
[19] "lightsalmon2"         "gray58"
These names can be used directly in plots.
# In base R
barplot(c(5,4,3,2), col = c("lightgoldenrodyellow", "mediumorchid1", "indianred2", "paleturquoise"))
Or we can give colours by their hex codes, explained in the next section.
barplot(c(2, 3, 4, 5), col = c("#fedcba", "#abcdef", "#123456", "#654321"))
The following plot shows 100 of the named colours, chosen at random.

title: Appendix D — Colours in R
text:
D.2 Colours by hex values
A colour can also be given by its hex code. This is a # followed by six hexadecimal digits.

The first two give the amount of red.
The next two give the amount of green.
The last two give the amount of blue.

Together they form the RGB (red, green, blue) value of the colour. There are sixteen hexadecimal digits, 0 to 9 and a to f, so two of them can represent \(16{\times}16 = 256\) levels of each colour, from 00 (none) to ff (full). Thus these codes give the basic colours.


#000000 is black, with no colour at all.

#ff0000 is red.

#00ff00 is green.

#0000ff is blue.

#ffffff is white.

Hex codes are useful when a report must follow a fixed house style, since the exact shade can be repeated in every chart.
See the following example.

barplot(2:6, col = c("#000000", "#ff0000", "#ffff00", "#00ffff", "#ff00ff"), main = "Some primary colour mixing")

title: Appendix D — Colours in R
text:
D.4 ColorBrewer palettes
Cynthia Brewer, an American cartographer who worked on the use of colour in maps, developed sets of colours that work well together and that are, in many cases, safe for readers with colour blindness. They are known as the Brewer palettes, and the package RColorBrewer makes them available in R.
Let us load the package and display all its palettes.

#install.packages("RColorBrewer")
library(RColorBrewer)
display.brewer.all()









They fall into three categories.


Sequential, for ordered values from low to high, like expenditure by district.

Qualitative, for categories with no order, like departments or schemes.

Diverging, for values on both sides of a meaningful middle, like savings and excesses against a budget.

To display a single palette, use display.brewer.pal(n, name), with the number of colours n and the palette’s name.

# View a single RColorBrewer palette by specifying its name
display.brewer.pal(n = 7, name = 'BrBG')







In charts, the palettes are used in two ways.


scale_fill_brewer() or scale_color_brewer() in ggplot2.

brewer.pal() in base R plots.

display.brewer.all(colorblindFriendly = TRUE) shows only the palettes that are safe for colour-blind readers.

library(RColorBrewer)
ggplot(mpg, aes(year, fill = class)) +
  geom_bar() +
  scale_fill_brewer(palette = "Dark2")








# Bar-plot using RColorBrewer
barplot(c(2,4, 5, 7, 3), col = brewer.pal(n = 5, name = "Accent"))

title: Appendix D — Colours in R
text:
D.5 Package colorspace

The package colorspace provides a broad toolbox for choosing colours and palettes, based on the HCL (hue, chroma, luminance) colour model, which matches the way people perceive colour.
The colorspace package provides three types of palettes based on the HCL model.


Qualitative palettes, from qualitative_hcl(), are for categories with no order, like schemes or departments. Every colour gets the same visual weight.

Sequential palettes, from sequential_hcl(), are for ordered numbers, where colours go from low to high.

Diverging palettes, from diverging_hcl(), are for numbers around a neutral middle. The colours move away from a neutral shade towards two extremes, like savings on one side and excesses on the other.

The function hcl_palettes() gives a quick overview.

library("colorspace")
hcl_palettes(plot = TRUE)







The package also gives ggplot2 scales for these palettes. Their names follow the pattern scale_<aesthetic>_<datatype>_<colorscale>(). Here <aesthetic> is fill, color or colour. <datatype> is discrete or continuous, the type of the variable plotted. <colorscale> is the type of palette, one of qualitative, sequential, diverging or divergingx.
A diverging palette suits Figure D.1 well, since mileage lies above or below a meaningful middle, the average. Here is the chart again, with red for below the average and blue for above. The colour now carries the right meaning, and the strength of the colour shows how far each class is from the average.

mpg |>
  summarise(hwy = mean(hwy), .by = class) |>
  mutate(class = fct_reorder(class, hwy)) |>
  ggplot(aes(y = class, x = hwy, fill = hwy)) +
  geom_col() +
  scale_fill_continuous_diverging(palette = "Blue-Red", rev = TRUE, mid = mean(mpg$hwy)) +
  geom_vline(aes(xintercept = mean(mpg$hwy)), linetype = "dashed", linewidth = 1) +
  theme_bw() +
  ggtitle("Class wise Mean Highway mileage of cars")







We have used the "Blue-Red" palette, not "Red-Green". Red and green together are hard for many colour-blind readers to tell apart. Blue and red stay distinct for them, and red still marks the weaker classes. The palette runs from blue to red, so rev = TRUE reverses it to put red at the low end. The strength of the colour also changes, which helps when the report is printed in black and white.

title: Appendix D — Colours in R
text:
Colours for audit charts
A few rules of thumb serve well in audit reports.

Use colour to carry one message, such as exceptions in red and everything else in grey, rather than giving every category its own bright colour.
Keep the usual meanings. Use red for shortfalls, losses and exceptions, and green or blue for normal or good.
Choose palettes that are safe for colour blindness and readable when printed in black and white, such as the Brewer palettes or the HCL palettes of colorspace.
Use a sequential palette for ordered values, a diverging one around a meaningful middle, and a qualitative one only for unordered categories.
